周浩〔貫浙江紹興府山陰縣，民籍，國子生，治書經，字允集，行四十二，年三十五，六月十五日生〕。曾祖永才，祖廷澤〔封翰林院檢討〕，父礽〔南京刑部郎中〕，母祁氏〔封安人〕。慈侍下，兄淑〔監生〕、澍〔引禮舍人〕、灌〔監生〕，弟沛、洄、沆、浡。聘朱氏，娶沈氏。浙江鄉試第六十四名，會試第二百六十二名。

林庭壆〔貫福建福州府閩縣，儒籍，國子生，治書經，字利節，行七，年二十八，四月十五日生〕。曾祖本〔訓導〕，祖元發〔義官〕，父潮，母藍氏。具慶下，兄庭㭿〔工部左侍郎〕、庭舉、庭譽、庭機〔同科進士〕，弟庭秠、庭學、庭黌、庭春。娶李氏。福建鄉試第八十五名，會試第四十九名。

張旦〔貫直隸揚州府高郵州寶應縣，民籍，增廣生，治易經，字子明，行三，年二十八，九月初六日生〕。曾祖震，祖岩，父禮〔遇例冠帶〕，母陳氏。重慶下，兄蘭、蕙、芷、葵、旬、易、習，弟菑、藻、蕃、茂、音。娶許氏。應天府鄉試第五十二名，會試第一百九十二名。

鄭富〔貫福建興化府莆田縣，民籍，府學附學生，治書經，字中虛，行一，年三十三，十一月初十日生〕。曾祖尚竒，祖永明，父轅，母陳氏。具慶下，弟寓、宿。娶林氏。福建鄉試第二名，會試第四十三名。
translation_en:
Zhou Hao, registered in Shanyin County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Yunji. Ranked forty-second in the family, he was thirty-five years old and was born on the fifteenth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Yongcai; his grandfather, Tingze, was granted the title of Examining Editor in the Hanlin Academy; his father, Reng, was a Bureau Director in the Nanjing Ministry of Justice; and his mother, née Qi, was granted the title of Lady of Peace (anren). His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Shu 淑, a student of the Directorate of Education; Shu 澍, a Ceremonial Usher; and Guan, a student of the Directorate of Education. His younger brothers were Pei, Hui, Hang, and Bo. He was betrothed to a woman née Zhu and married a woman née Shen. He placed sixty-fourth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 262nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lin Tingxue, registered in Min County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian, belonged to a Confucian scholar household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Lijie. Ranked seventh in the family, he was twenty-eight years old and was born on the fifteenth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather, Ben, was an Assistant Instructor; his grandfather, Yuanfa, held the honorary designation of Official for Righteousness (yiguan); his father was Chao; and his mother was née Lan. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Ting'ang, Left Vice Minister of Works; Tingju; Tingyu; and Tingji, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the same examination year. His younger brothers were Tingpi, Tingxue 庭學, Tinghong, and Tingchun. He married a woman née Li. He placed eighty-fifth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and forty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Dan, registered in Baoying County, Gaoyou Subprefecture, Yangzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan territory, belonged to a civilian household and was an expanded-quota government student. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Ziming. Ranked third in the family, he was twenty-eight years old and was born on the sixth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Zhen; his grandfather was Yan; his father, Li, had been accorded the privilege of wearing official cap and girdle under the applicable regulations; and his mother was née Chen. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His elder brothers were Lan, Hui, Zhi, Kui, Xun, Yi, and Xi; his younger brothers were Zai, Zao, Fan, Mao, and Yin. He married a woman née Xu. He placed fifty-second in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 192nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zheng Fu, registered in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian, belonged to a civilian household and was an attached student of the prefectural school. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Zhongxu. Ranked first in the family, he was thirty-three years old and was born on the tenth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Shangqi; his grandfather was Yongming; his father was Yuan; and his mother was née Chen. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yu and Su. He married a woman née Lin. He placed second in the Fujian Provincial Examination and forty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Quan Yuanli, registered in Yin County, Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Ruli; he ranked second among his brothers and was aged thirty-eight, born on the thirtieth day of the intercalary tenth month. His great-grandfather was Lun; his grandfather was Wenyu, an honorary official recognized for longevity; his father was Zheng, an Instructor; and his mother was née Song. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His elder brother was Yuanfang, and his younger brothers were Yuanwen and Yuanliang. He married a woman née Xu and subsequently women née Guan and Ding. He placed eighty-eighth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 307th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Yuyin, registered in Ji County, Weihui Prefecture, Henan, belonged to a civilian household and was a native of Liangxiang County, Shuntian Prefecture. He was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Ruhe; he ranked fourth among his brothers and was aged forty-five, born on the eighteenth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Guangzu; his grandfather was Mo, a Department Magistrate; his father was Wei, an Assistant Surveillance Commissioner; and his mother was née Tan, invested with the title Lady of Repose. Both his parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Yuhong, Yuyi, and Yulong, and his younger brother was Yuyan. He married a woman née Yan. He placed forty-fifth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 297th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lan Jiqing, registered in Houguan County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian, belonged to a civilian household and was an attached student of the county school specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Yongji; he ranked fifth among his brothers and was aged twenty-two, born on the twelfth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Sen; his grandfather was Lian, an honorary official recognized for public beneficence; his father was Ruxue; and his mother was née Guo. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His elder brothers were Fangqing, Xiuqing, and Maoqing, and his younger brothers were Xianqing, Zeqing, Yongqing, and Diaoqing. He married a woman née Xue. He placed sixty-seventh in the Fujian Provincial Examination and ninety-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zheng Jiong, registered in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household and was a county-school student specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Zhangfu; he ranked first among his brothers and was aged twenty-nine, born on the sixteenth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Shan; his grandfather was Decui; his father was Zhongyi; and his mother was née Zou. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers were Shuo, Huan, and Ling. He married a woman née Xu. He placed eighty-third in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 314th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Xu Shoudao, registered in a civilian household in Changyuan County, Kai Subprefecture, Daming Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan territory, was originally from Jinxian County, Jiangxi. A county government school student specializing in the Book of Changes, he had the courtesy name Zizhong, was first in birth order, and was aged thirty-four, born on the sixteenth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Rucheng; his grandfather, Hua; his father, Jiang; his mother, née Wang; and his stepmother, née Sun. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Shouzhi and Shouyi, and his wife was née Gao. He placed fifty-third in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 102nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Gui was registered in a civilian household in Qianshan County, Anqing Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan territory. A county government school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he had the courtesy name Zifang, was third in birth order, and was aged twenty-four, born on the twenty-fifth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Fu; his grandfather, Wenchang; his father, Pei; and his mother, née Wang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Kuo and Bai; his younger brothers were Bang and Wu; and his wife was née Chen. He placed ninety-ninth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 269th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhao Jiben was from Licheng County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong. A government school student specializing in the Book of Changes, he had the courtesy name Xiaofu, was second in birth order, and was aged thirty-seven, born on the seventh day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xuan, a subprefect; his grandfather, Kai; his father, Qi, an honorary official; and his mother, née Zhang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Jizong and Jizhi, and his wife was née Zhang. He placed twenty-seventh in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 207th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Gao Jie was registered in a military household in Xinzheng County, Jun Subprefecture, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan. A county government school student specializing in the Book of Documents, he had the courtesy name Jianqing, was first in birth order, and was aged thirty-four, born on the sixth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wang, posthumously granted the title of bureau director in the Ministry of Works; his grandfather was Kui, a bureau director in the Ministry of Works, advanced to the rank of Grand Master for Exemplary Service; his father was Shangxian, vice minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments; and his mother was née Shen, invested with the title Lady of Suitability. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers were Duo, a ceremonial usher; Gong, a tribute scholar; Cai; and Jian. His wife was née Shao, and his subsequent wife was née Wang. He placed twelfth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 222nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zhu Shangzhi, registered in a military household of the Shenyang Central Station Guard in Hejian Prefecture, Zhili, was a native of Jurong County, Yingtian Prefecture. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he had the courtesy name Zongshang and was first in birth order, aged forty-one, born on the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Fu; his grandfather, Qin, was a county magistrate; his father, Wei, was a tribute student; and his mother was née Li. His father was deceased, and he attended his surviving mother. His wife was née Zhang. He ranked thirtieth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 126th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Peng Xiang was registered in a military household in Anping County, Jinzhou Subprefecture, Zhending Prefecture, Zhili. A county school instructor specializing in the Book of Documents, he had the courtesy name Liangzhong and was fourth in birth order, aged thirty-nine, born on the twenty-ninth day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhen, his grandfather Yi, his father Qian, and his mother née Lu. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Fu, Yue, and Ren, and his wife was née Wu. He ranked sixty-second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 275th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Tianran was registered in a civilian household in Luoyang County, Henan Prefecture, Henan. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he had the courtesy name Yizhong and was first in birth order, aged forty-one, born on the twenty-fifth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Gui, his grandfather Ying, his father Zhang, and his mother née Zhang. Both parents were deceased. His wife was née Pan. He ranked forty-eighth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 141st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Yingqi was registered in a military household in Xiayi County, Guide Subprefecture, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he had the courtesy name Shiwang and was first in birth order, aged forty-three, born on the seventh day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather, Wei, was a prefectural school professor honorifically appointed Assistant in the Court of Judicial Review; his grandfather, De, was a surveillance vice commissioner; and his father, Shen, was a county vice magistrate. His father's former wife was née Liu, and his mother was née Wang. His father was deceased, and he attended his surviving mother. His elder brothers were Yingfeng, an honorary official, and Yingpeng; his younger brothers were Yinghong, Yinglong, Yingji, Yinghe, and Yingtu. His wife was née Duan. He ranked thirty-third in the Henan Provincial Examination and 319th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wang Sanpin was registered in a civilian household in Zhouzhi County, Xi’an Prefecture, Shaanxi, and was a county school student. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Mengshen. Listed as first in birth order, he was aged thirty-five and was born on the fourteenth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Lian, his grandfather Zai, and his father Yu; his mother was née Xin. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Laifang, Sangu, and Sanchong, and his younger brother was Sanhuai. His wife was née Deng. He placed first in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and sixty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Wensheng was registered in a military household of Ningshan Guard in Zhili, was a native of Xun County, and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Ziwei. Second in birth order, he was aged thirty-six and was born on the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Guang, his grandfather Ming 〔an honorary official recognized for longevity〕, and his father Jie; his mother was née Chen and his stepmother née Zhang. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Wenjin, and his younger brothers were Wentong, Wenxian, and Wenkui. His wife was née Qin; he subsequently married a woman née Sun. He placed eighty-seventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and thirty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Niu Heng was registered in a civilian household in Wugong County, Qian Subprefecture, Xi’an Prefecture, Shaanxi, and was a supplementary student of the county school. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Zizhen. First in birth order, he was aged twenty-six and was born on the twenty-second day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Zong, his grandfather Jing 〔a prefectural Registrar〕, and his father Zhaoxiang 〔a prefectural Judge〕; his mother and stepmother were both née Wang. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Hui, Wei, Tian, Zao, Yi, and Shen. His wife was née Li. He placed forty-second in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 131st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Gongwen was registered in a civilian household in Taihe County, Dali Prefecture, Yunnan, and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals; his courtesy name was Xianren. Listed as first in birth order, he was aged thirty-six and was born on the sixth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Zhen 〔granted the honorary cap and girdle in absentia〕, his grandfather Xuan 〔an honorary official recognized for longevity〕, and his father Yunlong 〔a School Instructor〕; his mother was née Kang. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Gongyao 〔a Professor〕 and Gongtang, and his younger brothers were Gongwu, Gongzhou, Gongchao, Gongshi, Gongming, and Gongji. His wife was née Dong; he subsequently married a woman née Zhu. He placed twenty-sixth in the Yunnan–Guizhou Provincial Examination and 285th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Li Bi, registered in Qi County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Ze’an, and he ranked second among his brothers. He was forty-four years old, born on the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Xin, posthumously granted the title of Bureau Director in the Ministry of Works; his grandfather was Weicong, Vice Commissioner of a Provincial Surveillance Commission; his father was Zhuo, and his mother was née Ren. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Tang, and his younger brothers were Shu, Bao, and He. His wife was née Ning. He placed ninth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 226th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Guo Chaobin, registered in Wenshang County, Dongping Subprefecture, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a military household and was an affiliated student of the county school. He specialized in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Shangfu, and he ranked seventh among his brothers. He was twenty-three years old, born on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Yu, his grandfather was Shun, his father was Xu, and his mother was née Lu. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Chaoyong, Chaoqing, Chaofu, Chaopin, Chaochen, and Chaoxian; his younger brothers were Chaomian and Chaozong. His wife was née Liu. He placed fifty-fourth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 288th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Weng Shijing, registered in Fuqing County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian, belonged to a military salt-producing household and was an affiliated student. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Kezhen, and he ranked fifth among his brothers. He was twenty-seven years old, born on the twenty-sixth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Fu, his grandfather was Bao, his father was Guang, and his mother was née Lin. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Shihe, and his younger brothers were Shixian, Shiji, Shijin, Shishuo, Shihao, and Shifang. His wife was née Lin. He placed sixty-sixth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 161st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Tianlun, registered in an official household in Zhenwu Guard, Shanxi, was a native of Mianyang Subprefecture, Huguang, and an added student of the Daizhou school. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Ruming, and he ranked first among his brothers. He was thirty-four years old, born on the seventh day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather Neng, grandfather Xuan, and father Yin each held the office of Battalion Commander. His mother, née Zhou, was posthumously granted the title of Lady of Suitability. His father was living and his mother deceased. His younger brother was Tianyi, and his wife was née Zeng. He placed first in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 175th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Che Bangyou, courtesy name Yiqing, was registered in a military household in Boluo County, Huizhou Prefecture, Guangdong. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked third among his brothers and was aged twenty-nine, born on the tenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yi, his grandfather Guangyun, and his father Ting; his mother was née Huang, and his stepmothers were née Han and née Zhou. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Bangxian, a Steward of Food, and Bangxian (邦獻); his younger brothers were Bangji (邦計), Bangji (邦佶), Bangding, and Bangping. His wife was née Li. He placed forty-fourth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and sixty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lu Pian, courtesy name Mubo, was registered in a medical household in Changshu County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and was a native of Kunshan County. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked first among his brothers and was aged thirty-two, born on the twenty-sixth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Fu; his grandfather Chang was posthumously appointed Assistant Director of the Imperial Medical Office; and his father Zhi was a former Assistant Director of that office. His mother, née Chen, held the title Lady of Tranquility (anren); his birth mother was née Xue. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Nan, and his wife was née Xu. He placed fifty-sixth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and fifty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Hui, courtesy name Shaozhi, was registered in a military household in Guang Subprefecture, Runing Prefecture, Henan. A subprefectural government school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked second among his brothers and was aged thirty-one, born on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather Zhong was posthumously appointed Assistant Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud; his grandfather Jin was Vice Minister of that court; and his father was Tingpei. His father's former wife was née Chen, and his mother was née Zhong. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His elder brother was Jing, and his wife was née Hu. He placed first in the Henan Provincial Examination and seventy-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Zhen, courtesy name Pinzhi, was registered in a military household in Danyang County, Zhenjiang Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. A county government school student specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked sixth among his brothers and was aged thirty-two, born on the twenty-sixth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Binnan, his grandfather Yue, and his father Yi; his mother was née Wang, and his stepmother was née Jiang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Qiong, Jing, and Rui; his younger brothers were Li, Ying, and Wei. His wife was née Lu. He placed sixty-sixth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and seventy-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wang Yiyan, courtesy name Xingshu, was registered in a civilian household in Fuqing County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian. He was an additional student of the county school and specialized in the Book of Rites. Second in birth order, he was aged thirty-three and born on the twenty-seventh day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zuo (Vice Prefect), his grandfather Shiyong, and his father Yu; his mother was née Shi. His mother alone was still living. His younger brothers were Yigun, Yiqi, Yibi, Yichen, Yiqing, Yilin, and Yiqi. His wife was née Shi. He placed fourth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 191st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Cui Guan, courtesy name Maode, was registered in a military household of the Guard Battalion in Baoning Prefecture, Sichuan, and was a native of Langzhong County. He was an additional student of the prefectural school and specialized in the Book of Odes. Second in birth order, he was aged twenty-four and born on the sixteenth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Gao, his grandfather Yan, and his father Tian’en; his mother was née Xu. Both parents were still living. His elder brother was Jue, and his younger brothers were Han, Cai, Yin, and Xian. His first wife was née Zhang, and his subsequent wife was also née Zhang. He placed twenty-fourth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and twenty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Zhaolong, courtesy name Ruizheng, was registered in a civilian household in Nanhai County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong. He was a student of the county school and specialized in the Book of Odes. Third in birth order, he was aged twenty-four and born on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yanxiang, his grandfather Xuan, and his father Qiao; his mother was née Luo, and his stepmother née Cai. Both parents were still living. His elder brothers were Yuelong and Conglong, and his younger brother was Weilong. His wife was née Jian. He placed twelfth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 258th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shu Pengyi, courtesy name Yunan, was registered in a military household of the Baoning Guard Battalion, Sichuan, and was a native of Langzhong County. He was a student of the Directorate of Education and specialized in the Book of Odes. Fifth in birth order, he was aged thirty and born on the fifth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Rong, his grandfather Ang, and his father Quan; his mother was née Shen. Both parents were still living. His elder brothers were Eyi, Luanyi, Yueyi, and Fengyi, and his younger brothers were Yuanyi, Heyi, Guyi, and Hongyi. His wife was née Dong. He placed sixtieth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and fifty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Hu Bin, courtesy name Ruguan, was registered in a civilian household in Guangzhou, Runing Prefecture, Henan. A student of the subprefectural school specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he ranked first among his brothers and was aged twenty-nine, born on the twelfth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Man; his grandfather was Qiu, a District Magistrate; his father was Yongzhong; and his mother was née Liu. His parents and grandparents were living. His younger brothers were Xian, Shi, Zhi, Gong, and Zi, and his wife was née Zhang. He placed eleventh in the Henan Provincial Examination and fifty-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ma Sen, courtesy name Kongyang, was registered in a military household in Huai'an County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Documents, he ranked fifth among his brothers and was aged thirty, born on the twenty-seventh day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jun 鈞; his grandfather was Jun 俊, a tribute scholar; his father was Cong; his legal mother was née Li; and his birth mother was née He. His father was deceased, and he attended upon his living mother. His younger brother was Zhi 栺, and his wife was née Ren. He placed fifteenth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 160th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhou Dai, courtesy name Ruzhen, was registered in a civilian household in Macheng County, Huangzhou Prefecture, Huguang. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Changes, he ranked second among his brothers and was aged thirty-eight, born on the twenty-second day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jian, a Surveillance Vice Commissioner; his grandfather was Si; his father was Tingyi; his mother was née Zhu; and his birth mother was née Peng. His father was deceased, and he attended upon his living mother. His elder brother was Chuan, a District Magistrate, and his younger brother was Ting; his wife was née Zhao. He placed seventy-seventh in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 297th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Guo Wancheng, courtesy name Zichang, was registered in a civilian household in Fuqing County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian. An annual tribute student specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he ranked fifth among his brothers and was aged twenty-nine, born on the twentieth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jian; his grandfather was Ding; his father was Shizhi; and his mother was née He. His father was deceased, and he attended upon his living mother. His younger brother was Wanhua, and his wife was née Lu. He placed thirty-seventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and forty-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Qian Xuan, registered in Haiyan County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, under military-and-civilian household registration, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Maoxiao; he ranked third in his family and was thirty-three years old, born on the eighteenth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Shi; his grandfather, Da, was posthumously granted the title of Bureau Director in the Nanjing Ministry of Justice; his father, Qi, was a Prefect; and his mother, née Wang, received the additional title of Lady of Suitability. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Yong, Yue, Zhu, Lan, Meng (a student of the Directorate of Education), Hui, Qin (a tribute scholar), and Wei (a Messenger); his younger brothers were Kui and Fei. He married a woman née Sun. He placed sixth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and seventy-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lu Xiaoda, registered in Dongyang County, Jinhua Prefecture, Zhejiang, under civilian household registration, was an annual tribute student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Weizhou; he ranked forty-fifth in his family and was thirty-two years old, born on the tenth day of the intercalary fourth month. His great-grandfather was Cong, his grandfather Liang, his father Chao, and his mother née Lü. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Xiaotong, and his younger brothers were Xiaoyi and Xiaoxun. He married a woman née Gong. He placed ninetieth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and ninety-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Yunqu, registered in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian, under civilian household registration, was a county government school student specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Bangying; he ranked first in his family and was thirty-four years old, born on the thirteenth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Mengyan; his grandfather, Heng, was an Assistant Instructor; his father was Wenchao, and his mother née Lin. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Shuwei, and his younger brothers were Yuncheng and Yunjie. He married a woman née Wu. He placed fifty-eighth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and three hundred seventeenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Cao Heng, registered in Xincai County, Runing Prefecture, Henan, under civilian household registration, was a county government school student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Bozhen; he ranked fourth in his family and was twenty-nine years old, born on the twelfth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather, Duan, was granted the title of Investigating Censor and advanced to the privilege of wearing second-rank robes; his grandfather, Feng, was Right Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate; his father was Daxia, and his mother née Zhang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Li, Kuo, and Xin; his younger brothers were Ting, Wei, Gao, Yong, Bian, Yi, Wen, Lian, and Geng. He married a woman née Wang. He placed twenty-second in the Henan Provincial Examination and one hundred thirteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Liu Yong 劉永, courtesy name Jifu, was from Liquan County, Xi’an Prefecture, Shaanxi, and belonged to a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he ranked first among his brothers and was aged thirty-eight, born on the twenty-fourth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jin, a County Magistrate; his grandfather was Tingxi; his father was Da, a Police Chief; and his mother was née Wang. His father was deceased, and he attended upon his surviving mother. His younger brothers were Dong, Fang, and Ye. He married a woman née Han and subsequently a woman née Luo. He placed thirty-seventh in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 240th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Sun Guo 孫國, courtesy name Daofu, was from Kai Subprefecture, Daming Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and belonged to a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Documents, he ranked fifth among his brothers and was aged thirty-three, born on the fifth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ying; his grandfather was Sheng, an Assistant Instructor who was additionally granted the posthumous title of Prefect; his father was Yu; and his mother was née Chang. His father was deceased, and he attended upon his surviving mother. His elder brothers were Yin, Kun, Jiong, and Bai; his younger brothers were Xiang, Ke, Zhao, Shi, and Zhan. He married a woman née Chang. He placed ninety-seventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 120th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xian Guiqi 洗桂竒, courtesy name Yiqian, was from Nanhai County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, and belonged to a civilian household. An added student of the county Confucian school specializing in the Classic of Changes, he ranked fifth among his brothers and was aged twenty-seven, born on the tenth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xian; his grandfather was Yu; his father was Guan; and his mother was née Chen. His father was deceased, and he attended upon his surviving mother. His elder brothers were Guiyu, Guirong, Guikui, and Guichang; his younger brothers were Guicong, Gui’e, and Guibiao. He married a woman née He. He placed twenty-eighth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 157th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Huang Ao 黃鰲, courtesy name Shizhen, was from Jinjiang County, Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian, and belonged to a military household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Changes, he ranked fourth among his brothers and was aged forty-nine, born on the fourteenth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ronggui; his grandfather was Duan and his father was Xun, both holders of honorary official titles conferred for longevity. His father’s former wife was née Chen, and his mother was née Cai. Both his parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Li, Peng, and Kun; his younger brother was Jing. He married a woman née Wu. He placed thirtieth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and twenty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

臣對：臣聞人君所以致天下之治者，法天而已矣；所以保天下之治者，法祖而已矣。善法天者，善致治者也；善法祖者，善保治者也。不法乎天，則致治者無其具；不法乎祖，則保治者無其具。如是而欲望天下之治，善其始以成開創之功，善其終以隆繼承之譽，祗見其難矣。且古今言致天下之治與其所以保天下之治者，莫善於三代。三代之治，夫豈無因而致哉？蓋其始也，思垂統之難而法天以立其極；終也，思創業之難而法祖以守其成。法天以立其極，是故其始之也，致天下之治而不見其化之塞；法祖以守其成，是故其終之也，保天下之治而不見其法之弊。自是而下，駁乎無以議為矣。欽惟皇帝陛下策士於廷，而以三代以後歷世久近之故為問，且及於創業守成之道，誠圖治之盛心也。臣也竊伏草茅，思見德化之成久矣，敢無言以對？臣伏讀聖制，有曰：「朕思昔自三代以來，迄于宋終，中間雖歷世有久近

Imperial comment: This accords with the original intent of the question. He may be ranked first in the first class.
Your servant, Han Yinglong.
Your servant replies: I have heard that the means by which a ruler brings order to All-under-Heaven is simply to model himself on Heaven; the means by which he preserves that order is simply to model himself on his ancestors. One who is good at following Heaven is good at bringing about order; one who is good at following his ancestors is good at preserving order. Without following Heaven, one lacks the means to establish order; without following one’s ancestors, one lacks the means to preserve it. Under such circumstances, to hope for order in All-under-Heaven—to begin well and accomplish the work of founding a dynasty, and to end well and enhance the reputation of its successors—would surely be difficult. Moreover, among those past and present who have brought order to All-under-Heaven and preserved it, none surpassed the Three Dynasties. Could their order possibly have arisen without a cause? At the beginning, they reflected on the difficulty of transmitting the dynastic succession and followed Heaven to establish their supreme standard; later, they reflected on the difficulty of founding the dynasty and followed their ancestors to preserve what had been achieved. By following Heaven to establish their supreme standard, they initially brought order to All-under-Heaven without their transforming influence becoming obstructed. By following their ancestors to preserve what had been achieved, they subsequently maintained order in All-under-Heaven without their institutions becoming corrupt. Thereafter, governance became so mixed and impure that it scarcely merits discussion.
I reverently observe that Your Imperial Majesty is examining scholars through policy questions at court, asking why the dynasties after the Three Dynasties endured for longer or shorter periods, and also addressing the ways of founding a dynasty and preserving its achievements. This truly expresses your profound desire to bring about good government. Your servant, living humbly in obscurity, has long wished to witness the full realization of your transforming moral influence. How could I dare offer no words in reply? 皇言其誠有見於治天下保天下之極者矣臣則以為三代之
所以久長與其治之所以隆盛者善法天而已矣善法祖
而已矣後世之所以祚短與其治之所以不振者不善法
天而已矣不善法祖而已矣法天法祖雖
皇言之所未及而實
聖心之所獨見者也臣請舉其大畧而言之夏之有天下也而
貽子孫者以典則商之有天下也而肇脩者人紀周之有
天下也而不顯之謨丕承之烈咸正無缺夫其典則也人
紀也謨烈也何者而非致治之法則亦何者而非法天之

Your servant believes that the Three Dynasties endured so long and their government flourished so greatly simply because they rightly modeled themselves on Heaven and on their ancestors. These statutes and standards, these principles of human relationships, these plans and achievements—were any of them not rules for bringing about good government? 正而繼立之不明崇事姑息而武功之不競其如天之道
何創業如是則其守成之所以不善其終如紹聖如靖康
者無惑也夫開創於前者不知所以法其天則守成於後
者亦將何以法其祖是以歷世雖久而治不古若也
聖問及此得非有慨於漢唐宋之治之弊而欲復三代之舊矣
乎然三代之治純矣而
聖意尤重有感於成周之盛顧以傳之所稱歷世最多傳祚恒
久而推本於文武之所積累者為言上以例夏商之治之
所以久而下以例漢唐宋之治之所以弊臣又於是而仰

聖心之所蘊尤有慕於成周之治矣夫周之有天下也自后稷
===
以來其君子則焦勞於外以躬稼穡之業其后妃則焦勞
於內以躬織紝之勤為絺為綌服之無斁葛覃之所以詠
也三之日于耜四之日舉趾豳風之所以歌也周之有天
下其恤民之心勤民之事類如此則德澤之洽於民者誠
深而嗣王持盈慎滿之道亦不容外厥祖以為法者也夫
其始之創業也以天為心而以民為心故其終之守成也
以祖為心而以天為心
聖問若此其亦心是心矣乎臣以為徒善不足以為政徒法不

正，而繼立之不明，崇事姑息而武功之不競，其如天之道何？創業如是，則其守成之所以不善其終，如紹聖、如靖康者，無惑也。夫開創於前者不知所以法其天，則守成於後者亦將何以法其祖？是以歷世雖久，而治不古若也。
聖問及此，得非有慨於漢、唐、宋之治之弊，而欲復三代之舊矣乎？然三代之治純矣，而聖意尤重有感於成周之盛，顧以傳之所稱「歷世最多，傳祚恒久」，而推本於文、武之所積累者為言，上以例夏、商之治之所以久，而下以例漢、唐、宋之治之所以弊。臣又於是而仰探聖心之所蘊，尤有慕於成周之治矣。
夫周之有天下也，自后稷以來，其君子則焦勞於外，以躬稼穡之業；其后妃則焦勞於內，以躬織紝之勤。「為絺為綌，服之無斁」，葛覃之所以詠也；「三之日于耜，四之日舉趾」，豳風之所以歌也。周之有天下，其恤民之心、勤民之事類如此，則德澤之洽於民者誠深，而嗣王持盈慎滿之道，亦不容外厥祖以為法者也。夫其始之創業也，以天為心而以民為心；故其終之守成也，以祖為心而以天為心。
聖問若此，其亦心是心矣乎？臣以為，徒善不足以為政，徒法不能以自行。陛下心其心矣，而欲有以法其法，不必遠有所慕，法乎祖而已矣。蓋我

With such a founding, it is no wonder that its subsequent preservation of the inheritance failed to reach a good conclusion, as in the Shaosheng and Jingkang eras. If those who first establish a dynasty do not know how to model themselves on Heaven, how can those who later preserve its inheritance model themselves on their ancestors? Thus, although these dynasties lasted many generations, their government did not equal that of antiquity.
Your Majesty’s sacred question touches upon this. Is it not because you deplore the defects in the government of Han, Tang, and Song and wish to restore the ancient ways of the Three Dynasties? Yet, while the government of all Three Dynasties was pure, Your Majesty is particularly moved by the flourishing age of Zhou. You cite the statement in the commentary that it “lasted the most generations and transmitted the imperial succession for an enduring span,” tracing this back to what Kings Wen and Wu had accumulated. You use this to illustrate, looking backward, why the government of Xia and Shang endured, and, looking forward, why that of Han, Tang, and Song became defective. From this, your servant ventures reverently to discern what lies within your sacred heart: an especial admiration for the government of Zhou.
As for Zhou’s possession of All under Heaven, from Hou Ji onward its noble men labored anxiously outside, personally undertaking the work of sowing and reaping, while its royal consorts labored anxiously within, personally undertaking the toil of weaving. “Making fine cloth and coarse cloth, wearing them without growing weary”: this is what ‘The Spreading Kudzu’ (Ge tan) celebrates. “In the days of the third month, they ready the plows; in the days of the fourth, they set their feet to work”: this is what the ‘Airs of Bin’ (Bin feng) sings. Such were Zhou’s concern for the people and its diligent efforts on their behalf when it possessed All under Heaven. Its beneficence truly reached deeply among the people. The way by which succeeding kings maintained prosperity and remained cautious at its height likewise could not dispense with taking their ancestors as models. At the beginning, when establishing the dynasty, they took Heaven’s heart and the people’s heart as their own. Thus, afterward, when preserving the inheritance, they took their ancestors’ heart and Heaven’s heart as their own.

太祖高皇帝之興也，代天復世，重造中華，舉天下被髮腥羶之民而歸之衣冠禮樂之域，是誠振古所無之功德也。太宗繼述于草創之初，列聖遵承于大定之後，重熙累洽百有六十餘載，振古所無之治化也。今我皇上以精明純粹之資、剛健中正之德，因天下之心，以理天下之政，治化之盛，比隆唐虞三代而上之矣，而猶不以至治之盛自滿。
臣伏讀聖制曰：「朕以宗支，方在冲昧之年，入承祖位，幼弱不才，多招災害於民。」夫災害之相乘，堯湯所不免，臣不敢謂無是也。然以災害之招而謂不才所致，自咎者謙謙之志耳。董仲舒曰：「天心仁愛人君，則出災異以警動之。」惟陛下益修厥德，以格天，以安民，可也。若曰災害之招，適然之數，則公孫弘之諛，非臣之所以事陛下也。
聖制又曰：「兹來思祖宗創造萬艱，惕然悚懼，欲長保洪業於無窮，且欲使民咸有以遂其生，物咸有以適其所，而求良法美意，可以行之當時、垂之後世者。」顧臣何人而當

聖明亦順承已耳復何言哉而臣猶惓惓以
法
祖為獻者盖我
皇祖之所以致天下之治者法天而已矣何者心者天之所以
與我者也我
皇祖觀心有亭以事心也民者天之所以視聽者也我
皇祖恤民有章以勤民也諸如此類無非緣法以致治則亦無
非因天以立法是皆
創業以傳諸後者也今我
===
皇上敬一有箴四箴有註即
皇祖之所以事心也
親耕有郊親蠶有室即
皇祖之所以勤民也推而至於一念慮之微一政事之著無往
而非
皇祖之所行者為道法
祖之善卓哉無容議矣區區草茅之見其將何以仰裨
聖德於萬一乎臣竊聞之民之所以遂其生者在厚其生而已
也物之所以適其所者在順其性而已也寒而不虞其衣饑
而不虞其食厚生之道也
今之民果皆厚其生矣乎順其所欲違其所惡因其材質之

皇祖恤民有章以勤民也諸如此類無非緣法以致治則亦無
非因天以立法是皆
創業以傳諸後者也今我
===
皇上敬一有箴四箴有註卽
皇祖之所以事心也
親耕有郊親蠶有室卽
皇祖之所以勤民也推而至於一念慮之微一政事之著無往
而非
皇祖之所行者爲道法
祖之善卓哉無容議矣區區草茅之見其將何以仰裨
聖德於萬一乎臣竊聞之民之所以遂其生者在厚其生而已
也物之所以適其所者在順其性而已也寒而不虞其衣饑
而不虞其食厚生之道也
今之民果皆厚其生矣乎順其所欲違其所惡因其材質之
punctuated:
大問。然臣竊聞之：臣賢於君，則輔君以所不能；臣不賢於君，則將順以承休德。臣也遭遇聖明，亦順承已耳，復何言哉？而臣猶惓惓以法祖為獻者，盖我皇祖之所以致天下之治者，法天而已矣。何者？心者，天之所以與我者也。我皇祖觀心有亭，以事心也。民者，天之所以視聽者也。我皇祖恤民有章，以勤民也。諸如此類，無非緣法以致治，則亦無非因天以立法。是皆創業以傳諸後者也。

今我皇上敬一有箴，四箴有註，即皇祖之所以事心也；親耕有郊，親蠶有室，即皇祖之所以勤民也。推而至於一念慮之微、一政事之著，無往而非皇祖之所行者，為道法祖之善，卓哉，無容議矣。區區草茅之見，其將何以仰裨聖德於萬一乎？臣竊聞之：民之所以遂其生者，在厚其生而已也；物之所以適其所者，在順其性而已也。寒而不虞其衣，饑而不虞其食，厚生之道也。今之民果皆厚其生矣乎？順其所欲，違其所惡，因其材質之
translation_en:
…Your Majesty’s great question. Yet your servant has humbly heard this: if a minister is worthier than his ruler, he assists the ruler in what the ruler cannot accomplish; if a minister is less worthy than his ruler, he supports and follows him, upholding his admirable virtue. Having encountered Your Majesty’s sagely enlightenment, your servant can only follow and uphold it. What more is there to say? Nevertheless, I earnestly persist in offering the counsel to emulate your ancestor, because the means by which our august ancestor brought order to all under Heaven was simply to emulate Heaven. Why is this? The mind is what Heaven has bestowed upon us. Our august ancestor had a pavilion for contemplating the mind, thereby attending to its cultivation. The people are those through whom Heaven sees and hears. Our august ancestor had writings on solicitude for the people, thereby devoting himself to their welfare. All such measures achieved good government through established standards, and all likewise established those standards in accordance with Heaven. These were all foundations laid to be handed down to later generations.

Now Your Majesty has composed an Admonition on Reverent Unity and commentaries on the Four Admonitions: these embody our august ancestor’s means of cultivating the mind. You have a site in the suburbs for personally ploughing and a chamber for personally tending silkworms: these embody our august ancestor’s devotion to the people’s welfare. Extending this to the smallest stirrings of thought and the manifest actions of government, nothing departs from what our august ancestor practised. Such excellence in following the Way and emulating your ancestor [?] is outstanding indeed and leaves no room for criticism. How could the insignificant views of a man from the countryside such as myself contribute even the slightest measure to Your Majesty’s sagely virtue? Your servant has humbly heard that enabling the people to fulfil their lives depends simply on enriching their livelihoods, and enabling all things to find their proper places depends simply on accommodating their natures. To have no anxiety about clothing when cold or food when hungry is the way to enrich livelihoods. Have the livelihoods of all the people today indeed been enriched? To accord with what things desire, avoid what they dislike, and act in accordance with their inherent qualities …

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
宜以置其用制其取用之節以遂其生順性之道也
今之物果皆順其性矣乎昔帝舜命棄以播時百穀正慮夫
民之不遂其生也命益以若上下草木鳥獸正慮夫物之
不適其所也
今之在位者多矣果皆如棄如益之臣矣乎若猶未也惟在
皇上節費以裕天下之財慎動以端天下之極明法以立天下
之紀懋德以召天下之和虛心以用天下之賢闢聰以納
天下之言明目以袪天下之蔽則萬民自遂其生萬物自
適其所而天下之化成億萬載無疆之業端在是矣然其
要則又在於無斁蓋天之行也健而不息故能成其大日
月之行也運而有常故能溥其照惟
===
皇上奮天道健行之勇
普日月久照之明勇以致其決明以察其幾不以始勤不以
終怠不以暫勉不以久忘則
皇猷允塞而法
祖法
天之心創業守成之道兼舉而無遺矣此非臣之過為是言以
欺
陛下也居安者易危處平者易傾人之情也故臣敢為是言也
臣冒瀆
天聽不勝戰慄隕越之至臣謹對

punctuated:
宜以置其用，制其取用之節以遂其生，順性之道也。今之物果皆順其性矣乎？昔帝舜命棄以播時百穀，正慮夫民之不遂其生也；命益以若上下草木鳥獸，正慮夫物之不適其所也。今之在位者多矣，果皆如棄、如益之臣矣乎？若猶未也，惟在皇上節費以裕天下之財，慎動以端天下之極，明法以立天下之紀，懋德以召天下之和，虛心以用天下之賢，闢聰以納天下之言，明目以袪天下之蔽，則萬民自遂其生，萬物自適其所，而天下之化成，億萬載無疆之業，端在是矣。然其要則又在於無斁。蓋天之行也，健而不息，故能成其大；日月之行也，運而有常，故能溥其照。惟皇上奮天道健行之勇，普日月久照之明，勇以致其決，明以察其幾，不以始勤，不以終怠，不以暫勉，不以久忘，則皇猷允塞，而法祖法天之心、創業守成之道，兼舉而無遺矣。此非臣之過為是言以欺陛下也。居安者易危，處平者易傾，人之情也，故臣敢為是言也。
臣冒瀆天聽，不勝戰慄隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…to employ them as suits their inherent qualities, and to regulate the extent of their taking and use so that they may fulfill their lives: this is the way to accord with their natures. But do all things today truly enjoy conditions that accord with their natures? In former times, Emperor Shun commanded Qi to sow the various grains precisely because he feared that the people might not fulfill their lives. He commanded Yi to tend in due accord with their natures the plants, trees, birds, and beasts above and below, precisely because he feared that things might not find their proper places. Many now hold office, but are they truly all ministers like Qi and Yi? If they are not yet so, it rests with Your Majesty to restrain expenditure to enrich the resources of the realm; to act cautiously to set right its supreme standard; to make the laws clear to establish its order; to cultivate virtue diligently to bring about its harmony; to maintain an open mind to employ its worthy men; to open your hearing to receive its counsel; and to sharpen your vision to dispel what obscures it. Then all the people will naturally fulfill their lives, and all things will naturally find their proper places. The fulfillment of the realm’s moral transformation and the boundless imperial enterprise enduring for countless ages depend precisely upon this.
Yet the essential point lies further in never growing weary. Heaven moves vigorously and without cessation, and thus achieves its greatness. The sun and moon move with constancy, and thus spread their light everywhere. May Your Majesty rouse the vigor of Heaven’s unceasing course and extend widely the enduring illumination of the sun and moon, using courage to carry decisions through and discernment to perceive the first subtle signs of change. Be diligent beyond the beginning, do not grow slack at the end, exert yourself beyond a brief interval, and do not forget with the passage of time. Then the imperial plans will truly be fulfilled, and both the resolve to emulate your ancestor and Heaven and the ways of founding an enterprise and preserving its achievements will be fully realized, with nothing omitted. Your servant does not exaggerate in saying this to deceive Your Majesty. Those who dwell in security readily fall into danger, and those who enjoy stability readily fall into upheaval: such is human nature. Therefore your servant dares to speak these words.
Your servant has presumptuously offended the imperial hearing and is overwhelmed with trembling and dread of ruin. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
御批
說仁禮之意好可第一甲第二名
臣孫陞
臣對臣聞人君所以基命保業也有仁以聨天下之心而
有禮以示天下之軌禮也者經世之大典也大典既立夫
然後親疎隆殺品節詳明愈久而人習之不敢犯仁也者
生民之大徳也大德既敷夫然後中外遐邇恵澤洋溢愈
久而人思之不能忘思之而不能忘斯愛心生焉習之而
不敢犯斯敬心生焉上以仁禮使其下下以愛敬事其上
布濩流衍纏綿固結而至於不可解夫豈一朝一夕強為
而襲取之乎是必開創者懋植其本深濬其源而繼之以
栽培疏瀹之善焉爾善創善守而繼世之君不能以皆賢
或靡以隤乖以紊斯本揺而源塞矣非大有為之君出乎
其間而栽培疏瀹以還善創善守之舊則深者失其所為
深懋者失其所為懋而何以凝天心延國祚也哉此三代
而下政治之得失而歴年修短因之者也欽惟
皇帝陛下秉天縱之資邃敬一之學膺歴御極兼總古今慨政
緒之隤以紊也於是乎飭勵而振起之綱正目張百度具
舉十有四年於兹矣圖至治以永
天祚復何明有弗燭隱有弗究耶顧以是進多士策之於

臣對：臣聞人君所以基命保業也，有仁以聨天下之心，而有禮以示天下之軌。禮也者，經世之大典也。大典既立，夫然後親疎隆殺，品節詳明，愈久而人習之不敢犯。仁也者，生民之大徳也。大德既敷，夫然後中外遐邇，恵澤洋溢，愈久而人思之不能忘。思之而不能忘，斯愛心生焉；習之而不敢犯，斯敬心生焉。上以仁禮使其下，下以愛敬事其上，布濩流衍，纏綿固結，而至於不可解，夫豈一朝一夕強為而襲取之乎？是必開創者懋植其本，深濬其源，而繼之以栽培疏瀹之善焉爾。善創善守，而繼世之君不能以皆賢，或靡以隤，乖以紊，斯本揺而源塞矣。非大有為之君出乎其間，而栽培疏瀹，以還善創善守之舊，則深者失其所為深，懋者失其所為懋，而何以凝天心、延國祚也哉？此三代而下政治之得失，而歴年修短因之者也。

translation_en:
Imperial comment: “The explanation of the meaning of benevolence and ritual propriety is good. He may be placed second in the first class.”
Your servant, Sun Sheng.
Your servant replies: I have heard that a ruler establishes his mandate and preserves his undertaking through benevolence, which unites the hearts of all under Heaven, and ritual propriety, which shows all under Heaven the rules they should follow. Ritual propriety is the great canon for ordering the world. Once this great canon is established, distinctions between close and distant relationships, degrees of greater and lesser observance, and gradations of conduct become clearly defined. The longer it endures, the more people become accustomed to it and dare not transgress it. Benevolence is the great virtue that sustains the people. Once this great virtue is spread abroad, its benefits overflow within and beyond the realm, far and near. The longer it endures, the more people cherish it and cannot forget it. From cherishing it and being unable to forget it arises love; from becoming accustomed to it and not daring to transgress it arises respect. Those above direct those below through benevolence and ritual propriety, and those below serve those above with love and respect. These influences spread and flow, intertwining and binding them firmly together until they cannot be separated. How could this be contrived by force and acquired all at once? The founder must vigorously plant the roots and deeply dredge the source, and those who follow must skillfully nurture the growth and keep the channels clear. Yet even where the founding and preservation have been well accomplished, succeeding rulers cannot all be worthy. Some lapse into decline through laxity, or into disorder through waywardness; then the roots are shaken and the source obstructed. Unless a ruler of great accomplishment emerges among them to nurture the growth and clear the channels, restoring the former excellence of founding and preservation, what was deep will lose its depth, and what was flourishing will lose its vigor. How then can Heaven’s favor be secured and the dynasty’s allotted span prolonged? Such have been the successes and failures of government since the Three Dynasties, upon which the length or brevity of dynastic rule has depended.
I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor possesses Heaven-bestowed gifts and profound learning in reverent concentration on the One. You have received the dynastic succession and ascended the throne, comprehensively embracing past and present. Deploring the decline and disorder of government, you have applied yourself diligently to revive it. The guiding principles have been rectified, their particulars set in order, and all institutions put into operation. Fourteen years have now passed. As you seek perfect government to perpetuate Heaven’s blessing upon the dynasty, what manifest matter remains unilluminated, what hidden matter unexplored? title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
廷使驗往推来以陳當時之政
好問好察樂取諸人誠謂治無底極是以望治之深求治之
切亦不自知其無底極爾善治必待於真儒臣豈其人哉
雖然竊有感焉傅說進言於高宗曰王忱不艱惟說不言
有厥咎今
陛下宵旰孜孜必欲身致成周久安長治之盛以光我
祖宗謨烈問察之下少有裨益亟欲措之行矣忱不艱何如也
幸際其會而無以自獻曷從委其咎乎臣敢忘其鄙陋披
瀝肝膽為
陛下陳之臣惟治天下有體而致之有漸握之有幾體有三漸
有二幾則一而已矣何言乎體也有創業垂統之體有繼
===
===
世守成之體有更化善治之體是之謂三何言乎漸也有
更張之漸有化成之漸是之謂二今夫創業垂統之君受
天命於甚衰極亂之世綱紀蕩然人心渙散必新天下之
耳目以一其視聽夫然後足以慰来蘇之望而佑啓其後
人盖慮無弗周而為之無有弗盡者也當其治定功成法
制大備世濟熈皥民樂有生是宜與時休息遵先世之遺
烈而申勅其畫一之規以益臻隆平之治始稱守成有道
之令主而後世有述焉及夫四海無虞熈皥已極時易趨
於玩愒事恒狃於因仍斯群小欝欝待逞之會也而君德
少弗協于大中柔闇必為所制剛毅則為所激佞倖伺其
便姦逆附其末而綱紀復蕩然矣此更化善治之時也然

punctuated:
廷，使驗往推来，以陳當時之政。好問好察，樂取諸人，誠謂治無底極，是以望治之深、求治之切，亦不自知其無底極爾。善治必待於真儒，臣豈其人哉？雖然，竊有感焉。傅說進言於高宗曰：「王忱不艱，惟說不言，有厥咎。」今陛下宵旰孜孜，必欲身致成周久安長治之盛，以光我祖宗謨烈。問察之下，少有裨益，亟欲措之行矣。忱不艱何如也！幸際其會，而無以自獻，曷從委其咎乎？臣敢忘其鄙陋，披瀝肝膽，為陛下陳之。

臣惟治天下有體，而致之有漸，握之有幾。體有三，漸有二，幾則一而已矣。何言乎體也？有創業垂統之體，有繼世守成之體，有更化善治之體，是之謂三。何言乎漸也？有更張之漸，有化成之漸，是之謂二。今夫創業垂統之君，受天命於甚衰極亂之世，綱紀蕩然，人心渙散，必新天下之耳目，以一其視聽。夫然後足以慰来蘇之望，而佑啓其後人。盖慮無弗周，而為之無有弗盡者也。當其治定功成，法制大備，世濟熈皥，民樂有生，是宜與時休息，遵先世之遺烈，而申勅其畫一之規，以益臻隆平之治，始稱守成有道之令主，而後世有述焉。及夫四海無虞，熈皥已極，時易趨於玩愒，事恒狃於因仍，斯群小欝欝待逞之會也。而君德少弗協于大中，柔闇必為所制，剛毅則為所激，佞倖伺其便，姦逆附其末，而綱紀復蕩然矣。此更化善治之時也。然
translation_en:
…at court, having them examine the past and infer what is to come, so as to set forth policies for the present. You delight in questioning and examining, gladly drawing upon others. Truly, good government knows no limit; thus, in the depth of your hopes for good government and the urgency of your pursuit of it, you yourself do not realize that these, too, know no limit. Good government must depend upon a true Confucian scholar. How could your servant be such a man? Nevertheless, I venture to express what moves me. Fu Yue advised Gaozong: “If the king is sincere, there will be no difficulty. If I, Yue, fail to speak, the fault will be mine.” Now Your Majesty labors diligently from before dawn until late at night, determined personally to achieve the enduring peace and lasting good government that flourished under the Zhou, thereby bringing glory to our ancestors’ plans and achievements. If your questioning and examination yield anything of even slight benefit, you urgently wish to put it into practice. How fully this exemplifies the saying that sincerity leaves no difficulty! Having fortunately encountered such an opportunity, if I offer nothing of myself, upon whom could I shift the blame? Your servant ventures to put aside his own ignorance and inadequacy, lay bare his innermost thoughts, and present them to Your Majesty.

Your servant considers that governing All under Heaven has its forms, that bringing it to fruition has its stages, and that grasping it depends upon a crucial pivot. There are three forms and two stages, but only one crucial pivot. What do I mean by forms? There is the form of founding a dynasty and handing down its succession; the form of succeeding to the throne and preserving what has been achieved; and the form of reforming government to govern well. These are the three. What do I mean by stages? There is the stage of reform and the stage in which transformation is brought to completion. These are the two. A ruler who founds a dynasty and hands down its succession receives Heaven’s Mandate in an age of profound decline and extreme disorder. The guiding principles of government have utterly collapsed, and the people’s hearts are scattered. He must renew what the people throughout the realm see and hear, so as to unite their attention. Only then can he satisfy their hope that his coming will restore them to life, and protect and open the way for his descendants. His deliberations must therefore encompass everything, and his actions leave nothing undone. Once order is established, his achievement complete, and laws and institutions fully provided, successive generations enjoy harmony and prosperity, and the people rejoice in being alive. It is then fitting to allow rest in keeping with the times, follow the achievements bequeathed by earlier generations, and reaffirm their uniform regulations, so as to attain still greater peace and prosperity. Only then may a ruler be called an excellent sovereign who possesses the Way of preserving what has been achieved, leaving something for later generations to carry forward. But when all within the Four Seas is free from danger and harmony and prosperity have reached their height, time is easily frittered away in idleness, and affairs habitually become mired in routine. This is the opportunity for petty men, long chafing in frustration, to realize their ambitions. If the ruler’s virtue departs even slightly from the great mean, then, if he is weak and benighted, he will inevitably be controlled by them; if firm and resolute, he will be provoked by them. Flatterers and favorites watch for their opportunity, while traitors and rebels follow in their wake, and the guiding principles of government once again utterly collapse. This is the time for reforming government to govern well. Yet…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄

其所以更之也惟振起其頹廢釐正其紊亂還祖宗創
始之善而復開守成之令緒焉爾因天之道察民之心
盖有不得不一為之者而政由其舊民安其常又何嘗
有為之之迹乎伏讀
聖制有曰昔自三代以來迄於宋終中間雖歷世有久近而
其君之歷年亦有長短惟周之歷世最多國祚恒久
陛下之及此言也
宗社無疆之福也行有所稽志有所慕古今媲美夫復何言
然周之所以享國長久者果何道哉司馬光謂講禮施
仁植本固而發源深爾常考周禮一書其大者曰辨方
正位體國經野設官分職以為民極自米鹽酒漿無一
===

籥無一不統於宗伯兵戎廋圉匡襌無一不統於司馬
盟約薙剪修閭禁暴無一不統於司寇輪輿築冶桃鳬
無一不統於司空則其禮以示天下者何廣大而悉備
乎然后稷建邦啓土公劉克篤前烈太王肇基王迹王
季其勤王家文王惠鮮懷保而咸和萬民武王順天應
人而永清四海繼承之君又皆盡持盈慎滿之道逮於
宣王號稱中興聯屬天下之仁益深益懋引而弗替上
匹夏商下陋唐宋傳世三十而歷年至八百焉猗與盛
哉肆我
太祖高皇帝龍飛淮甸建功德之隆

punctuated: 其所以更之也，惟振起其頹廢，釐正其紊亂，還祖宗創始之善，而復開守成之令緒焉爾。因天之道，察民之心，盖有不得不一為之者；而政由其舊，民安其常，又何嘗有為之之迹乎？伏讀聖制有曰：「昔自三代以來，迄於宋終，中間雖歷世有久近，而其君之歷年亦有長短。惟周之歷世最多，國祚恒久。」陛下之及此言也，宗社無疆之福也。行有所稽，志有所慕，古今媲美，夫復何言？然周之所以享國長久者，果何道哉？司馬光謂：「講禮施仁，植本固而發源深爾。」常考《周禮》一書，其大者曰：「辨方正位，體國經野，設官分職，以為民極。」自米鹽酒漿，無一不統於冢宰；稍委士誦，無一不統於司徒；鐘鏄鼙梲笙籥，無一不統於宗伯；兵戎廋圉匡襌，無一不統於司馬；盟約薙剪修閭禁暴，無一不統於司寇；輪輿築冶桃鳬，無一不統於司空。則其禮以示天下者，何廣大而悉備乎！然后稷建邦啓土，公劉克篤前烈，太王肇基王迹，王季其勤王家，文王惠鮮懷保而咸和萬民，武王順天應人而永清四海。繼承之君又皆盡持盈慎滿之道，逮於宣王，號稱中興，聯屬天下之仁益深益懋，引而弗替。上匹夏商，下陋唐宋，傳世三十，而歷年至八百焉。猗與盛哉！肆我太祖高皇帝龍飛淮甸，建功德之隆
translation_en:
…As for how such reform should be undertaken, it consists only in reviving what has fallen into decay, correcting what has become disordered, restoring the good foundations laid by the ancestors, and opening anew an auspicious course for preserving their achievements. Following Heaven’s way and discerning the people’s hearts, there are indeed measures that must be undertaken once; yet government follows its established course, and the people rest content in their accustomed ways. What trace of intervention is there?

I have reverently read these words in the imperial composition: “From the Three Dynasties of antiquity down to the end of the Song, the intervening dynasties endured for differing lengths of time, and their rulers’ reigns likewise varied in length. Zhou alone continued through the most generations, and its dynastic tenure endured long.” That Your Majesty should raise this matter is a boundless blessing for the ancestral temples and the altars of state. With precedents to guide your actions and ideals toward which to aspire, antiquity and the present may rival one another in excellence. What more need be said?

Yet by what way did Zhou actually enjoy such lasting rule? Sima Guang said: “They cultivated ritual and practiced benevolence; they planted their roots firmly and established their source deep.” I have often examined the Rites of Zhou. Its broad principles are stated thus: “Distinguish the directions and establish the proper positions; lay out the capital and delimit the countryside; establish offices and allocate duties, thereby providing a standard for the people.” Rice, salt, wine, and beverages all came under the Minister of State. Grain allowances and stores, instruction and recitation [?], all came under the Minister of Education. Bells, large bells [?], small drums, beaters [?], mouth organs, and pipes all came under the Minister of Rites. Arms and military affairs, stables and horse keeping, and ‘kuang dan’ [?] all came under the Minister of War. Covenants and agreements, cutting vegetation, maintaining neighborhood gates, and suppressing violence all came under the Minister of Justice. Wheelwrights and carriage builders, metalworkers and smelters, swordsmiths and bell founders all came under the Minister of Works. How extensive and comprehensive, then, were the rites they set before the realm!

Furthermore, Hou Ji established the state and opened its territory; Gong Liu firmly carried forward his predecessor’s achievements; King Tai laid the foundations of the royal enterprise; King Ji labored diligently for the royal house; King Wen showed kindness to the distressed, cherished and protected the people, and brought harmony to all; and King Wu followed Heaven and responded to the people, bringing enduring peace within the Four Seas. Their successors likewise fully observed the way of safeguarding prosperity and exercising caution at its height. By the time of King Xuan, whose reign was celebrated as a restoration, the benevolence that bound the realm together had grown ever deeper and more abundant, continuing without decline. Zhou matched Xia and Shang before it and made Tang and Song after it appear inferior. Its succession continued for thirty generations, and its years reached eight hundred. Ah, how flourishing it was!

Then our Emperor Taizu Gao rose like a dragon in the Huai region and established lofty achievements and virtue…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
太宗文皇帝鼎定幽燕弘繼述之孝興道致治上倣成周是故
初立
郊廟即文之惠于宗公也繼冊
太子即武之以燕翼子也罷中書而設六部分職率屬之典
也
封諸王而錄功臣列爵分土之制也巖穴之士罔不招致其
克知灼見者乎忠藎之臣率見褒錄其表墓式閭者乎定
吉禮十有四凶禮二軍賓禮三嘉禮五則損益周宗伯之
職矣製樂九章自本太初以至樂清寧則彷佛大武之協
矣是其所講之禮使民罔不約之於軌而
君臣上下咸有一德所以舉是禮而措之
===
朝廷之上以及四海之遠伸縮運用莫非關雎麟趾之意周
流貫徹於其間也盖禮以齊之則固有仁以先之矣所謂
與治同道罔不興不亦可徵也哉
列聖相承守而弗失禮以敷典立天下之大防仁以昭德宏天
下之大化重煕累洽以共成乎博厚高明之績然而承平
日久積習相因至
先朝則奸逆逞便紊於更張漸亦不能無可議者
陛下入繼
大統適應中興之期天下跂焉望治不啻飢渴而
維新之詔舉措宜民大慰天下之願天下忻忻然咸奔走而相
告曰

===
朝廷之上以及四海之遠伸縮運用莫非關雎麟趾之意周
流貫徹於其間也蓋禮以齊之則固有仁以先之矣所謂
與治同道罔不興不亦可徵也哉

下之大化重熙累洽以共成乎博厚高明之續然而承平
日久積習相因至
先朝則奸逆逞便系於更張漸亦不能無可議者
陛下入繼
大統適膺中興之期天下跂焉望治不啻飢渴而
陛下與一詔舉措宜民大慰天下之願天下忻忻然咸奔走而相
告曰
punctuated:
太宗文皇帝鼎定幽燕，弘繼述之孝，興道致治，上倣成周。是故初立郊廟，即文之惠于宗公也；繼冊太子，即武之以燕翼子也。罷中書而設六部，分職率屬之典也；封諸王而錄功臣，列爵分土之制也。巖穴之士罔不招致，其克知灼見者乎？忠藎之臣率見褒錄，其表墓式閭者乎？定吉禮十有四、凶禮二、軍賓禮三、嘉禮五，則損益周宗伯之職矣；製樂九章，自本太初以至樂清寧，則彷佛大武之協矣。是其所講之禮，使民罔不約之於軌，而君臣上下咸有一德。所以舉是禮而措之朝廷之上，以及四海之遠，伸縮運用，莫非《關雎》《麟趾》之意周流貫徹於其間也。盖禮以齊之，則固有仁以先之矣。所謂「與治同道罔不興」，不亦可徵也哉？
列聖相承，守而弗失，禮以敷典，立天下之大防；仁以昭德，宏天下之大化。重煕累洽，以共成乎博厚高明之績。然而承平日久，積習相因，至先朝，則奸逆逞便，紊於更張，漸亦不能無可議者。
陛下入繼大統，適應中興之期，天下跂焉望治，不啻飢渴。而維新之詔，舉措宜民，大慰天下之願。天下忻忻然咸奔走而相告曰：
translation_en:
…Emperor Taizong Wen firmly established the imperial seat in You and Yan, magnified the filial devotion of carrying forward his predecessor’s undertakings, promoted the Way, and brought about good government, taking the perfected Zhou order as his model. Thus, the initial establishment of the suburban sacrificial altars and ancestral temples corresponded to King Wen’s benevolence toward the ancestral lords; the subsequent investiture of the heir apparent corresponded to King Wu’s provision for the security of his descendants. Abolishing the Secretariat and establishing the Six Ministries instituted the allocation of duties and direction of subordinate officials. Enfeoffing the princes and recognizing meritorious ministers instituted the ordering of noble ranks and distribution of territories. No scholar dwelling in secluded caves went unsummoned: was this not the discernment that truly knows and clearly perceives worthy men? Loyal and devoted ministers were generally commended and honored: was this not like marking their graves and bowing from one’s carriage at the gates of their neighborhoods? Fourteen auspicious rites, two mourning rites, three military and guest rites, and five celebratory rites were established, adapting the duties of the Zhou Minister of Rites. Nine musical movements were composed, from Rooted in the Primordial Beginning to Rejoicing in Clarity and Tranquillity, approximating the harmony of the Great Martial Dance. The rites thus cultivated brought all the people within proper bounds, while ruler and ministers, superiors and inferiors, shared a single virtue. Thus, when these rites were put into practice at court and extended to the farthest reaches of the realm, their adaptation and application everywhere embodied the spirit of the Odes “Guanju” and “Linzhi,” which circulated through and permeated them. For when ritual brings people into order, benevolence must already have led the way. Is this not evidence for the saying, “None who follow the same Way as good government fail to flourish”?
The successive sage emperors inherited and preserved this without loss. Through ritual they promulgated institutions and established the great safeguards of the realm; through benevolence they manifested virtue and extended its great transforming influence throughout the realm. Successive ages of brilliance and accumulated harmony together produced achievements of breadth and depth, loftiness and illumination. Yet, as peace endured for many years, ingrained habits perpetuated one another. By the preceding reign, treacherous and rebellious men pursued their own advantage, bringing disorder through changes to established arrangements; gradually, matters could no longer remain beyond criticism.
Your Majesty entered upon the great imperial succession precisely at the moment for a restoration. All under Heaven stood on tiptoe awaiting good government, with a longing greater than hunger or thirst. Your edict of renewal introduced measures suited to the people and greatly fulfilled the wishes of the realm. All under Heaven rejoiced and hurried to tell one another, saying: …

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
帝王自有真太平於是有象矣然猶恐
天位之樂久而或移其初爾乃今
勵精圖治有加無巳側身修行無異周宣請得而歷舉之則
召問元老衮職之有補也申命帥臣玁狁之北伐也嚴飭兵
衛車攻之選師徒也親信正人張仲孝友之維在也彗星
示異而恐懼修省雲漢之畏天也天下孰不延頸以覩
中興之盛乎而
聖制乃曰幼弱不才多招災害是何
謙冲自抑而言之一至此也然以耳目之所睹記則亦竊有
疑焉而不敢深以為不然者
陛下亦嘗思及之否乎
藩封盛而常禄不繼
國費冗而內帑不充西北則田野多蕪東南則賦斂日急悍
卒雖殲於朔漠而兵巳疲戎羌雖挫於甘凉而機可畏是
皆上厪
當宁之慮而下切書生之隱憂者也夫災不存於物異而存
於事之曠弛害不生於幻妄而生於民之窮困握其幾而
圖之以漸則災不蔓害不滋失今弗為將有不勝其深遠
之虞焉者則夫臣所陳之六事可無善後之策也哉
聖制又曰上之良法要道
朕心慕之思之不知何以得此臣意
陛下躬親蹈之而復疑之

謙沖自抑而言之一至此也然以耳目之所睹記則亦竊有
疑焉而不敢深以爲不然者
陛下亦嘗思及之否乎
===
藩封盛而常祿不繼
國費冗而內帑不充西北則田野多蕪東南則賦歛日急犳
卒雖殲於朔漠而兵已疲戎羗雖挫於甘凉而機可畏是
皆上厪
當宁之慮而下切書生之隱憂者也夫災不存於物異而存
於事之曠弛害不生於苟安而生於民之窮困握其幾而
圖之以漸則災不蔓害不滋失今弗爲將有不勝其深遠
之虞焉者則夫臣所陳之六事可無善後之策也哉
聖制又曰上之良法要道
朕心慕之思之不知何以得此臣意
陛下躬親蹈之而復疑之
punctuated:
帝王自有真太平，於是有象矣。」然猶恐天位之樂，久而或移其初爾。乃今勵精圖治，有加無巳；側身修行，無異周宣。請得而歷舉之：則召問元老，衮職之有補也；申命帥臣，玁狁之北伐也；嚴飭兵衛，車攻之選師徒也；親信正人，張仲孝友之維在也；彗星示異而恐懼修省，雲漢之畏天也。天下孰不延頸以覩中興之盛乎？而聖制乃曰：「幼弱不才，多招災害。」是何謙冲自抑，而言之一至此也！然以耳目之所睹記，則亦竊有疑焉，而不敢深以為不然者。陛下亦嘗思及之否乎？

藩封盛而常禄不繼，國費冗而內帑不充；西北則田野多蕪，東南則賦斂日急；悍卒雖殲於朔漠而兵巳疲，戎羌雖挫於甘凉而機可畏。是皆上厪當宁之慮，而下切書生之隱憂者也。夫災不存於物異，而存於事之曠弛；害不生於幻妄，而生於民之窮困。握其幾而圖之以漸，則災不蔓，害不滋；失今弗為，將有不勝其深遠之虞焉者。則夫臣所陳之六事，可無善後之策也哉？

聖制又曰：「上之良法要道，朕心慕之思之，不知何以得此。」臣意陛下躬親蹈之，而復疑之，
translation_en:
…“The emperors and kings truly had an age of Great Peace; now its signs are manifest.” Yet there remained the fear that prolonged enjoyment of the imperial throne might perhaps alter Your Majesty’s original resolve. Now, however, your devoted efforts to achieve good government continually increase, and your vigilant cultivation of your conduct is no different from that of King Xuan of Zhou. Allow me to enumerate these parallels. Summoning and consulting the elder statesmen supplies what is lacking in the sovereign’s discharge of his duties. Renewing commands to the military commanders recalls the northern expedition against the Xianyun. Strictly disciplining the palace guards recalls the selection of troops in “Our Chariots Were Strong” (Che gong). Trusting upright men recalls the presence of Zhang Zhong, filial and devoted to his brothers. Responding to the ominous appearance of a comet with fear, self-cultivation, and examination recalls the reverence for Heaven in “The Milky Way” (Yun han). Who throughout the realm does not crane his neck to behold the splendor of this restoration? Yet the Emperor’s decree reads: “Young, weak, and without ability, I have brought on many calamities and afflictions.” How profound is the humility and self-restraint that brings Your Majesty to speak thus! Nevertheless, judging by what I have seen, heard, and recorded, I too privately harbor doubts, and dare not firmly dismiss these words as untrue. Has Your Majesty ever considered these matters?

The princely establishments multiply, but their regular stipends cannot be sustained; state expenditures are excessive, but the palace treasury is insufficiently stocked. In the northwest, much farmland lies waste; in the southeast, the exaction of taxes grows more pressing daily. Though the fierce enemy troops have been annihilated in the northern desert, our soldiers are already exhausted; though the Rong and Qiang have been defeated at Gan and Liang, the potential turn of events remains alarming. These are all matters that burden the sovereign’s thoughts above and cause a scholar below deep, unspoken anxiety. Calamity resides not in anomalous phenomena, but in the neglect and lax administration of affairs; harm arises not from phantasms and delusions, but from the people’s destitution. If one grasps the first signs and addresses them by degrees, calamities will not spread and harm will not increase. If the present opportunity is lost through inaction, there will be cause to fear consequences of incalculable depth and reach. Can the six matters your servant has presented, then, be left without policies to secure their lasting resolution?

The Emperor’s decree further reads: “The excellent institutions and essential principles mentioned above—I admire them and ponder them in my heart, but do not know how to attain them.” Your servant believes that Your Majesty personally puts them into practice, yet still doubts this…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
聖不自聖夫亦過焉爾矣
陛下所謂良法非臣之所謂禮乎
陛下所謂要道非臣之所謂仁乎周祚之所以久長
皇祖之所以創立
列聖之所以守成而
陛下今日所以中興焉者率不外此但謹於前或忽於後銳於
作或怠於成董仲舒曰王者之道必有偏廢不舉之處非
其道不善也久而或有失之也惟
陛下講禮施仁率典昭德竟其更化善治之緒以要之於極俾
民各遂其生物各適其所至治馨香通於神明協氣嘉生
徧於宇宙斯
===
聖帝明王之能事而祈
天永
命之極功
陛下所以策臣欲長保洪業於無窮有隆弗替延
宗社萬禩之固永家國千世之傳者行將見之而成周不得專
美於前矣雖然心者治之本也幾者動之微也所動雖微
所關實大臣又敢以慎微之說進焉一或不慎則幽獨得
肆之地投間抵隙將不自知其此心之累而施仁講禮皆
為彌文可不逆為之慮乎怠荒遊逸益嘗舉以戒舜矣是
非古人之過計也危平易傾理所必至而兢業萬幾正舜
之所以為聖焉者狂瞽之言弗識忌諱

punctuated:
聖不自聖，夫亦過焉爾矣。陛下所謂良法，非臣之所謂禮乎？陛下所謂要道，非臣之所謂仁乎？周祚之所以久長，皇祖之所以創立，列聖之所以守成，而陛下今日所以中興焉者，率不外此。但謹於前，或忽於後；銳於作，或怠於成。董仲舒曰：「王者之道，必有偏廢不舉之處，非其道不善也，久而或有失之也。」惟陛下講禮施仁，率典昭德，竟其更化善治之緒，以要之於極，俾民各遂其生，物各適其所，至治馨香通於神明，協氣嘉生徧於宇宙，斯聖帝明王之能事，而祈天永命之極功。陛下所以策臣，欲長保洪業於無窮，有隆弗替，延宗社萬禩之固，永家國千世之傳者，行將見之，而成周不得專美於前矣。
雖然，心者治之本也，幾者動之微也。所動雖微，所關實大。臣又敢以慎微之說進焉。一或不慎，則幽獨得肆之地，投間抵隙，將不自知其此心之累，而施仁講禮皆為彌文，可不逆為之慮乎？怠荒遊逸，益嘗舉以戒舜矣。是非古人之過計也。危平易傾，理所必至，而兢業萬幾，正舜之所以為聖焉者。狂瞽之言，弗識忌諱。
translation_en:
…Though a sage, you do not regard yourself as a sage; yet this humility goes too far. Are not what Your Majesty calls good laws what your servant calls ritual propriety? Is not what Your Majesty calls the essential Way what your servant calls benevolence? The long endurance of the Zhou dynasty, the founding achievement of the Imperial Progenitor, the preservation of that achievement by successive sage emperors, and Your Majesty’s present restoration all depend upon these alone. Yet care at the outset may give way to neglect later, and zeal in undertaking a task may give way to indolence in completing it. Dong Zhongshu said: “In the way of kings, there will inevitably be aspects that are neglected and left unpracticed. This is not because the Way is defective, but because, over time, departures from it may occur.” May Your Majesty cultivate ritual propriety and practice benevolence, follow the established canons and manifest virtue, and bring your undertaking of reform and good government to its fullest completion. Let every person fulfill the course of life and every creature find its proper place; let the sweet fragrance of consummate government reach the spirits, and harmonious vital forces and flourishing life pervade the universe. This is the achievement of sage emperors and enlightened kings, and the supreme accomplishment in praying to Heaven for an enduring mandate. What Your Majesty desires in posing this policy question to your servant—to preserve the great imperial enterprise forever, flourishing without decline, to secure the ancestral temples and altars of state for ten thousand years, and to perpetuate the transmission of the ruling house and realm for a thousand generations—will soon be realized. Then the perfected Zhou will no longer hold an exclusive claim to such glory in antiquity.
Nevertheless, the mind is the root of government, and incipient impulses are the subtle beginnings of action. Though the initial movement is slight, its consequences are great. Your servant therefore ventures further to submit an argument for vigilance over the slightest beginnings. Should vigilance lapse even once, secluded and solitary moments will afford scope for self-indulgence; exploiting openings and slipping through gaps, it will burden the mind without your awareness. The practice of benevolence and cultivation of ritual propriety will then become mere elaborate forms. Can one fail to guard against this beforehand? Yi once warned Shun against indolence, neglect, pleasure-seeking, and ease. This was no excessive anxiety on the part of the ancients. “Precarious peace readily topples” [?]: this is an inevitable consequence of the underlying principles. Shun’s vigilant attention to the myriad incipient affairs of government was precisely what made him a sage. These rash and benighted words take no account of what it is forbidden to say…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
御批
敬為心學之極此論好可第一甲
第三名
臣吳山
臣對臣聞帝王之於天下其得之也必本於仁而其保之
也必本於敬仁以得天下則所以締造而固結之者無弗
至敬以保天下則所以繼承而持守之者無弗周是固法
之良道之要也苟得天下而不本於仁則是莫為之前雖
===
美弗彰何以為後人憑藉之地保天下而不本於敬則是
莫為之後雖盛弗傳且將墜先人創造之艱矣孟子曰三
代之得天下也以仁則夫得天下者孰有外於仁哉召公
之誥成王曰王敬作所不可不敬德則夫保天下者孰有
要於敬哉然仁也敬也匪在外也皆在乎吾之一心而已
是故心存則仁存矣仁存則敬無不存矣此三代所以有
道之長也此我
太祖高皇帝之所以肇造
太宗文皇帝之所以繼述
列聖之所以遵承
陛下之所以中興而與天無極者也是豈漢唐宋之所能及也

太宗文皇帝之所以繼述
列聖之所以遵承
陛下之所以中興而與天無極者也是豈漢唐宋之所能及也
punctuated:
御批：敬為心學之極，此論好，可第一甲。

第三名，臣吳山。

臣對：臣聞帝王之於天下，其得之也必本於仁，而其保之也必本於敬。仁以得天下，則所以締造而固結之者無弗至；敬以保天下，則所以繼承而持守之者無弗周。是固法之良、道之要也。苟得天下而不本於仁，則是莫為之前，雖美弗彰，何以為後人憑藉之地？保天下而不本於敬，則是莫為之後，雖盛弗傳，且將墜先人創造之艱矣。孟子曰：「三代之得天下也以仁。」則夫得天下者孰有外於仁哉？召公之誥成王曰：「王敬作所，不可不敬德。」則夫保天下者孰有要於敬哉？然仁也，敬也，匪在外也，皆在乎吾之一心而已。是故心存則仁存矣，仁存則敬無不存矣。此三代所以有道之長也。此我太祖高皇帝之所以肇造、太宗文皇帝之所以繼述、列聖之所以遵承、陛下之所以中興而與天無極者也。是豈漢唐宋之所能及也
translation_en:
Imperial comment: “Reverence is the highest attainment in the learning of the mind. This discussion is good; it merits placement in the First Class.”

Third place: your servant Wu Shan.

Your servant replies: I have heard that, in their relation to All under Heaven, emperors and kings must base their acquisition of it upon benevolence, and their preservation of it upon reverence. When they acquire All under Heaven through benevolence, their means of founding and firmly consolidating it are thorough in every respect. When they preserve All under Heaven through reverence, their means of succeeding to it and maintaining it are comprehensive in every respect. These are indeed excellent principles and the essentials of the Way. If one acquires All under Heaven without basing oneself upon benevolence, then there is no one to establish what comes before: however fine it may be, it will not be made manifest. How could this provide a foundation on which later generations might rely? If one preserves All under Heaven without basing oneself upon reverence, then there is no one to carry on what comes after: however flourishing it may be, it will not be transmitted. Moreover, one will bring to ruin what one’s predecessors labored so hard to create.

Mencius said: “The Three Dynasties acquired All under Heaven through benevolence.” Who, then, has acquired All under Heaven apart from benevolence? In his admonition to King Cheng, the Duke of Shao said: “Let the king reverently establish his place; he must not fail to revere virtue.” For preserving All under Heaven, then, what could be more essential than reverence? Yet benevolence and reverence are not external things: both reside solely in this one mind of ours. Thus, when the mind is preserved, benevolence is preserved; when benevolence is preserved, reverence is present in all things. This is why the Three Dynasties long possessed the Way.

This is how our Emperor Taizu Gao founded the dynasty, how Emperor Taizong Wen carried forward his predecessor’s work, how the successive sage emperors continued that inheritance, and how Your Majesty has brought about a restoration whose duration, like Heaven’s, knows no limit. Could this possibly be matched by the Han, Tang, or Song …

哉欽惟
陛下
稟聰明睿智之資
蘊剛健中正之德爰自
藩邸入繼
大統即位以來勵精化理百度惟貞萬邦咸乂真有以永
宗社於無窮保家國於弗替而
敬一之箴則又真得夫千聖相傳心法之要保天下之道信
無喻於此矣乃猶不自滿假惕然悚懼進臣等于
廷而以三代以來迄於宋終歷世之久近與其君歷年之長
短及我
===
祖宗
列聖之所以創守發為
明詔以求所以保業之良法要道顧臣何知而可以與此雖
然臣克聖臣不命其承矧
陛下命之如此臣雖至愚敢不罄竭以對揚於萬一乎臣聞惟
天生民必立之君是君也者天之命也天既命之以天下
而為天之子是必有祈天永命之道故曰惟皇上帝降衷
于下民若有恒性克綏厥猷惟后又曰亶聰明作元后元
后作民父母曰惟天聰明惟聖時憲則夫所以得之者固
難而所以保之者亦弗易也故曰天難諶命靡常曰惟天
無親克敬惟親苟失其所以得與夫所以保之道則雖

…indeed! I reverently consider that Your Majesty possesses the gifts of intelligence and sagely wisdom and harbors the virtues of strength, vigor, centrality, and rectitude. From your princely residence you came to succeed to the imperial throne. Since your accession, you have exerted yourself wholeheartedly in transforming and governing the realm. All institutions are properly ordered, and all states are at peace. You truly possess the means to perpetuate the ancestral temples and altars of state without end and to preserve the imperial house and realm from decline. Moreover, your Admonition on Reverent Oneness (Jingyi zhen) truly grasps the essentials of the teaching of the mind transmitted from sage to sage. Surely nothing surpasses this [?] as a way of preserving All-under-Heaven. Yet you remain neither complacent nor self-satisfied, but vigilant and apprehensive. You have summoned us, your servants, to court and issued an enlightened decree asking about the relative duration of successive dynasties from the Three Dynasties through the end of the Song, the lengths of their rulers’ reigns, and the means by which our founding ancestors and successive sage emperors established and preserved their rule. Thus you seek sound methods and essential principles for preserving the imperial enterprise. Yet what knowledge have I that would enable me to contribute to this? Nevertheless, ministers can make their ruler a sage, and ministers carry out his intentions without awaiting commands. How much more, then, when Your Majesty has commanded us in this manner! Though I am utterly foolish, dare I fail to exhaust my abilities in answering and honoring even the smallest part of your charge?
Your servant has heard that when Heaven brings forth the people, it must establish a ruler over them. The ruler is thus appointed by Heaven. Since Heaven entrusts him with All-under-Heaven and makes him the Son of Heaven, there must be a way for him to pray to Heaven for an enduring mandate. Thus it is said: “August Heaven on high bestows an upright nature upon the people below. It is the sovereign who enables them to follow their constant nature and peacefully pursue its proper course.” Again it is said: “One truly intelligent and discerning becomes the great sovereign; the great sovereign becomes the father and mother of the people.” It is also said: “Heaven is intelligent and discerning; the sage takes this as his model.” Thus the means of obtaining the realm are certainly difficult, and the means of preserving it are likewise not easy. title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
或與之亦或奪之雖或就之亦或去之雖或得之亦或失
之而崇高富貴之地有不可恃者矣今夫千金之家其始
也未有不自其祖宗之艱難勞苦以成之而其終也亦未
有不自其子孫之頑率奢傲以敗之况夫天下至大也兆
民至衆也四海至廣也以一人而偃然居於其上以統理
之使皆帖服順從惟其欲以治而為法於當時可傳於後
世是豈無道以致之哉臣嘗聞之夏有天下四百年矣其
始也則由禹之祗台德先文命誕敷以得之也一傳而為
啟則賢能敬承繼禹之道而遂以家天下太康逸豫滅德
而夏道以衰至桀之暴夏始轉而商矣非天私於商也桀
失其所以保之之道焉爾商有天下六百年矣其始也則
===
由湯之克寬克仁彰信兆民以得之也一傳而太甲則克
終允德而其間之太戊也祖乙盤庚也皆賢聖之君也至
於高宗則又不敢怠遑允協于先王成德而商道復興及
紂之暴商始轉而周矣非天私於周也紂失其所以保之
之道焉爾故曰我不可不監于有夏亦不可不監于有殷
乃若周之有天下也固本於文王之惠鮮懷保武王之不
泄不忘然遡而上之若后稷之克配彼天公劉之克篤前
烈太王之肇基王迹王季之其勤王家其積功累仁所由
來者遠矣而成王之基命宥密康王之敬忌天威其所以
繼承之者何如也况又有周公之制禮作樂其所以維持
之者又何如也厲王暴虐周道始衰宣王承之而側身脩
