punctuated:
或與之，亦或奪之；雖或就之，亦或去之；雖或得之，亦或失之。而崇高富貴之地，有不可恃者矣。今夫千金之家，其始也，未有不自其祖宗之艱難勞苦以成之；而其終也，亦未有不自其子孫之頑率奢傲以敗之。况夫天下至大也，兆民至衆也，四海至廣也，以一人而偃然居於其上以統理之，使皆帖服順從，惟其欲以治，而為法於當時，可傳於後世，是豈無道以致之哉？

臣嘗聞之：夏有天下四百年矣，其始也，則由禹之「祗台德先，文命誕敷」以得之也。一傳而為啟，則賢能敬承，繼禹之道，而遂以家天下。太康逸豫滅德，而夏道以衰；至桀之暴，夏始轉而商矣。非天私於商也，桀失其所以保之之道焉爾。商有天下六百年矣，其始也，則由湯之「克寬克仁，彰信兆民」以得之也。一傳而太甲，則克終允德；而其間之太戊也，祖乙、盤庚也，皆賢聖之君也。至於高宗，則又「不敢怠遑」，允協于先王成德，而商道復興。及紂之暴，商始轉而周矣。非天私於周也，紂失其所以保之之道焉爾。故曰：「我不可不監于有夏，亦不可不監于有殷。」

乃若周之有天下也，固本於文王之惠鮮懷保、武王之不泄不忘。然遡而上之，若后稷之克配彼天、公劉之克篤前烈、太王之肇基王迹、王季之其勤王家，其積功累仁所由來者遠矣。而成王之基命宥密、康王之敬忌天威，其所以繼承之者何如也？况又有周公之制禮作樂，其所以維持之者又何如也？厲王暴虐，周道始衰；宣王承之，而側身脩
translation_en:
…it may grant it, yet may also take it away; though it may draw near, it may also depart; though one may obtain it, one may also lose it. Thus an exalted station of wealth and honor cannot be relied upon. Consider a household worth a thousand pieces of gold: at its beginning, it invariably owes its establishment to the hardships and toil of its ancestors; at its end, it invariably owes its ruin to the obstinacy, recklessness, extravagance, and arrogance of their descendants. How much more is this true of the realm, so vast, its people so numerous, and the lands within the Four Seas so extensive! For one man to sit securely above them and govern them all, making everyone submit and obey, bringing order as he intends, and establishing an example for his own age that can be transmitted to later generations—could this possibly be achieved without a guiding Way?

Your servant has heard that the Xia possessed the realm for four hundred years. At its beginning, Yu gained it by “reverently putting virtue first and spreading his civilizing teachings far and wide.” After one succession it passed to Qi, who worthily and ably received his charge with reverence, continued Yu’s Way, and thereby made rule of the realm hereditary within his family. Taikang destroyed his virtue through ease and indulgence, and the Way of the Xia declined. With Jie’s tyranny, rule finally passed from the Xia to the Shang. It was not that Heaven favored the Shang: Jie had simply lost the Way by which he could preserve his rule. The Shang possessed the realm for six hundred years. At its beginning, Tang gained it by “being magnanimous and humane, and manifesting his trustworthiness to the myriad people.” After one succession came Taijia, who ultimately attained true virtue. Among the intervening rulers, Taiwu, Zuyi, and Pangeng were all worthy and sagely sovereigns. Gaozong, moreover, “dared not indulge in idleness or leisure,” and truly conformed to the perfected virtue of the former kings, so that the Way of the Shang flourished again. With Zhou’s tyranny, rule finally passed from the Shang to the Zhou dynasty. It was not that Heaven favored the Zhou: the tyrant Zhou had simply lost the Way by which he could preserve his rule. Thus it is said: “We cannot fail to take warning from the Xia, nor can we fail to take warning from the Yin.”

As for the Zhou’s possession of the realm, its foundations certainly lay in King Wen’s kindness toward the forlorn and his care and protection of the people, and in King Wu’s freedom from laxity and forgetfulness. Yet tracing its origins further back, we find Houji, who could match Heaven in virtue; Gongliu, who could consolidate the achievements of his predecessors; King Tai, who laid the foundations of the royal enterprise; and Wang Ji, who labored diligently for the royal house. Their accumulated achievements and benevolence had very distant origins indeed. Then King Cheng established the mandate with magnanimity and quiet deliberation, and King Kang revered and stood in awe of Heaven’s majesty. How admirable were the means by which they carried on this inheritance! Moreover, the Duke of Zhou established rites and created music: how admirable, too, were the means by which he sustained it! King Li was violent and tyrannical, and the Way of the Zhou began to decline. King Xuan succeeded him and, with anxious humility, cultivated…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
行宗周復赫赫矣綿至春秋陵夷已極而天下之民猶依
依然不忍離去是其德澤之深風化之美不可企及而傳
稱其歷世最多國祚恒久良有以也向使其子若孫不失
其保之之道焉則周雖至今存可也自周而下享國之久
者漢唐宋耳以漢言之高帝之寬仁大度得國正矣而其
繼體之君若文景之恭儉光武之中興亦粗得夫保之之
道此所以歷年四百也以唐言之太宗之力行仁義創業
善矣而其守成之主若玄宗之勵精政事憲宗之光復舊
物亦僅得夫保之之道此所以歷年三百也宋太祖以忠
厚立國矣而繼以仁宗四十二年仁厚之政有以培植其
命脉此所以享有三百餘年也如使其子若孫皆不失其
===
保之之道焉則雖如周之過其歷亦可也是則三代也漢
唐宋也其歷世之久近歷年之長短雖有不同至要其所
以得之與夫所以保之之道則未有不本於仁敬者也而
聖策所謂皆基之於先王德澤洽於民心亦繼之嗣王能盡持
盈慎滿之道者是已然創守無二道仁敬無二理第舉其
重而言則創業垂統惟仁為最大繼體守成惟敬為最切
是故言仁則敬在其中能敬則仁在其中夫非有二也我
太祖高皇帝獨禀全智應運而興廓清天地之大變恢復帝王
之正統功德之隆振古無比其所以肇造而為根本之地
者固矣

行宗周復赫赫矣綿至春秋陵夷已極而天下之民猶依
依然不忍離去是其德澤之深風化之美不可企及而傳
稱其歷世最多國祚恒久良有以也向使其子若孫不失
其保之之道焉則周雖至今存可也自周而下享國之久
者漢唐宋耳以漢言之高帝之寬仁大度得國正矣而其

道此所以歷年四百也以唐言之太宗之力行仁義創業
善矣而其守成之主若玄宗之勵精政事憲宗之克復舊
物亦僅得夫保之之道此所以歷年三百也宋太祖以忠
厚立國矣而繼以仁宗四十二年仁厚之政有以培植其

保之之道焉則雖如周之過其歷亦可也是則三代以漢
唐宋也其歷世之久近歷年之長短雖有不同至要其所
以得之與夫所以保之之道則未有不本於仁敬者也而

是故言仁則敬在其中言敬則仁在其中夫非有二也我

者固矣

punctuated:
行，宗周復赫赫矣。綿至春秋，陵夷已極，而天下之民猶依依然不忍離去。是其德澤之深、風化之美，不可企及，而傳稱其歷世最多，國祚恒久，良有以也。向使其子若孫不失其保之之道焉，則周雖至今存可也。
自周而下，享國之久者，漢、唐、宋耳。以漢言之，高帝之寬仁大度，得國正矣，而其繼體之君，若文、景之恭儉，光武之中興，亦粗得夫保之之道，此所以歷年四百也。以唐言之，太宗之力行仁義，創業善矣，而其守成之主，若玄宗之勵精政事，憲宗之光復舊物，亦僅得夫保之之道，此所以歷年三百也。宋太祖以忠厚立國矣，而繼以仁宗四十二年仁厚之政，有以培植其命脉，此所以享有三百餘年也。如使其子若孫皆不失其保之之道焉，則雖如周之過其歷亦可也。是則三代也，漢、唐、宋也，其歷世之久近、歷年之長短雖有不同，至要其所以得之與夫所以保之之道，則未有不本於仁敬者也。而聖策所謂「皆基之於先王德澤洽於民心，亦繼之嗣王能盡持盈慎滿之道」者，是已。然創守無二道，仁敬無二理。第舉其重而言，則創業垂統，惟仁為最大；繼體守成，惟敬為最切。是故言仁則敬在其中，能敬則仁在其中，夫非有二也。
我太祖高皇帝獨禀全智，應運而興，廓清天地之大變，恢復帝王之正統，功德之隆，振古無比。其所以肇造而為根本之地者固矣。太宗文皇帝載靖內難，奄奠兩京，其所以繼述而培植之者深
translation_en:
…his conduct, and the ancestral Zhou realm once again shone in splendor. By the Spring and Autumn period, its decline had reached the utmost extreme, yet the people throughout the realm remained affectionately attached to it and could not bear to leave. Such were the incomparable depth of its beneficence and excellence of its moral influence. The tradition therefore had good reason to say that it endured for the most generations and that its dynastic mandate long continued. Had its sons and grandsons never lost the way to preserve it, Zhou might even have survived to this day.
After Zhou, the dynasties that enjoyed lengthy rule were Han, Tang, and Song alone. To speak of Han: Emperor Gao, through his generosity, benevolence, and magnanimity, acquired the realm uprightly. Among the rulers who succeeded him, Wen and Jing, with their reverence and frugality, and Guangwu, with his restoration of the dynasty, also attained some measure of the way to preserve it. This is why it lasted four hundred years. To speak of Tang: Taizong vigorously practiced benevolence and righteousness and founded the dynasty well. Among the rulers who maintained his achievement, Xuanzong, through his earnest attention to government, and Xianzong, through his recovery of the former inheritance, likewise attained only some measure of the way to preserve it. This is why it lasted three hundred years. Song Taizu founded his dynasty on loyalty and generosity, and Renzong followed with forty-two years of benevolent and generous government, thereby nurturing its lifeblood. This is why it enjoyed more than three hundred years of rule. Had their sons and grandsons all maintained the way to preserve their dynasties, they too might, like Zhou, have outlasted their allotted span. Thus, although the Three Dynasties and Han, Tang, and Song differed in the number of generations and years they endured, the essential ways by which they acquired and preserved the realm were invariably rooted in benevolence and reverence. This is precisely what Your Majesty’s policy question means by saying: “All were founded upon the beneficence of former kings, which suffused the people’s hearts, and were continued by succeeding kings who fully practiced the way of holding a brimming vessel and remaining cautious amid fullness.” Yet founding and preserving a dynasty are not two different ways, nor are benevolence and reverence two separate principles. If we speak only of their relative emphasis, benevolence is paramount in founding a dynasty and handing down its succession; reverence is most pressing in succeeding to the throne and preserving what has been achieved. Thus, when one speaks of benevolence, reverence is included within it; when one practices reverence, benevolence is included within it. They are not two separate things.
Our Taizu, the Exalted Emperor, uniquely endowed with complete wisdom, arose in response to Heaven’s appointed time. He swept away the great upheaval between Heaven and earth and restored the rightful imperial succession. The grandeur of his achievements and virtue was unequaled since antiquity. Firm indeed were the foundations he laid in establishing the dynasty. Taizong, the Cultured Emperor, then pacified the internal troubles and brought lasting stability to the two capitals. Profound was his work in carrying forward and nurturing that inheritance…

列聖相承守而勿失其所以率循而灌溉之者篤矣是其創守
之道仁敬兼盡真有以建億萬載無疆之休也于今百六
十餘年矣
陛下踐阼以來大孝尊
親
至仁饗
帝
聖敬日躋十四年來有如一日深仁厚澤浹洽於民心
峻德成功昭布於海宇蓋真所謂赫然中興之盛而不特守
成之美而已
===
聖策乃以為多招災害於民者此特
陛下憂勤惕勵視民如傷之心也臣雖愚昧亦知其無是事矣
又以為思
祖宗創造萬艱惕然悚懼欲長保鴻業於無窮有隆弗替永
宗社萬禩之固保家國千世之傳民得以遂生物得以適所如
上之良法要道朕心慕之思之不知何以得此此特
陛下憂勤惕勵望道未見之心也臣雖愚昧亦知其無以加矣
何也蓋保天下之道誠不外於敬焉爾矣在昔堯之兢兢
舜之業業率用此道而周公無逸之篇言殷之中宗高宗
祖甲及周文王享國之長久與厥後王之罔或克壽亦惟
在於無逸乃逸之分召公之誥言夏商之墜厥命亦惟在

punctuated:
矣。列聖相承，守而勿失，其所以率循而灌溉之者篤矣。是其創守之道，仁敬兼盡，真有以建億萬載無疆之休也。于今百六十餘年矣。
陛下踐阼以來，大孝尊親，至仁饗帝，聖敬日躋，十四年來有如一日。深仁厚澤，浹洽於民心；峻德成功，昭布於海宇。蓋真所謂赫然中興之盛，而不特守成之美而已。
聖策乃以為多招災害於民者，此特陛下憂勤惕勵、視民如傷之心也。臣雖愚昧，亦知其無是事矣。又以為：「思祖宗創造萬艱，惕然悚懼，欲長保鴻業於無窮，有隆弗替，永宗社萬禩之固，保家國千世之傳，民得以遂生，物得以適所。如上之良法要道，朕心慕之思之，不知何以得此。」此特陛下憂勤惕勵、望道未見之心也。臣雖愚昧，亦知其無以加矣。
何也？蓋保天下之道，誠不外於敬焉爾矣。在昔堯之兢兢、舜之業業，率用此道。而周公《無逸》之篇，言殷之中宗、高宗、祖甲及周文王享國之長久，與厥後王之罔或克壽，亦惟在於無逸、乃逸之分。召公之誥，言夏商之墜厥命，亦惟在
translation_en:
…indeed. The successive sage emperors inherited and preserved it without loss; their adherence to its precedents and their nurturing of it were devoted indeed. Thus, in both founding and preserving the dynasty, they fully realized benevolence and reverence alike, truly establishing boundless blessings for countless ages. More than one hundred and sixty years have now passed.
Since Your Majesty ascended the throne, you have honored your parent with supreme filial devotion and offered sacrifice to the Supreme Deity with utmost benevolence. Your sagely reverence has increased daily, remaining constant throughout these fourteen years as though they were a single day. Your profound benevolence and abundant bounty have thoroughly permeated the people’s hearts; your exalted virtue and accomplished achievements shine throughout the realm. This is truly what is called the splendor of a brilliant dynastic resurgence, exceeding even the excellence of preserving an established inheritance.
Yet the imperial policy question speaks of having brought many calamities upon the people. This merely expresses Your Majesty’s anxious diligence and vigilant self-discipline, and your care for the people as though they were injured. Though your servant is ignorant, even I know that no such thing has occurred. It further states: “Reflecting on the countless hardships through which my ancestors founded the dynasty, I tremble in apprehension. I wish to preserve their great undertaking forever, ensuring that it flourishes without decline; to secure the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain for ten thousand years; and to ensure that the ruling house and state are transmitted for a thousand generations, so that the people may fulfill their lives and all things find their proper places. My heart yearns for and ponders the excellent methods and essential principles described above, but I do not know how to attain them.” This merely expresses Your Majesty’s anxious diligence and vigilant self-discipline, and your pursuit of the Way as though you had yet to perceive it. Though your servant is ignorant, even I know that nothing could surpass this.
Why is this so? The way to preserve All under Heaven truly consists in nothing beyond reverence. In antiquity, Yao’s circumspection and Shun’s vigilance both followed this way. The Duke of Zhou’s chapter “Against Ease” discusses the long reigns of Zhongzong, Gaozong, and Zu Jia of Yin, and King Wen of Zhou, alongside the failure of their successor kings to attain longevity. This too depended solely on the distinction between avoiding ease and indulging in it. The “Announcement of the Duke of Shao” says that Xia and Shang lost their Mandate solely because of…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
於不敬厥德且拳拳欲其君疾敬德以祈天永命二公之
所以告其君者如此是知人君一念敬肆之間而天下之
治亂生民之休戚壽命之長短皆繫於此是不可不慎也
大哉敬乎其合内外貫創守之道乎蓋能敬則心無不存
而仁無不全天下之道備於我矣故曰敬也者聖學所以
成始成終之要也此在
陛下固已超然遠覽淵然深識身體而力行之矣臣愚復何言
哉雖然臣又聞之詩曰靡不有初鮮克有終伊尹之告太
甲曰終始惟一時乃日新傅說之復高宗曰念終始典于
學厥德脩罔覺臣愚無知伏願
陛下常存此心謹終如始於凡
===
聖箴之所載如所謂惟敬惟一執之甚固畏天勤民不遑寧處
與夫郊則恭誠廟嚴孝趨肅于明廷慎于閒居省躬察咎
儆戒無虞之說益焉弗懈則夫所謂天親民懷光前裕後
者皆自此而得之而雍熙泰和之盛亦在於此又豈特所
謂庶幾湯孫底于嘉靖而已哉雖然此亦
陛下嘗言之矣其曰行顧其言終如其始者是已而臣復以為
言者蓋以傅說之復高宗又曰非知之艱行之惟艱王忱
不艱允協于先王成德惟說不言有厥咎此臣所以於終
篇而申言之也臣誠愚昧無所知識拳拳芹曝之私如此
而已伏惟
陛下謹厥終而力行之無忽實

punctuated:
於不敬厥德，且拳拳欲其君疾敬德，以祈天永命。二公之所以告其君者如此，是知人君一念敬肆之間，而天下之治亂、生民之休戚、壽命之長短，皆繫於此，是不可不慎也。大哉，敬乎！其合内外、貫創守之道乎！蓋能敬，則心無不存，而仁無不全，天下之道備於我矣。故曰：「敬也者，聖學所以成始成終之要也。」此在陛下，固已超然遠覽，淵然深識，身體而力行之矣，臣愚復何言哉！

雖然，臣又聞之，《詩》曰：「靡不有初，鮮克有終。」伊尹之告太甲曰：「終始惟一，時乃日新。」傅說之復高宗曰：「念終始典于學，厥德脩罔覺。」臣愚無知，伏願陛下常存此心，謹終如始。於凡聖箴之所載，如所謂「惟敬惟一，執之甚固，畏天勤民，不遑寧處」，與夫「郊則恭誠，廟嚴孝趨，肅于明廷，慎于閒居，省躬察咎，儆戒無虞」之說，益焉弗懈，則夫所謂「天親民懷，光前裕後」者，皆自此而得之，而雍熙泰和之盛亦在於此，又豈特所謂「庶幾湯孫底于嘉靖」而已哉！

雖然，此亦陛下嘗言之矣，其曰「行顧其言，終如其始」者是已。而臣復以為言者，蓋以傅說之復高宗又曰：「非知之艱，行之惟艱。王忱不艱，允協于先王成德。惟說不言，有厥咎。」此臣所以於終篇而申言之也。臣誠愚昧，無所知識，拳拳芹曝之私，如此而已。伏惟陛下謹厥終而力行之，無忽，實
translation_en:
…in failing to revere their virtue; he also earnestly wished his ruler to apply himself urgently to revering virtue, thereby praying to Heaven for an enduring mandate. Such were the admonitions these two dukes addressed to their rulers. We thus know that the difference between reverence and heedlessness in a ruler’s single thought determines order or disorder throughout the realm, the well-being or suffering of the people, and the length or brevity of his life. One cannot be incautious about this. Great indeed is reverence! Is it not the Way that unites the inner and the outer and runs through both founding and preserving a dynasty? For if one can maintain reverence, the mind remains fully present and benevolence remains whole: the Way of all under Heaven is complete within oneself. Thus it is said: “Reverence is the essential means by which the learning of the sages achieves both its beginning and its completion.” Your Majesty has already surveyed this with lofty vision, understood it with profound insight, and embodied it through strenuous practice. What more can your foolish servant say?

Nevertheless, your servant has also heard these words. The Book of Odes says: “None fail to make a beginning; few can bring matters to completion.” Yi Yin admonished Tai Jia: “Be consistent from beginning to end, and you will renew yourself daily.” Fu Yue replied to Gaozong: “Keep your thoughts, from beginning to end, constantly upon learning, and your virtue will improve without your noticing it.” Foolish and ignorant as your servant is, I humbly pray that Your Majesty will always preserve this disposition and be as careful at the end as at the beginning. As for everything recorded in the Imperial Admonition—such sayings as “Maintain reverence and singleness of purpose, holding firmly to them; stand in awe of Heaven and labor for the people, allowing yourself no leisure to rest,” and “At the suburban sacrifice be reverent and sincere; in the ancestral temple approach with solemn filial devotion; be solemn in the illustrious court and cautious in private; examine yourself and investigate your faults; remain vigilant even when there is no cause for alarm”—redouble your efforts without slackening. Then what is called “Heaven’s favor and the people’s allegiance, bringing glory to your predecessors and abundance to your successors” will all be attained through this. The flourishing of concord, prosperity, and great harmony likewise depends upon this. How could it amount merely to what is called “hoping that Tang’s descendant may attain excellent and tranquil government”?

Yet Your Majesty has also spoken of this before, in the words “Let conduct accord with speech, and let the end be like the beginning.” Your servant speaks of it again because Fu Yue also said in his reply to Gaozong: “Knowing is not difficult; putting knowledge into practice is difficult. If the king is sincere, it will not be difficult, and he will truly accord with the perfected virtue of the former kings. If I, Yue, do not speak, the fault will be mine.” This is why your servant reiterates this point at the close of his essay. Your servant is truly benighted and without knowledge; this is merely my earnest personal wish to offer something of use, like one offering humble celery or the warmth of the sun. I humbly beseech Your Majesty to take care to the very end and diligently put this into practice, without neglect. This would truly be…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
臣李璣
臣對臣聞帝王之於天下其創之也以仁其守之也亦以
仁而仁之為道有四焉曰公曰儉曰寬曰敏廣大而溥是
之謂公節制而當是之謂儉宏裕而容是之謂寬奮勵而
勇是之謂敏公則澤周儉則利溢寬則恩流敏則效著四
者合而成仁天德備矣天德備而法形王道章矣夫德之
備者可與語神神妙而應速焉夫道之章者可與語化化
達而績凝焉道洽政治民心日益懷而德盛業新邦基日
益固享國長久之道孰謂不在於此哉何也國保於民民
安而國自壽焉耳民保於仁仁普而民自安焉耳茍弗公
而僻其失也私弗儉而貪其失也侈弗寬而忍其失也刻
===
弗敏而徇其失也怠仁之實壅而民之心離矣天下可得
而強制之乎故創業而非仁弗可以創也守成而非仁弗
可以守也良法要道信莫有過於此者稽之於古驗之於
今又何有不然者哉臣跧伏草野學識疎淺豈曰素閑於
王政然志於用世講聞此說亦久矣每欲自獻而無由乃
今叨有司之薦
陛下進之廷而寵以問焉且勉令罄所知以告臣敢不披瀝素
所欲吐以效其一得之愚乎臣伏讀
聖制首以歷代享國之永繼以
祖宗創造之艱終之以求良法要道思育民物保洪業於無疆
夫欲仰纘

punctuated:
臣李璣。
臣對：臣聞帝王之於天下，其創之也以仁，其守之也亦以仁。而仁之為道有四焉：曰公，曰儉，曰寬，曰敏。廣大而溥，是之謂公；節制而當，是之謂儉；宏裕而容，是之謂寬；奮勵而勇，是之謂敏。公則澤周，儉則利溢，寬則恩流，敏則效著。四者合而成仁，天德備矣；天德備而法形，王道章矣。夫德之備者，可與語神，神妙而應速焉；夫道之章者，可與語化，化達而績凝焉。道洽政治，民心日益懷，而德盛業新，邦基日益固。享國長久之道，孰謂不在於此哉？何也？國保於民，民安而國自壽焉耳；民保於仁，仁普而民自安焉耳。茍弗公而僻，其失也私；弗儉而貪，其失也侈；弗寬而忍，其失也刻；弗敏而徇，其失也怠。仁之實壅，而民之心離矣，天下可得而強制之乎？故創業而非仁，弗可以創也；守成而非仁，弗可以守也。良法要道，信莫有過於此者。稽之於古，驗之於今，又何有不然者哉？
臣跧伏草野，學識疎淺，豈曰素閑於王政？然志於用世，講聞此說亦久矣。每欲自獻而無由，乃今叨有司之薦，陛下進之廷而寵以問焉，且勉令罄所知以告。臣敢不披瀝素所欲吐，以效其一得之愚乎？臣伏讀聖制，首以歷代享國之永，繼以祖宗創造之艱，終之以求良法要道，思育民物，保洪業於無疆。夫欲仰纘
translation_en:
Your servant, Li Ji.
Your servant replies: I have heard that sovereigns establish their rule over All-under-Heaven through benevolence, and preserve it likewise through benevolence. The Way of benevolence has four aspects: impartiality, frugality, forbearance, and diligence. To be broad and all-embracing is called impartiality; to exercise restraint appropriately is called frugality; to be magnanimous and accommodating is called forbearance; to exert oneself with courage is called diligence. Impartiality makes blessings universal; frugality makes benefits abundant; forbearance allows kindness to flow; diligence makes results manifest. These four together constitute benevolence, and thus the virtue of Heaven is complete. When the virtue of Heaven is complete and takes form in institutions, the Kingly Way becomes manifest. With one whose virtue is complete, one may discuss spiritual efficacy: its workings are wondrous and its responses swift. With one whose Way is manifest, one may discuss transformation: its influence reaches everywhere and its achievements become firmly established. As the Way pervades and government is well ordered, the people's hearts grow ever more attached; as virtue flourishes and accomplishments are renewed, the foundations of the state grow ever firmer. Who could say that the means of prolonging a dynasty's rule does not lie here? Why is this so? The state is preserved through the people: when the people are at peace, the state naturally endures. The people are preserved through benevolence: when benevolence extends everywhere, the people naturally enjoy peace. If one is partial rather than impartial, the failing is selfishness; if greedy rather than frugal, the failing is extravagance; if cruel rather than forbearing, the failing is harshness; if yielding to indulgence rather than diligent, the failing is indolence. When the substance of benevolence is obstructed and the people's hearts become estranged, can All-under-Heaven be held by force? Thus, without benevolence an undertaking cannot be founded, nor can an established achievement be preserved. Truly, no sound institutions or essential principles surpass this. Examining antiquity and testing it against the present, where could it prove otherwise?
Your servant has lived obscurely in the countryside, and my learning and understanding are shallow. How could I claim long familiarity with kingly government? Yet I aspire to serve the age, and have long discussed and heard this teaching. I have often wished to present myself in service but had no means to do so. Now, through the undeserved recommendation of the responsible officials, Your Majesty has brought me into the court and honored me with questions, further encouraging me to report all that I know. How could I dare not lay bare what I have long wished to express, offering the one insight that even my foolishness may possess? I have reverently read Your Majesty's decree. It begins with the long duration of past dynasties, proceeds to the difficulties your ancestors faced in founding this dynasty, and concludes by seeking sound institutions and essential principles, with the intention of nurturing the people and all things and preserving the great imperial enterprise without end. Now, to wish reverently to carry forward…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
先緒大孝也俯育民物至仁也道已至而望若未見至謙也持
此以為天下何所不濟臣請為
陛下陳之以備采擇之萬一幸容其愚妄而試聴之臣嘗謂得
天下無他存乎民心焉爾矣得民心無他存乎仁焉爾矣
究夫所以為仁亦大略如臣所言四者而已矣四者備而
民心不我附焉未之有也民心附而天下不我有焉亦未
之有也創業守成均之不可舍乎此臣請即以
聖制享祚最乆如周者證之可乎夫周之有國自后稷封邰始
及文武而後天下定于一其積功累仁由来有漸而周公
夾輔之力亦不可誣也觀乎周官六典與夫詩書之所稱
者渢渢乎一至仁之流行至今言治者稽焉故即其不泄
===
邇不忘遠可以知其公九式制用而日成月要歲會有攷
可以知其儉三典詰姦而平以八議三赦可以知其寬日
中昃不暇洛水講武不廢可以知其敏仁以經政政以顯仁
而民之衣被其休要非一日之積矣况其嗣世賢君迭作
而於所謂公儉寬敏者曾不少改其繩墨其間基命無逸
如成王率循對揚如康王車攻復古雲漢憂民如宣王者
盛而能傳尤不可以多見是則關雎麟趾之仁奕世彌光
固不獨見諸創造者然也夫惟其創之者仁則植本固而
發源深憑藉有其地而守之以仁則先德廣而遺澤遠上
之所以結其下者為益固是以下逮赧元諸君雖威令久
矣不伸於天下而天下依依不忍叛去者以有此具也傳

punctuated:
先緒，大孝也；俯育民物，至仁也；道已至而望若未見，至謙也。持此以為天下，何所不濟？臣請為陛下陳之，以備采擇之萬一，幸容其愚妄而試聴之。
臣嘗謂得天下無他，存乎民心焉爾矣；得民心無他，存乎仁焉爾矣。究夫所以為仁，亦大略如臣所言四者而已矣。四者備而民心不我附焉，未之有也；民心附而天下不我有焉，亦未之有也。創業守成，均之不可舍乎此。臣請即以聖制享祚最乆如周者證之，可乎？夫周之有國，自后稷封邰始，及文武而後天下定于一。其積功累仁，由来有漸，而周公夾輔之力亦不可誣也。觀乎《周官》六典與夫《詩》《書》之所稱者，渢渢乎一至仁之流行，至今言治者稽焉。故即其不泄邇、不忘遠，可以知其公；九式制用，而日成、月要、歲會有攷，可以知其儉；三典詰姦，而平以八議、三赦，可以知其寬；日中昃不暇，洛水講武不廢，可以知其敏。仁以經政，政以顯仁，而民之衣被其休，要非一日之積矣。况其嗣世賢君迭作，而於所謂公儉寬敏者，曾不少改其繩墨。其間基命無逸如成王，率循對揚如康王，車攻復古、雲漢憂民如宣王者，盛而能傳，尤不可以多見。是則《關雎》《麟趾》之仁，奕世彌光，固不獨見諸創造者然也。夫惟其創之者仁，則植本固而發源深，憑藉有其地；而守之以仁，則先德廣而遺澤遠，上之所以結其下者為益固。是以下逮赧元諸君，雖威令久矣不伸於天下，而天下依依不忍叛去者，以有此具也。傳
translation_en:
…the legacy of one’s forebears is great filial piety; to nurture the people and all living things below is supreme benevolence; to have attained the Way yet look toward it as though it remained unseen is supreme humility. With these principles employed in governing the realm, what could not be accomplished? I beg leave to set forth my views for Your Majesty, in the hope that some small part may merit selection. May you indulge my foolish presumption and give them a hearing.
I have always maintained that winning the realm depends on nothing other than the hearts of the people, and winning the hearts of the people depends on nothing other than benevolence. Examining how benevolence is practiced, it amounts broadly to the four qualities I have mentioned. Never has anyone possessed all four yet failed to gain the people’s allegiance; nor has anyone gained their allegiance yet failed to possess the realm. Neither founding a dynasty nor preserving its achievements can dispense with these. May I offer as evidence the Zhou, which your sagely decree mentions as enjoying an exceptionally long dynastic tenure?
The Zhou possession of a state began when Hou Ji was enfeoffed at Tai; only with Kings Wen and Wu was the realm finally united. Their accumulation of meritorious deeds and benevolence was a gradual process of long standing, and the assistance rendered by the Duke of Zhou cannot be denied. Looking at the six codes in the Offices of Zhou and what is celebrated in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents, one sees supreme benevolence flowing abundantly throughout. To this day, those who discuss government consult them. Their neither slighting those nearby nor forgetting those far away reveals their impartiality. Their regulation of expenditure through the nine standards, with daily accounts, monthly summaries, and annual audits available for scrutiny, reveals their frugality. Their punishment of wrongdoing through the three penal codes, tempered by the eight grounds for deliberation and the three grounds for pardon, reveals their leniency. Their having no leisure even as the sun declined past noon, and their maintaining military exercises by the Luo River, reveals their diligence. Benevolence ordered their government, and their government manifested benevolence. The blessings that clothed and sheltered the people were certainly not the accumulation of a single day.
Moreover, worthy rulers arose successively in later generations, never departing in the slightest from the standards of impartiality, frugality, leniency, and diligence. Among them were King Cheng, who consolidated the mandate and shunned ease; King Kang, who followed established precedents and extolled the legacy he had received; and King Xuan, who restored ancient practices, as in “Chariots Are Strong,” and showed concern for the people, as in “The Milky Way.” Such rulers, who flourished and could transmit their achievements, are especially rare. Thus the benevolence expressed in “The Ospreys” and “The Qilin’s Hoofs” shone ever more brightly through successive generations; it was certainly not manifested solely by the founders.
Because the founders were benevolent, they planted firm roots and established deep sources, providing a foundation upon which their successors could rely. When their successors preserved the dynasty through benevolence, the virtue of their forebears was extended and its beneficent legacy reached far. The bonds by which rulers attached their subjects to themselves became still stronger. Thus, even down to such rulers as Nan and Yuan [?], although their authority and commands had long ceased to prevail throughout the realm, the people remained attached to them and could not bear to rebel and abandon them, because this foundation remained. It was transmitted …

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
世三十歷年八百夫豈適然哉然前之曰夏曰商均之享
國之永者而詳考其故亦仁焉耳矣是故下車泣罪于患
困窮禹湯之仁既已素浹於民心而其嗣王如啓仲康大
甲盤庚中宗高宗者又能嗣守先訓敬承而懋戒焉允德
而敷德焉寅畏而恭默焉雖欲不謂之仁不可也此其創
守一道亦有以綿國祚之永至令言享國者必與成周並
誦於世而不衰是則創守必以仁者三代共之豈非彰灼
之大效也哉孟軻曰三代之得天下也以仁是可明其所
由創又曰其失天下也以不仁則其守之必以仁也自可
類推矣嗣是而漢而唐而宋雖非秦晉五代所能及而槩
以三代則未焉蓋漢高之豁達唐大宗之愛人宋祖之忠
===
厚庶幾仁以創業矣然漢高雜霸也大宗雜夷也宋祖武
畧不競也果有如三代之所創者乎文景之恭儉玄默玄
憲之勵精剛明真仁之簡易仁恕庶幾仁以守成矣然文
景溺於異端也玄憲鮮克有終也真仁剛勇不足也果有
如三代之所守者乎夫是以即其得仁之似固足壽其國
而仁有未純求如三代之盛且久不可也故臣嘗遡而考
之則漢唐宋之享祚俱不及三代析而觀之則唐宋享祚不
及漢漢之享祚不及夏商夏商享祚不及周故曰三代有
道之長又曰惟周之歷世最久國祚恒永而漢唐宋無稱
焉夏商周漢唐宋所以享祚之永者非倖也同乎其仁也
制所謂基於先王德澤洽於民心亦繼以嗣王能盡持盈慎

世三十，歷年八百，夫豈適然哉？然前之曰夏曰商，均之享國之永者，而詳考其故，亦仁焉耳矣。是故下車泣罪，于患困窮，禹湯之仁既已素浹於民心，而其嗣王如啓、仲康、大甲、盤庚、中宗、高宗者，又能嗣守先訓，敬承而懋戒焉，允德而敷德焉，寅畏而恭默焉，雖欲不謂之仁，不可也。此其創守一道，亦有以綿國祚之永，至令言享國者必與成周並誦於世而不衰。是則創守必以仁者，三代共之，豈非彰灼之大效也哉？孟軻曰：「三代之得天下也以仁。」是可明其所由創。又曰：「其失天下也以不仁。」則其守之必以仁也，自可類推矣。

嗣是而漢而唐而宋，雖非秦晉五代所能及，而槩以三代則未焉。蓋漢高之豁達，唐大宗之愛人，宋祖之忠厚，庶幾仁以創業矣。然漢高雜霸也，大宗雜夷也，宋祖武畧不競也，果有如三代之所創者乎？文景之恭儉玄默，玄憲之勵精剛明，真仁之簡易仁恕，庶幾仁以守成矣。然文景溺於異端也，玄憲鮮克有終也，真仁剛勇不足也，果有如三代之所守者乎？夫是以即其得仁之似，固足壽其國，而仁有未純，求如三代之盛且久，不可也。故臣嘗遡而考之，則漢唐宋之享祚俱不及三代；析而觀之，則唐宋享祚不及漢，漢之享祚不及夏商，夏商享祚不及周。故曰：「三代有道之長。」又曰：「惟周之歷世最久，國祚恒永。」而漢唐宋無稱焉。夏商周漢唐宋所以享祚之永者，非倖也，同乎其仁也。制所謂「基於先王德澤洽於民心，亦繼以嗣王能盡持盈慎
translation_en:
…for thirty generations and eight hundred years: could this possibly have been mere chance? Yet the earlier Xia and Shang likewise enjoyed long possession of the realm. Examining the reasons closely, we find that these too amounted simply to benevolence. Thus, through such acts as descending from the carriage to weep over an offender and showing concern for those in distress and poverty [?], the benevolence of Yu and Tang had already thoroughly permeated the people’s hearts. Their successors, such as Qi, Zhongkang, Tai Jia, Pan Geng, Zhongzong, and Gaozong, continued to uphold their predecessors’ instructions: reverently receiving them and diligently exercising caution, practicing genuine virtue and spreading it abroad, and remaining respectfully apprehensive and reverently silent. Even if one wished to deny that this was benevolence, one could not. Their founding and preservation of the dynasty followed a single Way, thereby prolonging its fortunes. Down to the present, anyone discussing long possession of the realm invariably praises them alongside Zhou, and this praise has never faded. Thus the necessity of benevolence in both founding and preserving a dynasty was common to the Three Dynasties. Is this not a conspicuously great demonstration of its efficacy? Meng Ke said, “The Three Dynasties gained All-under-Heaven through benevolence.” This makes clear how they founded their rule. He also said, “They lost All-under-Heaven through a lack of benevolence.” That preserving their rule likewise required benevolence can readily be inferred.

After them came Han, Tang, and Song. Although Qin, Jin, and the Five Dynasties could not match them, measured against the Three Dynasties they fell short. The magnanimity of Gaozu of Han, the love for others of Taizong of Tang, and the loyalty and generosity of the founding emperor of Song came close to founding a dynasty through benevolence. Yet Gaozu of Han mingled his rule with the methods of a hegemon; Taizong mingled his with barbarian ways; and the founding emperor of Song lacked strength in military strategy. Did their founding achievements truly equal those of the Three Dynasties? The reverence, frugality, and quiet reserve of Emperors Wen and Jing; the diligent resolve, firmness, and discernment of Xuanzong and Xianzong; and the simplicity, benevolence, and forbearance of Zhenzong and Renzong came close to preserving an established dynasty through benevolence. Yet Wen and Jing were immersed in heterodox teachings; Xuanzong and Xianzong failed to sustain a good course to the end; and Zhenzong and Renzong lacked firmness and courage. Did their preservation of the dynasty truly equal that of the Three Dynasties? Thus, even their attainment of a semblance of benevolence was sufficient to prolong their states. But because their benevolence was not pure, they could not hope to equal the Three Dynasties in both prosperity and duration. Your servant has therefore traced back and examined their histories: the dynastic fortunes of Han, Tang, and Song all lasted less long than those of the Three Dynasties. Considered separately, Tang and Song lasted less long than Han; Han less long than Xia and Shang; and Xia and Shang less long than Zhou. Hence the sayings, “The Three Dynasties long possessed the Way,” and “Zhou alone endured for the greatest number of generations, its dynastic fortunes lasting perpetually.” Han, Tang, and Song receive no mention in these sayings. That Xia, Shang, Zhou, Han, Tang, and Song enjoyed long dynastic fortunes was no accident: they shared benevolence. This is what the Emperor’s decree means by “being founded upon the former kings’ virtue and beneficence, which permeated the people’s hearts, and being continued by succeeding kings who could fully uphold prosperity and exercise caution…”

所以為仁也
聖制所謂歷世有久近而其君之歷年亦有長短要之皆自其
為君者何如是已向使漢唐宋之創守者純乎其仁焉於
臣之所謂公儉寬敏者無歉焉則民罔常懷懷于有仁常
厥德保厥位雖八百其曆亦可也復何享國不及於周耶
陛下兼舉漢唐宋以為問而獨詳於周臣知

為
陛下詳之而我
國家行將與天地相為無疆亦非可望以漢唐宋者也然豈
獨不屑於後世而已哉臣之於周亦每喜其創者之善而
竊悲其守之不常成康也何者創業雖由於先王而其守
之常賴於後世失於守而後創之者終也使周之嗣王世
守其仁焉舉無愧於成康之際焉則周雖至今存可也詎
止八百年已乎故曰道非亡也幽厲不繇也有天下者亦
可以監矣欽惟

滿之道者是已。漢唐宋享祚不及三代者，非他也，異乎其所以為仁也。聖制所謂歷世有久近，而其君之歷年亦有長短，要之皆自其為君者何如，是已。向使漢唐宋之創守者純乎其仁焉，於臣之所謂公儉寬敏者無歉焉，則民罔常懷，懷于有仁；常厥德，保厥位，雖八百其曆亦可也，復何享國不及於周耶？
陛下兼舉漢唐宋以為問，而獨詳於周，臣知聖意有所擇而不屑乎此。且區區駁雜如漢唐宋者，臣固不欲為陛下詳之，而我國家行將與天地相為無疆，亦非可望以漢唐宋者也。然豈獨不屑於後世而已哉？臣之於周，亦每喜其創者之善，而竊悲其守之不常成康也。何者？創業雖由於先王，而其守之常賴於後世；失於守，而後創之者終也。使周之嗣王世守其仁焉，舉無愧於成康之際焉，則周雖至今存可也，詎止八百年已乎？故曰：「道非亡也，幽厲不繇也。」有天下者亦可以監矣。
欽惟太祖高皇帝奉天理民，攘夷安夏，敷錫皇極，肇造丕基。當時之民之苦於元者，不啻脫水火而就諸衽席。其至仁天覆，難徧以疏舉。姑自其一二言之：罰不昵近，賞不遺遠，則載諸《大誥》；宮漏必碎，鞍轡必却，則紀諸
translation_en:
…the way of sustaining fullness and guarding against complacency: this is precisely what is meant. That the Han, Tang, and Song enjoyed shorter dynastic mandates than the Three Dynasties had no other cause than differences in how they practiced benevolence. Your Majesty’s sacred decree speaks of dynasties enduring for longer or shorter spans, and their rulers likewise reigning for longer or shorter periods, concluding that all depends upon what sort of rulers they were. This is precisely the point. Had the founders and successors of the Han, Tang, and Song been pure in their benevolence, lacking nothing in what your servant has called impartiality, frugality, generosity, and diligence, then, since “the people have no constant attachment, but attach themselves to those who possess benevolence,” they could have “made their virtue constant and preserved their throne.” Even a span of eight hundred years would have been possible. Why, then, should their dynasties have endured less long than the Zhou?
Your Majesty has included the Han, Tang, and Song in your question, yet has treated the Zhou alone in detail. Your servant knows that your sagely intention is discerning in its choice and disdains these lesser examples. Indeed, your servant would not wish to expound for Your Majesty upon such limited and impure achievements as those of the Han, Tang, and Song. Our dynasty is destined to endure without limit alongside Heaven and Earth; the Han, Tang, and Song cannot furnish the measure of its prospects. Yet is it only these later ages that merit disdain? As for the Zhou, your servant has often rejoiced in the excellence of its founders, yet privately grieved that its successors did not consistently equal Kings Cheng and Kang. Why is this? Although founding a dynasty is the work of earlier kings, its continued preservation depends upon later generations. Only when they fail to preserve it does the founders’ achievement come to an end. Had the succeeding kings of Zhou maintained their benevolence generation after generation, all measuring up to the age of Cheng and Kang, the Zhou might have survived even to the present. Why should it have lasted merely eight hundred years? Thus it is said: “The Way had not perished; Kings You and Li did not follow it.” Those who possess all under Heaven may take warning from this.
Reverently considering Emperor Taizu Gao: he obeyed Heaven and governed the people, drove back the barbarians and brought peace to the Chinese realm, widely bestowed the supreme standard of rule, and established the great dynastic foundation. For the people then suffering under the Yuan, it was nothing less than escaping flood and fire and being settled upon comfortable bedding. His consummate benevolence sheltered all like Heaven; it is difficult to enumerate its manifestations exhaustively. Let me speak of just one or two. 《聖政》。納詹同之奏，至取刑具焚之，而造福緩刑之戒則嚴諸《祖訓》。閑暇則閱經史，便殿則閱奏牘，而皇陵一碑又諄諄乎締造勤勞之由，以示後焉。是其仁儉寬敏，軒越往古，雖周莫或過之，而漢唐宋之創者不足望其萬一矣。繼而太宗潤色於草昧之初，列聖嗣興於守文之日，深仁厚澤漸被寰宇，百六十餘年如一日焉。天下之人亦如赤子之於父母而不忍釋者哉！國家億萬年無疆之休，不在此乎？
陛下臨御以来，深惟民瘼，凡積年之弊，又一洗而重新之。與天下相為休息之政，天下固已囿於皇仁之中，而莫知所為之者。而陛下策臣乃曰：「朕幼弱不才，多招災害于民。兹来思祖宗創造萬艱，惕然悚惧。朕欲長保洪業於無窮，有隆弗替，永宗社萬禩之固，保家國千世之傳，民得以遂生，物得以適所。如上之良法要道，朕心慕之思之，不知何以得此。」
陛下之言及此，天地神人之福也。此天下所願少須臾無死，以待德化之成者。臣雖庸譾，奚容以自黙？况遭逢有此，又可以肆其狂瞽而無所虞於罪者，敢不思所以副休命之一二乎？臣竊謂民者邦之本，仁者誠民永命之要道。非天下之至仁，不足以創業；非天下之至仁，亦不足以守成。且歴代
translation_en:
…the Record of Sagely Governance (Shengzheng). He accepted Zhan Tong’s memorial, even having instruments of punishment brought out and burned; and the admonitions concerning the conferring of blessings and the mitigation of punishments were strictly set forth in the Ancestral Instructions (Zuxun). In his leisure he read the classics and histories; in his private audience hall he read memorials. The inscription at the imperial mausoleum likewise earnestly recounted the toil involved in founding the dynasty, to instruct posterity. His benevolence, frugality, generosity, and diligence thus surpassed antiquity. Even the Zhou could not exceed him, while the founders of the Han, Tang, and Song could not aspire to one ten-thousandth of his achievement. Thereafter, Taizong refined the institutions of the dynasty’s unsettled beginnings, and successive sage sovereigns arose to preserve its established order. Profound benevolence and abundant favor gradually spread throughout the realm, remaining constant for more than 160 years. Were not the people of the realm like infants with their parents, unable to bear separation? Does not the state’s boundless prosperity for countless ages rest upon this?
Since ascending the throne, Your Majesty has given deep consideration to the people’s sufferings, sweeping away longstanding abuses and renewing affairs. Through policies that allow the realm rest and recuperation, all under Heaven have already been enfolded within imperial benevolence, without knowing who has brought this about. Yet in your policy question to your servant, Your Majesty says: “Young, weak, and lacking ability, I have brought many calamities upon the people. Lately, reflecting on the myriad hardships my ancestors endured in founding the dynasty, I tremble with apprehension. I wish to preserve this great enterprise forever, ensuring that it flourishes without decline; to secure the ancestral temples and altars of state for ten thousand years; and to ensure the transmission of the ruling house and state for a thousand generations, so that the people may fulfill their lives and all beings find their proper places. My heart admires and ponders the excellent methods and essential principles described above, but I do not know how to attain this.”
That Your Majesty should speak thus is a blessing for Heaven and Earth, spirits and people alike. This is what makes all under Heaven wish to be spared death a little longer, so that they may await the fulfillment of your moral transformation. Though your servant is mediocre and shallow, how could I permit myself to remain silent? Moreover, having encountered such an opportunity, when I may freely express my rash and unenlightened views without fear of punishment, how could I fail to consider how to fulfill even a small part of your gracious command? Your servant humbly holds that the people are the foundation of the state, and that benevolence is the essential way to win the people’s allegiance [?] and perpetuate Heaven’s mandate. Without the utmost benevolence in the realm, one cannot found a dynasty; without the utmost benevolence in the realm, neither can one preserve its accomplishments. 國家靈長之祚終必賴之於臣所謂四者復何議焉但自邇
===
者觀之
陛下愛民之心雖不少衰而弊端之在天下或已漸形而亦不
可不為之所者臣不暇毛舉其細而其大且急者則一曰
藩封之禄未理一曰工作之興大濫一曰刑罰失平一曰軍
伍不充四弊不去臣不敢欺
陛下以為果無所歉於仁也是則
陛下雖有仁天下之實心天下且得以其迹而議於
陛下矣何以言之蓋
藩封之禄未理民且以為私工作之興大濫民且以為侈刑
罰失平民且以為刻軍伍不充民且以為怠是
陛下雖無其心不幸已有其迹亦安能以其迹而自解於天下

臣仰見
陛下大德旁敷日照而月臨夙夤盡朔風飛而雷厲柔遠能邇
好惡予奪之不私親耕親蠶蠲租禁奢之有
詔疑獄必覆讞而減刑之使一歲一行視朝有常規而奏牘
之繁隨入隨閱盛德美政莫可殫述天下固已訢訢然決
聖主而
國家靈長之祚終必賴之於臣所謂四者復何議焉但自邇
===
者觀之
陛下愛民之心雖不少衰而弊端之在天下或已漸形而亦不
可不為之所者臣不暇毛舉其細而其大且急者則一曰
藩封之祿未理一曰工作之興大濫一曰刑罰失平一曰軍
伍不充四弊不去臣不敢欺
陛下以為果無所歉於仁也是則
陛下雖有仁天下之實心天下且得以其迹而辭於
陛下矣何以言之蓋
藩封之祿未理民且以為私工作之興大濫民且以為侈刑
罰失平民且以為刻軍伍不充民且以為怠是
陛下雖無其心不幸已有其迹亦安能以其迹而自解於天下
punctuated:
創守之故，臣已畧陳其槩，有足徴也。然則又奚俟於遠求哉？陛下欲保祖宗之業，亦惟思固民心而已耳；欲固民心，亦惟法祖廣仁而已耳。所謂廣仁者，毋亦於公儉寛敏加之意而已。然臣仰見陛下大德旁敷，日照而月臨；夙蠹盡剔，風飛而雷厲。柔遠能邇，好惡予奪之不私；親耕親蠶，蠲租禁奢之有詔；疑獄必覆讞，而减刑之使一歲一行；視朝有常規，而奏牘之繁隨入隨閲。盛德美政，莫可殫述。天下固已訢訢然决聖主，而國家靈長之祚終必賴之。於臣所謂四者，復何議焉？

但自邇者觀之，陛下愛民之心雖不少衰，而弊端之在天下，或已漸形，而亦不可不為之所者。臣不暇毛舉其細，而其大且急者，則一曰藩封之禄未理，一曰工作之興大濫，一曰刑罰失平，一曰軍伍不充。四弊不去，臣不敢欺陛下，以為果無所歉於仁也。是則陛下雖有仁天下之實心，天下且得以其迹而議於陛下矣。何以言之？蓋藩封之禄未理，民且以為私；工作之興大濫，民且以為侈；刑罰失平，民且以為刻；軍伍不充，民且以為怠。是陛下雖無其心，不幸已有其迹，亦安能以其迹而自解於天下？
translation_en:
…As for the circumstances of founding and preserving dynasties, your servant has already briefly set out their general outlines, providing sufficient evidence. Why, then, need one seek further afield? If Your Majesty wishes to preserve the enterprise of your ancestors, you need only consider how to secure the people's allegiance. To secure their allegiance, you need only emulate your ancestors and extend your benevolence. Extending benevolence means simply giving greater attention to impartiality, frugality, leniency, and diligence. Yet your servant respectfully observes that Your Majesty's great virtue spreads everywhere, illuminating like the sun and overlooking all like the moon; longstanding abuses are entirely rooted out, with the swiftness of wind and the force of thunder. You soothe those far away and bring those nearby into harmony, showing no partiality in your likes and dislikes, grants and deprivations. There are the personal performance of plowing and sericulture, and edicts remitting taxes and prohibiting extravagance. Doubtful criminal cases must undergo further review, and envoys charged with reducing sentences are dispatched once each year. Court audiences follow established procedures, and the numerous memorials are read as they arrive. Your magnificent virtue and admirable government cannot be exhaustively recounted. All under Heaven already rejoice in their sage sovereign [?], and the state's enduring good fortune must ultimately depend upon him. What further criticism could there be concerning the four qualities your servant has mentioned?

Judging by recent circumstances, however, although Your Majesty's love for the people has not diminished in the slightest, abuses within the realm may already be gradually taking shape, and these too must be dealt with. Your servant has no leisure to enumerate every minor instance. The major and urgent ones are these: first, the stipends of the enfeoffed princes have not been properly regulated; second, construction projects are undertaken with excessive prodigality; third, punishments lack equity; and fourth, military units are below strength. Unless these four abuses are removed, your servant dares not deceive Your Majesty by claiming that there is indeed no shortcoming in benevolence. Thus, although Your Majesty sincerely desires to treat all under Heaven benevolently, the realm will nevertheless be able to criticize Your Majesty on the evidence of these outward manifestations. Why do I say this? When the princes' stipends are not properly regulated, the people will regard it as partiality; when construction projects are undertaken with excessive prodigality, they will regard it as extravagance; when punishments lack equity, they will regard it as cruelty; and when military units are below strength, they will regard it as negligence. Thus, although Your Majesty has no such intentions, unfortunately their outward manifestations already exist. With such manifestations, how can you clear yourself before all under Heaven?…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
欲為國家綿久遠之福而此等不之釐臣不可得而知也
有以釐之而民復不遂其生物復不適其所者臣未之信
也臣請得熟數於前以為
陛下持盈慎滿之一助何謂
藩封之祿未理臣聞王政莫先於親親而親之欲貴愛之欲
富者此亦人情之自然故
祖宗時廣建
宗藩豐其祿秩者非以天下為私奉直以行其親愛富貴之
心耳且當時支派未盛固不容豫為之限亦曰後世自有
增節者今則支派之盛大非昔比而
宗藩之需動稱不足及今不為之計數世之後天下將益耗
===
竭而不可救何者上人之祿下民之膏脂也支派之盛日
增而田野之賦有限以有限之賦而周日增之祿其勢必
至於病民非仁也以日增之祿而制以有限之賦其勢必
至於儉親非孝也
陛下以仁孝治天下者何取於此臣願
陛下申明舊例制其妾御之數其有不如例者許有司舉劾以
聞一斷以法則其勢自不容於或濫至其諸不在五服之限
者聽其明經應舉祿之以官而又限之位若
藩親不使內補者然矣服制既遠則其相臨也便限之以位
則其制抑也周雖有懷三窟之異志者亦自戢而莫逞此
非惟祿可少殺而或亦誘之向善之一機括也如此則親

增飾者今則支派之盛大非昔比而

至於偸親非孝也
陛下以仁孝治天下者何取於此臣願
陛下申明舊例制其妄御之數其有不如例者許有司舉劾以
聞一斷以法則其勢自不容於或濫至其諸不在五服之限
者聽其明經應舉祿之以官而又限之位居
藩親不使內補者然夫服制既遠則其相臨也便限之以位
則其制御也周雖有懷二家之舉志者亦自戢而莫逞此
非惟祿可少殺而或亦誘之向善之一機括也如此則親
punctuated:
欲為國家綿久遠之福，而此等不之釐，臣不可得而知也。有以釐之，而民復不遂其生、物復不適其所者，臣未之信也。臣請得熟數於前，以為陛下持盈慎滿之一助。
何謂藩封之祿未理？臣聞王政莫先於親親，而親之欲貴、愛之欲富者，此亦人情之自然。故祖宗時廣建宗藩，豐其祿秩者，非以天下為私奉，直以行其親愛富貴之心耳。且當時支派未盛，固不容豫為之限，亦曰後世自有增節者。今則支派之盛大非昔比，而宗藩之需動稱不足。及今不為之計，數世之後，天下將益耗竭而不可救。何者？上人之祿，下民之膏脂也。支派之盛日增，而田野之賦有限，以有限之賦而周日增之祿，其勢必至於病民，非仁也；以日增之祿而制以有限之賦，其勢必至於儉親，非孝也。陛下以仁孝治天下者，何取於此？臣願陛下申明舊例，制其妾御之數。其有不如例者，許有司舉劾以聞，一斷以法，則其勢自不容於或濫。至其諸不在五服之限者，聽其明經應舉，祿之以官，而又限之位，若藩親不使內補者然矣。服制既遠，則其相臨也便；限之以位，則其制抑也周。雖有懷三窟之異志者，亦自戢而莫逞。此非惟祿可少殺，而或亦誘之向善之一機括也。如此則親
translation_en:
…If one wishes to secure enduring blessings for the state yet leaves these matters unrectified, your servant cannot understand how this could be achieved. If they were rectified, I do not believe that the people would still fail to obtain their livelihood or that other living things would still fail to find their proper places. I beg leave to enumerate these matters fully before Your Majesty, as an aid to preserving prosperity and exercising caution at its height.
What do I mean by saying that the stipends of the enfeoffed princes have not been properly regulated? Your servant has heard that, in kingly government, nothing takes precedence over affection for one's kin. To wish those to whom one is close to enjoy honor, and those whom one loves to enjoy wealth, is natural to human feeling. Thus, when the imperial ancestors established princely houses far and wide and endowed them with generous stipends, they were not treating the realm as a source of private support; they were simply giving effect to their desire to bestow wealth and honor upon their beloved kin. Moreover, at that time the branches of the imperial lineage were not yet numerous, so limits could hardly have been imposed in advance. It was also assumed that later generations would make additions or reductions as appropriate. Now, however, the proliferation of these branches is incomparably greater than before, and the princely houses constantly declare that their provision is insufficient for their needs. Unless plans are made now, within a few generations the realm will become ever more depleted, beyond remedy. Why? The stipends of those above are the very lifeblood of the common people below. The branches of the lineage multiply daily, while the revenue from the fields is limited. To meet ever-growing stipends from limited revenue must inevitably distress the people: this is not benevolence. To constrain ever-growing stipends within limited revenue must inevitably mean stinting one's kin: this is not filial piety. Your Majesty governs the realm through benevolence and filial piety; what could commend either course?
Your servant wishes Your Majesty to reaffirm the established regulations and restrict the number of their concubines and attendant women. Where anyone contravenes these regulations, permit the responsible officials to submit an impeachment for Your Majesty's information, and adjudicate every case according to law. Excess would then naturally become impossible. As for those whose kinship falls outside the five degrees of mourning, allow them to demonstrate their mastery of the Classics and compete in the examinations, receiving stipends through official appointments, while also restricting the offices they may hold—as with the rule that imperial relatives of the princely houses may not be appointed to posts in the capital [?]. Since their mourning relationship is already distant, it would be practicable for them to exercise authority over one another; restrictions on their offices would provide comprehensive control. Even those harboring disloyal designs of securing ‘three burrows’—multiple refuges for themselves—would restrain themselves and find no opportunity to act. This would not only permit some reduction in stipends; it might also provide a means of encouraging them toward goodness. In this way, affection for one's kin…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
親仁民一舉兩得庶幾不嫌於私而仁可以廣矣何謂工
作之興太濫臣聞國家舉事非財不濟而財非取之於民
不可是故聖王慎於造作非獨裕後且欲貽民以富耳今
陛下自以為天下之財何如也西北之民飢餓輾轉而東南困
於征斂且告竭矣夫民之財可竭而不可繼也
陛下曾不是念大內之役前後相仍程督之使冠蓋相望於道
路近自畿甸遠而窮鄉下邑日擾擾焉奉行
明詔之不暇夫事係重要固有不可已者然於其間亦豈無
可已而不已者乎可已不已臣恐太倉之儲無幾矣萬一
他變突起復何以應之且天地生財止有此數不在官則
在民民貧不已不得不取諸民民貧不已不得不入於盜
===
今
陛下之民將入於盜矣奈何其不節費以裕民乎昔漢文帝惜
十家之產露臺中輟而唐太宗監亡秦之轍一殿不為當
時由之以致富庶至今使人稱明
陛下德配堯舜嘗陋二帝於不為者何獨於此焉不省也臣願
停無益之作寬罷敝之民則庶幾不鄰於侈而仁可以廣
矣何謂刑罰失平臣聞刑之為道輕者笞掠重者編伍其
尤重者抵死然裸體笞掠為辱已極仁人之所深隱者況
編伍乎況抵死乎此而不審甚非所為體天而愛人者也
書曰刑期無刑又曰與其殺不辜寧失不經正謂此耳今
天下奸吏納賄恣意出入以傷和氣且不暇計至如往者

可已而不已者乎可已不已臣恐大倉之儲無幾矣萬一
他變猝起復何以應之且天地生財止有此數不在官則
在民國貧不已不得不取諸民民貧不已不得不入於盜
===
今
陛下之民將入於盜矣柰何其不節費以裕民乎昔漢文帝惜
十家之產露臺中輟而唐太宗監亡秦之轍一殿不為當
時由之以致富庶至今使人稱明
陛下德配堯舜嘗陋二帝於不為者何獨於此焉不省也臣願
停無益之作寬罷繳之民則庶幾不鄰於侈而仁可以廣
矣何謂刑罰失平臣聞刑之為道輕者笞掠重者編伍其
尤重者抵死然裸體笞掠為辱已極仁人之所深隱者況
編伍乎況抵死乎此而不審甚非所為體天而愛人者也
書曰刑期無刑又曰與其殺不辜寧失不經正謂此耳今
天下獄吏納賄恣意出入以傷和氣且不暇計至如往者
punctuated:
親仁民，一舉兩得，庶幾不嫌於私，而仁可以廣矣。
何謂工作之興太濫？臣聞國家舉事，非財不濟，而財非取之於民不可。是故聖王慎於造作，非獨裕後，且欲貽民以富耳。今陛下自以為天下之財何如也？西北之民飢餓輾轉，而東南困於征斂，且告竭矣。夫民之財可竭而不可繼也。陛下曾不是念，大內之役前後相仍，程督之使冠蓋相望於道路，近自畿甸，遠而窮鄉下邑，日擾擾焉，奉行明詔之不暇。夫事係重要，固有不可已者，然於其間亦豈無可已而不已者乎？可已不已，臣恐太倉之儲無幾矣。萬一他變突起，復何以應之？且天地生財，止有此數，不在官則在民。民貧不已，不得不取諸民；民貧不已，不得不入於盜。今陛下之民將入於盜矣，奈何其不節費以裕民乎？昔漢文帝惜十家之產，露臺中輟；而唐太宗監亡秦之轍，一殿不為。當時由之以致富庶，至今使人稱明。陛下德配堯舜，嘗陋二帝於不為者，何獨於此焉不省也？臣願停無益之作，寬罷敝之民，則庶幾不鄰於侈，而仁可以廣矣。
何謂刑罰失平？臣聞刑之為道，輕者笞掠，重者編伍，其尤重者抵死。然裸體笞掠，為辱已極，仁人之所深隱者，況編伍乎？況抵死乎？此而不審，甚非所為體天而愛人者也。《書》曰：「刑期無刑。」又曰：「與其殺不辜，寧失不經。」正謂此耳。今天下奸吏納賄，恣意出入，以傷和氣，且不暇計。至如往者，
translation_en:
…show affection for one’s kin and benevolence toward the people, achieving both at a single stroke. Thus one might escape the suspicion of partiality and extend benevolence more widely.
What is meant by saying that construction projects are undertaken too freely? Your servant has heard that affairs of state cannot be accomplished without wealth, and that this wealth must be obtained from the people. Therefore, sage kings were cautious about construction, not merely to leave ample resources to their successors, but also to leave the people prosperous. What does Your Majesty now consider the condition of the realm’s wealth to be? The people of the northwest languish in hunger, while the southeast is oppressed by levies and is approaching exhaustion. The people’s wealth can be exhausted, but cannot continually be replenished. Yet Your Majesty gives no thought to this. Building works within the imperial palace follow one another without pause, and the caps and carriages of commissioners supervising their progress are continually in sight along the roads. From the nearby capital region to remote villages and small towns, people are thrown into daily turmoil, scarcely able to keep up with carrying out Your Majesty’s illustrious edicts. Certainly, some projects of great importance cannot be stopped. Yet can there be none among them that could be stopped but are not? If projects that could be stopped continue, your servant fears that little will remain in the Court of the Imperial Granaries’ reserves. Should some other emergency suddenly arise, how could it be met? Moreover, the wealth produced by Heaven and Earth is limited: what is not held by the government is held by the people. As the people’s poverty continues, further wealth must be taken from the people [?]; as their poverty continues, they cannot help turning to banditry. Your Majesty’s people are now on the verge of becoming bandits. Why, then, do you not reduce expenditure to provide them with abundance? In former times, Emperor Wen of Han, unwilling to expend the equivalent of ten households’ property, abandoned the building of the Dew Terrace. Emperor Taizong of Tang, taking warning from the course that had brought Qin to ruin, refrained from building even a single palace hall. These measures brought prosperity in their own times, and to this day people praise their enlightened rule. Your Majesty’s virtue matches that of Yao and Shun, and you have regarded these two emperors as inferior in what they left undone [?]. Why, in this matter alone, do you fail to reflect? Your servant asks that you halt unprofitable works and give relief to the exhausted people. Thus one might avoid approaching extravagance and extend benevolence more widely.
What is meant by saying that punishments have lost their fairness? Your servant has heard that, among punishments, the lighter involve beating and flogging, the heavier involve assignment to the military ranks, and the gravest entail death. Yet to be stripped naked and flogged is already humiliation in the extreme, something that deeply pains a benevolent person. How much more so assignment to the military ranks! How much more so death! To fail to examine such matters carefully is altogether inconsistent with embodying Heaven’s intentions and loving the people. The Book of Documents says: “Punishment aims at there being no punishment.” It also says: “Rather than kill the innocent, better to err by departing from the norm.” This is precisely what those words mean. Throughout the realm today, corrupt officials accept bribes and arbitrarily acquit or convict, thereby injuring the harmonious qi; there is scarcely time even to enumerate these abuses. As for what happened previously, …

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
臺省諸臣言事失當上干
天怒遂而放之而重論之誠是矣然原厥初心亦欲忠於為國
非敢有他志者但意見或少差耳今舉事一不當而竟棄
不復遂使悔過無門似亦非先王欽恤之道也且君之於
臣猶父之於子方子之為不善也父固不免於怒甚且撻
而逐之矣及其知悔而懲也則未有忍於終棄者然則
陛下獨能忍於終棄乎况及今不宥則遠者將死於邊近者將
死於獄矣
陛下果忍令後世謂此輩皆以言獲罪而死乎臣願
陛下闢天地之量開悔過之門則庶幾不傷於刻而仁可以廣
矣何謂軍伍不充臣聞善謀國者必強其本善制夷者先
戢其兵兵不戢則外夷乘其釁而尾大不掉皆自其不知
強本者為之今在京之兵計七十餘衛分為三營至正統
間復有十二團營之設凡此皆為強本計也邇則勢豪者

臺省諸臣言事失當，上干天怒，遂而放之，而重論之，誠是矣。然原厥初心，亦欲忠於為國，非敢有他志者，但意見或少差耳。今舉事一不當，而竟棄不復，遂使悔過無門，似亦非先王欽恤之道也。且君之於臣，猶父之於子。方子之為不善也，父固不免於怒，甚且撻而逐之矣；及其知悔而懲也，則未有忍於終棄者。然則陛下獨能忍於終棄乎？况及今不宥，則遠者將死於邊，近者將死於獄矣。陛下果忍令後世謂此輩皆以言獲罪而死乎？臣願陛下闢天地之量，開悔過之門，則庶幾不傷於刻，而仁可以廣矣。

… the officials of the Censorate and the central ministries spoke inappropriately on affairs of state and thereby incurred Your Majesty’s wrath. That they were consequently banished and sentenced severely was indeed right. Yet, if we examine their original intentions, they too wished to serve the state loyally and dared harbor no other purpose; their views were merely somewhat mistaken. Now, for a single inappropriate action, they are cast aside forever, with no reinstatement, leaving them no avenue to repent of their faults. This, it seems, also falls short of the former kings’ principle of reverent care and compassion in punishment. A ruler’s relation to his ministers is like a father’s relation to his sons. When a son does wrong, his father naturally cannot avoid anger and may even beat him and drive him away. But once the son recognizes his fault, repents, and reforms, no father has the heart to abandon him forever. Can Your Majesty alone bear to abandon them forever? Moreover, if they are not pardoned now, those far away will die on the frontier, and those nearby will die in prison. Can Your Majesty truly bear to have later generations say that all these men were convicted for their words and died? Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would display a magnanimity as broad as Heaven and Earth and open the door to repentance. Then, perhaps, Your Majesty’s benevolence would escape the injury of harshness and could be extended more widely.

What is meant by the ranks of the army being under strength? Your servant has heard that those skilled in planning for the state must strengthen its foundations, and those skilled in controlling foreign peoples first bring their own troops under discipline. If the troops are not disciplined, foreign peoples exploit the resulting openings, while the tail grows too large to be moved: all this results from a failure to understand how to strengthen the foundations. The troops now stationed in the capital comprise more than seventy guards, divided among three encampments. During the Zhengtong reign, twelve regimental encampments were additionally established. All these measures were intended to strengthen the foundations. Recently, however, powerful men have selected the able-bodied soldiers for private service and used nominal entries on the rolls to secure actual profits. Those said to be available for muster are all old, weak, exhausted, or sick, without even the strength to bear armor. As for troops serving their rotation at the capital, their resources are exhausted by exploitation and their strength by excessive duties; there are further circumstances that one cannot bear to recount. Under such conditions, can one expect the army to be strong? Thus, when disturbances occur in the interior, they cannot be quelled without frontier troops. Your servant cannot see how it is acceptable to expose this situation to distant peoples. As for abuses in the frontier garrisons, your servant has also examined their causes. In ordinary, peaceful times, the care of the soldiers is entrusted to unsuitable men, fodder and grain arrive irregularly, and even half the material benefits bestowed by the court end up in the baskets of crafty rogues. When a soldier seizes an opportunity to distinguish himself and earns merit by taking an enemy head, the powerful berate him and take it away, appropriating it as their own achievement. Now, from soldiers one wishes to obtain …

其死力者也欲其力之足以正死不先得其心而内兵又不
足以鎮壓之是宜其群譟而屢爲變矣兵不戢而又何惑
於夷之肆也哉故欲攘夷必自戢邊兵始欲戢邊兵必自
強本始臣願大釐此弊簡罷卒以歸農慎清理以剔姦時

補弊以廣大其仁則麟趾符祥鳧鷖歌治光媲
祖宗道軼邃古百姓大和而無不遂其生也萬物咸若而無不
適其所也諸福日集後祿永綏天德布而王道終將有傳

其死力者也。欲其力之足以正死，不先得其心，而内兵又不足以鎮壓之，是宜其群譟而屢爲變矣。兵不戢，而又何惑於夷之肆也哉？故欲攘夷，必自戢邊兵始；欲戢邊兵，必自強本始。臣願大釐此弊，簡罷卒以歸農，慎清理以剔姦，時拊循以昭恩，嚴紀綱以肅度，而又屯閑田、通鹽法以足餉。斯則庶幾不流於怠，而仁可以廣矣。陛下果不以臣言爲妄且迂，勅下有司，擇其所可行，而益興滯補弊，以廣大其仁，則麟趾符祥，鳧鷖歌治，光媲祖宗，道軼邃古，百姓大和而無不遂其生也，萬物咸若而無不適其所也。諸福日集，後祿永綏，天德布而王道終，將有傳記所不及載者，而宗社萬禩之固、國家千世之傳在是矣。豈特如成周歷年八百已哉？

良法要道，或不能越諸此。然臣愚之見，尚有進於此者，敢申其說於清問之下，幸無厭焉。臣謂人君之道，莫要於正聖學，莫急於開言路。夫聖學不正，則無以建天下之極，其見也隘，隘且塞，仁斯壅上矣。然不開，則無以通天下之情，其見也隘，隘且塞，仁斯壅上矣。然臣見陛下日御經筵，箴嚴敬一，甚者手不釋卷，至夜分始寐，則所謂正聖學者，陛下固已優爲矣。群下建白，每見嘉納；至於國有大政，必反覆謀議始行，則所謂開言路者，
translation_en:
…their utmost exertions, even unto death. If one wishes their strength to suffice for facing death [?], yet does not first win their hearts, while the troops of the interior are themselves insufficient to suppress them, it is only to be expected that they should gather in uproar and repeatedly mutiny. If the troops are not restrained, why be surprised at the unbridled conduct of the foreign peoples? Thus, to repel foreign peoples, one must begin by restraining the frontier troops; to restrain the frontier troops, one must begin by strengthening the foundation. Your servant wishes these abuses to be thoroughly remedied: select the unfit soldiers and return them to farming; carefully investigate and rectify affairs to root out wrongdoing; regularly comfort and care for the troops to manifest imperial kindness; and enforce discipline strictly to uphold the regulations. Furthermore, establish military agricultural colonies on unused land and improve the operation of the salt laws to provide sufficient military supplies. In this way, perhaps we may avoid lapsing into negligence and extend benevolence. If Your Majesty indeed does not regard your servant’s words as reckless and impractical, issue an edict to the responsible officials to select those proposals that can be implemented, further revive neglected undertakings, and remedy abuses, thereby enlarging your benevolence. Then the auspicious signs of “The Qilin’s Hoofs” will be fulfilled, and “Wild Ducks and Gulls” will sing of good government. Your glory will equal that of your ancestors, and your Way will surpass remote antiquity. The people will enjoy great harmony, and none will fail to fulfill their lives; all things will flourish in accord, and none will fail to find their proper place. Every blessing will gather daily, enduring bounty will bring lasting peace [?], Heaven’s virtue will spread, and the kingly Way will reach fulfillment. There will be achievements beyond what historical records can recount. Herein will lie the security of the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain for ten thousand years, and the transmission of the state through a thousand generations. How could this amount merely to eight hundred years, as under the Zhou?

Sound laws and essential principles may not go beyond these measures. Yet your servant’s humble understanding has something further to offer. I venture to set forth this view in response to your august inquiry, hoping that you will not tire of it. Your servant holds that, in the ruler’s Way, nothing is more essential than setting sagely learning aright, and nothing more urgent than opening channels for remonstrance. If sagely learning is not correct, there is no means to establish the supreme standard for all under Heaven; one’s vision is narrow—narrow and obstructed—and benevolence is thus dammed up above. Yet if these channels are not opened [?], there is no means to comprehend the circumstances of all under Heaven; one’s vision is narrow—narrow and obstructed—and benevolence is thus dammed up above. [The transcription appears defective here and repeats a clause.] Yet your servant observes that Your Majesty attends the Classics Colloquium daily and rigorously observes the admonition to maintain single-minded reverence. Indeed, you sometimes do not put down your books and retire only at midnight. Thus, as for what is called setting sagely learning aright, Your Majesty has certainly already accomplished it admirably. Whenever your officials submit proposals, these regularly receive your appreciative acceptance; and whenever the state faces a major policy decision, you invariably deliberate repeatedly before acting. Thus, as for what is called opening channels for remonstrance…

而體諸身心也難無所忤而用人也易有所忤而用言也
難況帝王之道法天立極厥終少有懈焉前美將盡棄矣

矣翕受敷施皐陶之所以勸禹者諄如也臣子愛君無已
之心類如此臣之愚何敢自比於古人而
陛下之明則兼夫舜禹臣烏敢不以舜禹望其君父乎故臣更
願
陛下究理亂之源察是非之極密慎獨之功全躬行之實而文
藝之末則姑以後焉斯可也夫是之謂正聖學壮正人之
===
===

於用者亦姑勿究焉斯可也夫是之謂開言路夫正學以

精明聞見日益充拓天下事將惟吾所建而仁且底於如
天之盛矣於去目前四弊何有哉是則仁以守成而其道

===
於用者亦姑勿究焉斯可也夫是之謂開言路夫正學以
端其本用言以虛其受合人己以成其德焉則神智日益
精明聞見日益充拓天下事將惟吾所建而仁且底於如
天之盛矣於去目前四弊何有哉是則仁以守成而其道
在於正聖學開言路如此是固無有新奇可喜之說且狂
率不識忌諱冒犯
天威罪在不赦然直意
陛下以制策求士必將有取於凱切時務之論而不貴於勦說
雷同之者故敢畧獻其愚如此惟諒其朴直而采覽焉則臣
愚不勝幸甚臣謹對
punctuated:
陛下亦旣優為矣。但臣私憂過計，竊謂學而習其文藝也易，學而體諸身心也難；無所忤而用人也易，有所忤而用言也難。況帝王之道，法天立極，厥終少有懈焉，前美將盡棄矣。

臣嘗讀書，見舜之聖，重華協帝，無所虞於敗度者，禹且以無怠無荒者戒之。而禹之不自滿假，亦非拒人自賢者明矣，翕受敷施，皐陶之所以勸禹者諄如也。臣子愛君無已之心類如此。臣之愚，何敢自比於古人？而陛下之明則兼夫舜禹，臣烏敢不以舜禹望其君父乎？

故臣更願陛下究理亂之源，察是非之極，密慎獨之功，全躬行之實，而文藝之末則姑以後焉，斯可也。夫是之謂正聖學。壮正人之氣，養公論之鋒，容峻激之辭，大茹納之量，而言雖有不適於用者，亦姑勿究焉，斯可也。夫是之謂開言路。夫正學以端其本，用言以虛其受，合人已以成其德焉，則神智日益精明，聞見日益充拓，天下事將惟吾所建，而仁且底於如天之盛矣。於去目前四弊何有哉？是則仁以守成，而其道在於正聖學、開言路如此。

是固無有新竒可喜之說，且狂率不識忌諱，冒犯天威，罪在不赦。然直意陛下以制策求士，必將有取於剴切時務之論，而不貴於勦說雷仝者，故敢畧獻其愚如此。惟諒其朴直而采覽焉，則臣愚不勝幸甚。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…Your Majesty has likewise already accomplished this admirably. Yet your servant, privately anxious and perhaps excessively concerned, humbly believes that it is easy to study and acquire literary accomplishments, but difficult to embody one's learning in mind and person; easy to employ men when they give no offense, but difficult to act upon words that do offend. Moreover, the way of emperors and kings is to model themselves upon Heaven and establish the supreme standard. Should they grow even slightly negligent toward the end, all their previous excellence will be thrown away.

Your servant has read in the Book of Documents that Shun's sageliness continued Yao's brilliance and accorded with that emperor's virtue, so that there was no reason to fear he would violate proper standards. Yet Yu still admonished him against negligence and neglect. Yu, for his part, was neither complacent nor presumptuous, and plainly did not reject others while considering himself alone worthy. Nevertheless, Gao Yao earnestly urged him to receive counsel broadly and put it widely into practice. Such is the unceasing love that ministers bear their ruler. Foolish as your servant is, how dare I compare myself to the ancients? Yet Your Majesty's wisdom combines that of Shun and Yu: how could your servant dare not hold up Shun and Yu as the standard for his ruler and father?

Thus your servant further wishes that Your Majesty would investigate the sources of order and disorder, discern the ultimate grounds of right and wrong, exercise meticulous vigilance over yourself even when alone, and fully realize your learning in personal conduct. The lesser matter of literary accomplishments may appropriately be put afterward. This is what is meant by rectifying sagely learning. Strengthen the resolve of upright men, sustain the incisiveness of public judgment, tolerate stern and vehement language, and enlarge your capacity to accommodate and accept counsel. Even when words are unsuitable for practical use, it would be proper to refrain from pursuing the matter against their speakers. This is what is meant by opening the channels of remonstrance. By rectifying learning, you set the foundation straight; by acting upon counsel, you receive others' contributions with an open mind. By bringing together others and yourself [?], you perfect your virtue. Then your spiritual insight will grow ever clearer, and your knowledge ever broader. The affairs of the realm will take shape through your initiatives, and your benevolence will attain a grandeur like that of Heaven. What difficulty would there then be in eliminating the four present abuses? Such is the way to preserve established achievements through benevolence: it lies in rectifying sagely learning and opening the channels of remonstrance.

There is certainly nothing novel or striking in these proposals to give you pleasure. Moreover, in my rashness and ignorance of what must be avoided, I have offended Your Majesty's awe-inspiring authority, an offense beyond pardon. Yet I simply suppose that, in seeking men through an imperially issued policy question, Your Majesty will surely value arguments that address current affairs directly and pertinently, rather than prize borrowed opinions and unthinking agreement. I have therefore ventured to present these few foolish observations. If you would graciously understand their plain sincerity and consider them, your foolish servant would count himself exceedingly fortunate. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

臣趙貞吉
臣對臣聞天下勢也運勢者機也握機者志也建志者時
也時也者事之會也聖人之所競也唯聖人能速赴時以
成天下之務其志一定而不可移而天下之勢常固而不
離也勢也者天下之命也聖人之所重也且天下大器也
勢離則或昂而不可挽或低而不可舉低昂之間誠有機
焉惟聖人能研先幾以平天下之勢而常不失時也此古
之人所以欲帝而帝欲王而王欲守成而不愆不忘者也
成其道常歷百世而不廢非有暴亂之裔不即敗也後世
循其迹則合而稱曰聖王治天下之良法要道也夫求聖
王之法於千載之上其勢變矣臣得其機焉學聖王之道
===
於千載之下其時異矣臣得其志焉勢也者伏於無形者
也其來也不可豫其去也不可追其倏然而聚也不可度
其忽然而散也不可合也非有機焉以運之則亦漫漶瞶
眊而終不可執也時也者藏於有待者也其蓄也或發之
矣其張也或弛之矣或行而尼之或塞而通之矣非有志
焉以隨之則亦顛倒錯亂而會不逢其適也機以持勢志
以發機時以建志得其說者天下國家之治可幾也
陛下發
德音求歷世長久之數持盈保成之道思
祖宗創業之艱念民物望治之願此愚臣之所懷蓄而欲以獻
之於

臣趙貞吉。

臣對：臣聞天下，勢也；運勢者，機也；握機者，志也；建志者，時也。時也者，事之會也，聖人之所競也。唯聖人能速赴時，以成天下之務。其志一定而不可移，而天下之勢常固而不離也。勢也者，天下之命也，聖人之所重也。且天下大器也，勢離則或昂而不可挽，或低而不可舉。低昂之間，誠有機焉。惟聖人能研先幾，以平天下之勢，而常不失時也。此古之人所以欲帝而帝，欲王而王，欲守成而不愆不忘者也。成其道，常歷百世而不廢；非有暴亂之裔，不即敗也。後世循其迹，則合而稱曰：聖王治天下之良法要道也。夫求聖王之法於千載之上，其勢變矣，臣得其機焉；學聖王之道於千載之下，其時異矣，臣得其志焉。勢也者，伏於無形者也。其來也不可豫，其去也不可追，其倏然而聚也不可度，其忽然而散也不可合也。非有機焉以運之，則亦漫漶瞶眊而終不可執也。時也者，藏於有待者也。其蓄也或發之矣，其張也或弛之矣，或行而尼之，或塞而通之矣。非有志焉以隨之，則亦顛倒錯亂而會不逢其適也。機以持勢，志以發機，時以建志。得其說者，天下國家之治可幾也。

Your servant, Zhao Zhenji.

Your servant replies: I have heard that the realm depends upon the configuration of circumstances; what moves that configuration is the pivotal mechanism; what commands that mechanism is resolve; and what establishes resolve is the moment. The moment is the convergence of affairs, which the sage strives to seize. Only the sage can promptly meet the moment and thereby accomplish the affairs of the realm. Once his resolve is established, it cannot be shifted, and the configuration of the realm remains secure and does not fall apart. This configuration is the lifeblood of the realm, and the sage sets great store by it. Moreover, the realm is a great vessel. When its configuration falls apart, it may rise beyond recall or sink beyond recovery. Between its sinking and rising there is indeed a pivotal mechanism. Only the sage can discern the earliest signs of change, thereby bringing the configuration of the realm into balance and never missing the moment. This is why the men of antiquity could, when they wished, rule as emperors or as kings, and could preserve their accomplishments without transgression or forgetfulness. Once their Way was established, it commonly endured for a hundred generations without being abandoned; unless there were violent and disorderly descendants, it did not readily fail. Later generations followed their precedents and agreed in calling them the sound methods and essential Way by which sage kings governed the realm. Yet if we seek the methods of the sage kings more than a thousand years in the past, the configuration of circumstances has changed; I apprehend their pivotal mechanism. If we study the Way of the sage kings more than a thousand years afterward, the times are different; I apprehend their resolve.

The configuration of circumstances lies hidden in what has no visible form. Its coming cannot be anticipated, its departure cannot be pursued, its sudden convergence cannot be reckoned, and its abrupt dispersal cannot be gathered back together. Without a pivotal mechanism to move it, all remains obscure and indistinct, leaving one deaf and dim-sighted, and it can never finally be grasped. The moment lies concealed in what awaits fulfillment. What has accumulated may be released; what has been stretched taut may be slackened; what is proceeding may be checked, and what is obstructed may be opened. Without resolve to follow these developments, there will likewise be confusion and disorder, and one will fail to meet the fitting opportunity. The pivotal mechanism sustains the configuration of circumstances; resolve activates the mechanism; and the moment establishes resolve. For one who grasps this principle, good government of the realm, the state, and the family is within reach.

Your Majesty has issued your gracious pronouncement, seeking the principles of endurance through successive generations and the Way to maintain fullness and preserve accomplishment. You reflect upon the hardships your ancestors faced in founding the dynasty and bear in mind the desire of the people and all living things for good government. These are matters that your foolish servant has long cherished within and wishes to present to …

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
陛下者也臣嘗自謂讙讙諤諤思與天下返朴還淳盡忠竭愚
可夙夜無怠也恭遇
陛下拔之於塗泥而以縉紳彌綸之謀大人御世之規
詢之如是而不言則臣之自棄甚矣言而不詳擇而不精則
臣之無具明矣夫士莫大乎有自棄負
君之罪有不學無具之恥也臣請以
聖策所及者條對之而後及臣之說幸
陛下詳擇其中焉臣伏讀
聖策朕思昔自三代以來迄於宋終中間雖歷世有久近而其
君之歷年亦有長短要之皆自其為君者何如耳夫歷世
永命之道詩書備矣臣敢冒昧億對曰上世風氣淳固貴
===
===
道秉德其君皆清明在躬志氣如神心之精神迺與造化
流通故能其壽皆百其在位皆六七十年或四五十年而
天下大治物不夭厲民不彫喪後世稱曰治安未巳也夫
人君居崇高富貴之地故驕奢易生而逸欲乃興也彼其
宮室之壯麗服器之繪飾車馬田獵之侈縱聲色子女之
艷美固自以為盡天下之腴養安宅矣抑豈知憒聰明而
壞氣志已包藏天下之大毒而不自覺哉是以高識遠覽
之主必求大道之原知性命之貴儉以自奉不過乎物雖
以尊貴之極而其恬愉簡靜無以異於山林修潔者之為
是以精神充盈年壽益堅德性堅定外誘不入天下有奇
袤之術淫蕩之巧舉無所入之故天下陰受其休養綏寧

陛下者也。臣嘗自謂：讙讙諤諤，思與天下返朴還淳，盡忠竭愚，可夙夜無怠也。恭遇陛下拔之於塗泥，而以縉紳彌綸之謀、大人御世之規詢之。如是而不言，則臣之自棄甚矣；言而不詳，擇而不精，則臣之無具明矣。夫士莫大乎有自棄負君之罪，有不學無具之恥也。臣請以聖策所及者條對之，而後及臣之說，幸陛下詳擇其中焉。
臣伏讀聖策：「朕思昔自三代以來，迄於宋終，中間雖歷世有久近，而其君之歷年亦有長短，要之皆自其為君者何如耳。」夫歷世永命之道，《詩》《書》備矣。臣敢冒昧億對曰：上世風氣淳固，貴道秉德，其君皆清明在躬，志氣如神，心之精神迺與造化流通。故能其壽皆百，其在位皆六七十年，或四五十年，而天下大治，物不夭厲，民不彫喪，後世稱曰治安，未巳也。夫人君居崇高富貴之地，故驕奢易生，而逸欲乃興也。彼其宮室之壯麗、服器之繪飾、車馬田獵之侈縱、聲色子女之艷美，固自以為盡天下之腴養安宅矣。抑豈知憒聰明而壞氣志，已包藏天下之大毒而不自覺哉？是以高識遠覽之主，必求大道之原，知性命之貴，儉以自奉，不過乎物。雖以尊貴之極，而其恬愉簡靜，無以異於山林修潔者之為。是以精神充盈，年壽益堅，德性堅定，外誘不入。天下有奇袤之術、淫蕩之巧，舉無所入之，故天下陰受其休養綏寧
translation_en:
…to Your Majesty. Your servant has often said to himself: speaking earnestly and forthrightly, I aspire to join all under Heaven in returning to simplicity and sincerity, exhausting my loyalty and humble understanding, and remaining diligent morning and night. I have respectfully received Your Majesty’s favor in raising me from the mud and consulting me about the comprehensive plans of scholar-officials and the principles by which great men govern the world. If, under these circumstances, I did not speak, my abandonment of my own responsibilities would be grave indeed. If I spoke without thoroughness and chose my arguments without discernment, my lack of preparation would be plain. For a scholar, no offense is greater than abandoning his responsibilities and failing his ruler, and no disgrace greater than being unlearned and unprepared. I ask leave to answer, point by point, the matters raised in Your Majesty’s policy question, and then to present my own views. I hope Your Majesty will carefully select what is sound among them.
Your servant has reverently read the imperial policy question: “I reflect that, from the Three Dynasties down to the end of the Song, although dynasties endured for different lengths of time, their rulers’ reigns also varied in length. Ultimately, this all depended on what sort of rulers they were.” The way to endure through successive generations and perpetuate the Mandate is fully set out in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents. Your servant ventures presumptuously to offer this conjectural reply: in high antiquity, prevailing customs were simple and steadfast; the Way was honored and virtue upheld. The rulers all embodied purity and illumination, and their purpose and vital energy were like those of spirits. The spiritual essence of their hearts thus flowed in communion with the transforming processes of Heaven and Earth. Consequently, they could all live to a hundred and reign for sixty or seventy years, or forty or fifty years. All under Heaven was well governed; living things suffered neither premature death nor pestilence, and the people neither dwindled nor perished. Later generations have never ceased praising this as good government and peace.
A ruler occupies a position of supreme eminence, wealth, and honor. Arrogance and extravagance therefore arise easily, and indolence and desire flourish. With magnificent palaces, richly ornamented garments and utensils, extravagant indulgence in carriages, horses, and hunting, and the alluring beauty of music, sensual pleasures, and young companions, he naturally thinks that he enjoys the richest sustenance and most comfortable dwelling the world can provide. Yet how could he realize that these cloud his perceptions and ruin his vital energy and resolve—that he has already harbored the greatest poison in the world without knowing it?
Thus, a ruler of lofty understanding and far-reaching vision invariably seeks the source of the Great Way and recognizes the preciousness of his nature and life. He provides for himself frugally and avoids excess in material things. Although he occupies the highest position of honor, his tranquil contentment, simplicity, and stillness are no different from the conduct of those who cultivate purity in the mountains and forests. His spiritual energies are therefore abundant, his longevity more secure, and his virtuous nature firmly established; external temptations cannot enter. Whatever strange practices [?] or licentious contrivances exist in the world find no opening at all. Thus, all under Heaven quietly receives the benefits of his nurturing care and pacification…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
之福而歷世之久近亦從可卜也是歷年之久與歷世之
久固相須也臣又伏讀
聖策唯周之歷世最多國祚恒久然周之所以久本於文武之
積累亦後之繼承者能保持之耳上至夏商垂及唐宋亦
若是焉皆基於先王德澤洽於民心亦繼之以嗣王能盡
持盈慎滿之道者也夫創業守成之事當塗之士爭言之
矣臣敢冒昧臆對曰創業之君得天下於至難而守成之
主失天下於至易何其不相及也臣嘗伏而求其故矣賈
誼曰三代之王所以有道之長者以其諭教太子而導之
術業也斯言可謂根極理要者矣故周公教成王至老而
不倦也豳風之詩無逸之篇是周之所以貽永年之具也
===
漢唐宋之君其始也皆百戰而有之憂勤惕厲若可述也
然亦有身親為之而身變其初者矣況其子孫之繼體者
皆出於婦人狎習之手其於正人正言心不相洽而意不
相安不見王業之所以難安得不以易心乘之不原天命
之不可忽安得不以怠心處之老成忠愛之臣起而救其
遺餘末流已無及矣雖其間英主誼辟不無有之然或得
於天資之似矜飾之粗依倣假借間斷者眾也是以不逮
於三代之美也是故古之帝王不恃其積之厚而恃其繼
之者賢也不恃其德澤入人之深而恃其子孫維持之有
其具也謹擇人選任使以教諭之必祈其無逸必知稼穡
之艱難必知道術仁義之正雖歷百世而天下蒙其福也

之福，而歷世之久近亦從可卜也。是歷年之久與歷世之久，固相須也。臣又伏讀聖策：「唯周之歷世最多，國祚恒久。」然周之所以久，本於文武之積累，亦後之繼承者能保持之耳。上至夏商，垂及唐宋，亦若是焉。皆基於先王德澤洽於民心，亦繼之以嗣王能盡持盈慎滿之道者也。夫創業守成之事，當塗之士爭言之矣。臣敢冒昧臆對曰：創業之君得天下於至難，而守成之主失天下於至易，何其不相及也！臣嘗伏而求其故矣。賈誼曰：「三代之王所以有道之長者，以其諭教太子而導之術業也。」斯言可謂根極理要者矣。故周公教成王，至老而不倦也。《豳風》之詩、《無逸》之篇，是周之所以貽永年之具也。

漢唐宋之君，其始也皆百戰而有之，憂勤惕厲，若可述也。然亦有身親為之而身變其初者矣。況其子孫之繼體者，皆出於婦人狎習之手，其於正人正言，心不相洽而意不相安。不見王業之所以難，安得不以易心乘之？不原天命之不可忽，安得不以怠心處之？老成忠愛之臣起而救其遺餘末流，已無及矣。雖其間英主誼辟不無有之，然或得於天資之似、矜飾之粗，依倣假借、間斷者眾也，是以不逮於三代之美也。是故古之帝王不恃其積之厚，而恃其繼之者賢也；不恃其德澤入人之深，而恃其子孫維持之有其具也。謹擇人，選任使，以教諭之，必祈其無逸，必知稼穡之艱難，必知道術仁義之正。雖歷百世，而天下蒙其福也。
translation_en:
…the blessings of nurture and peace, and from this one may also predict whether the succession of generations will be long or short. Thus longevity in years and longevity across generations necessarily depend upon one another. Your servant has again reverently read the imperial policy question: “Zhou alone endured for the greatest number of generations, and its dynastic mandate lasted long.” Yet Zhou’s endurance rested upon what Kings Wen and Wu had accumulated, and also upon the ability of their successors to preserve it. This was likewise true as far back as Xia and Shang and down through Tang and Song. All rested upon the virtue and beneficence of former kings having permeated the people’s hearts, followed by succeeding kings who fully practiced the way of preserving fullness and remaining cautious amid prosperity. Men in positions of power vie with one another in discussing the founding of a dynasty and the preservation of its achievements. Your servant ventures presumptuously to offer his own judgment: founding rulers obtain the realm through the greatest difficulty, while rulers charged with preserving it lose it with the greatest ease. How far the latter fall short! Your servant has humbly sought the reason. Jia Yi said: “The kings of the Three Dynasties long maintained good government because they instructed the crown prince and guided him in the arts and duties of rulership.” These words may indeed be said to reach the very root and essentials of the matter. Thus the Duke of Zhou taught King Cheng tirelessly even into old age. The poems of the Airs of Bin and the chapter Against Idleness were the means by which Zhou bequeathed lasting years to its descendants.

The founding rulers of Han, Tang, and Song all gained possession of the realm through a hundred battles. Their anxious diligence, vigilance, and self-discipline would seem worthy of recounting. Yet even among them were those who personally accomplished this and then themselves departed from their original principles. How much more was this so with the descendants who succeeded them, all raised in the hands of women who indulged them in excessive familiarity. Their hearts found no accord with upright men and upright words, and their minds felt no ease with them. Failing to see how difficult the royal enterprise was, how could they avoid taking it up with a careless heart? Failing to consider that Heaven’s Mandate must not be slighted, how could they avoid treating it with a negligent heart? By the time seasoned ministers, loyal and devoted, arose to salvage what remained in the final stages of decline, it was already too late. There were indeed enlightened sovereigns and righteous rulers among them. Yet some attained only a semblance of goodness through natural endowment or a superficial display through studied adornment [?]; many merely imitated and borrowed, with frequent lapses. Hence they fell short of the excellence of the Three Dynasties.

For this reason, the emperors and kings of antiquity relied not upon the abundance of what they had accumulated, but upon the worthiness of their successors; not upon the depth to which their virtue and beneficence had entered the people’s hearts, but upon their descendants’ possessing the means to sustain them. They carefully chose suitable men and appointed them to instruct and guide their heirs, earnestly seeking to ensure that the heirs shunned idleness, understood the hardships of sowing and reaping, and knew the correct principles of the Way, benevolence, and righteousness. Even after a hundred generations, all under Heaven would enjoy the blessings of this.

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
歷年所永天命之道實在于此臣又伏讀
聖策洪惟朕
皇祖高皇帝代
天復世重肇中華建振古無比之功德朕
太宗繼述於草創之初
列聖遵承於大定之後百有六十餘載傳之於今朕以沖昧之年入承
祖位幼弱不才多招災害於民臣於此有以仰窺
聖孝之大
聖德之謙也臣謹冒昧獻言曰
陛下之繼位也是中興之運治忽之機也然而不能大有為臣
竊以為過矣
===
陛下聰明英哲迥出前古
踐祚以來十四年間講學師古更化善治君臣之間未嘗不
以堯舜相期高宗傅說蓋屢歌而咏嘆之矣臣嘗觀高宗
之學方其退於默也藏其精至不測也養其明至不撓也
所精義者至神也所研幾者至變也宣不縕原挈本直截
簡易哉以是言治無難矣是故力定者必先為之強也見
定者必先為之明也守定者必先為之植也今時學士文
儒彬彬然會于此矣非必無古說沃王心者也
陛下誠留神於此以光
太祖以繼
太宗至孝也以承

歷年所永，天命之道實在于此。臣又伏讀聖策：「洪惟朕皇祖高皇帝，代天復世，重肇中華，建振古無比之功德。朕太宗繼述於草創之初，列聖遵承於大定之後，百有六十餘載，傳之於今。朕以沖昧之年，入承祖位，幼弱不才，多招災害於民。」臣於此有以仰窺聖孝之大、聖德之謙也。臣謹冒昧獻言曰：陛下之繼位也，是中興之運、治忽之機也。然而不能大有為，臣竊以為過矣。
