translation_en:
…Herein truly lies the way to prolong the years of the dynasty and retain Heaven’s Mandate. Your servant has also reverently read the imperial policy question: “We solemnly reflect that Our imperial ancestor, the Emperor Gao, acting on Heaven’s behalf, restored the world, founded China anew, and established achievements and virtue unmatched since antiquity. Our Taizong continued his work in the early days of the founding; the successive sage emperors carried it forward after order had been firmly established. It has been transmitted down to the present for more than a hundred and sixty years. At a young and unenlightened age, We succeeded to the ancestral throne. Young, weak, and without ability, We have brought many calamities upon the people.” In these words your servant can discern something of the greatness of Your Majesty’s filial piety and the humility of your sagely virtue. Your servant respectfully ventures to submit: Your Majesty’s accession marked an opportunity for dynastic revival, a turning point between good government and disorder. Yet you have not accomplished great things; your servant privately considers this a failing.

Your Majesty’s intelligence, wisdom, and discernment far surpass those of earlier ages. During the fourteen years since your accession, you have pursued learning, taken antiquity as your teacher, reformed government, and sought good order. Sovereign and ministers have constantly looked to one another to attain the standards of Yao and Shun. Surely you have repeatedly sung the praises of Gaozong and Fu Yue and reflected admiringly upon them. Your servant has studied Gaozong’s learning. When he withdrew into silence, he stored up his inner essence until it became unfathomable and nurtured his discernment until it became unshakable. In refining his understanding of moral principles, he attained spiritual subtlety; in examining the first intimations of events, he attained mastery of change. The following words are unclear, but appear to concern tracing origins and grasping fundamentals [?]—how direct and simple! With this as the basis for discussing government, there would be no difficulty. Thus, to make one’s capacity steadfast, one must first strengthen it; to make one’s judgment settled, one must first clarify it; to make one’s adherence firm, one must first root it securely. Today, scholars and learned Confucians have gathered here in cultivated abundance. Surely among them there are those who, like Fu Yue of old, can refresh their sovereign’s heart. If Your Majesty would truly attend to this, thereby bringing glory to Taizu and continuing the work of Taizong, that would be the utmost filial piety; thereby to uphold…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
祖廟以育群生至明也修之乎一時而名譽垂之無窮聲光著
而不磨至美也幸毋曰積累之者厚矣可恃而安也臣又
伏讀
聖策茲來思
祖宗創造萬艱惕然悚懼朕欲長保弘業於無窮有隆弗替永
宗社萬禩之固保家國千世之傳民得以遂生物得以適所如
上之良法要道朕心慕之恐之不知何以得此臣於此可
以窺仰
陛下大有為之志欲建萬世之長策也臣敢冒昧獻言曰天下
之事其深遠切至者非臣之愚所能覩然其指歸要領之
地不過曰法
===
祖敬天勤民而已夫欲思其創造萬艱惕然悚懼不可徒有是
心必實有是事可也然而恭儉盡之矣夫創業之君與守
成之主其求賢裕財以成天下之務道未始有異也然而
每不相及者其故可知已彼以難處之而此以易乘之而
已也夫人君之於臣也如其不賢則急去之矣如其賢也
烏可不改容貌而禮之也哉臣嘗觀之小者至於奴隸臧
獲至卑賤也一不得其歡心則不能致其動力而況於天
下耆艾魁偉之士其視爵祿榮進已不足以羈其逸氣而
豢之矣又況接之以勢而震之以威何以能要其忠貞而
俾之自盡也哉盖末季之君嘗自以為賢為聖為天下莫
已若也挾是心也安往而非其振矜驕忽之地也哉佞諛

已若也挾是心也安往而非其振矜驕忽之地也哉佞諛
punctuated:
祖廟，以育群生，至明也。修之乎一時，而名譽垂之無窮，聲光著而不磨，至美也。幸毋曰：「積累之者厚矣，可恃而安也。」
臣又伏讀聖策：「茲來思祖宗創造萬艱，惕然悚懼。朕欲長保弘業於無窮，有隆弗替，永宗社萬禩之固，保家國千世之傳，民得以遂生，物得以適所。如上之良法要道，朕心慕之，恐之，不知何以得此。」臣於此可以窺仰陛下大有為之志，欲建萬世之長策也。臣敢冒昧獻言曰：「天下之事，其深遠切至者，非臣之愚所能覩。然其指歸要領之地，不過曰法祖、敬天、勤民而已。」
夫欲思其創造萬艱，惕然悚懼，不可徒有是心，必實有是事可也。然而恭儉盡之矣。夫創業之君與守成之主，其求賢裕財，以成天下之務，道未始有異也。然而每不相及者，其故可知已：彼以難處之，而此以易乘之而已也。
夫人君之於臣也，如其不賢，則急去之矣；如其賢也，烏可不改容貌而禮之也哉？臣嘗觀之，小者至於奴隸臧獲，至卑賤也，一不得其歡心，則不能致其動力，而況於天下耆艾魁偉之士？其視爵祿榮進，已不足以羈其逸氣而豢之矣。又況接之以勢，而震之以威，何以能要其忠貞，而俾之自盡也哉？盖末季之君，嘗自以為賢、為聖，為天下莫已若也。挾是心也，安往而非其振矜驕忽之地也哉？佞諛
translation_en:
…the ancestral temples, and to nurture all living beings: this is the utmost discernment. To cultivate these things within a single age, yet leave a reputation extending without end, its renown and splendor manifest and never effaced: this is the utmost excellence. May Your Majesty never say, “What has been accumulated is abundant; I may rely on it and rest at ease.”
Your servant has also reverently read the imperial policy question: “Now, reflecting [?] upon the myriad hardships through which Our ancestors founded the dynasty, We feel apprehensive and fearful. We wish to preserve this great undertaking forever, that it may flourish without decline; to secure the ancestral temples and altars of state for ten thousand years; and to preserve the transmission of the ruling house and realm for a thousand generations, so that the people may fulfill their lives and all things find their proper places. Such excellent methods and essential principles as those mentioned above—Our heart longs for them and fears them [?], yet We do not know how to attain this.” From this your servant can glimpse and look up to Your Majesty’s ambition to accomplish great things and establish a lasting plan for ten thousand generations. Your servant ventures presumptuously to offer these words: “The most profound, far-reaching, and urgent affairs of the realm lie beyond your foolish servant’s understanding. Yet their essential direction and governing principles amount to no more than following the ancestors, revering Heaven, and diligently caring for the people.”
If one wishes to reflect upon the myriad hardships of their founding undertaking with apprehension and fear, one must not merely harbor these sentiments; one must give them substance in actual deeds. Reverence and frugality encompass all that is required. The ruler who founds a dynasty and the sovereign who preserves its achievements have never differed in their way of seeking worthy men and making resources abundant to accomplish the affairs of the realm. Yet the reason why the latter so often fails to equal the former is plain: the founder approaches these affairs as difficult, while his successor takes them up as easy.
As for a ruler’s treatment of his ministers: if a minister is unworthy, he should promptly dismiss him; if he is worthy, how can the ruler fail to compose his countenance and treat him with courtesy? Your servant has observed that even those of the lowest station, down to male and female slaves, are utterly humble and lowly, yet once one loses their goodwill, one cannot obtain their labor [?]. How much more is this true of the venerable and outstanding men of the realm! In their eyes, rank, emoluments, honor, and advancement are already insufficient to bridle their free spirits and keep them dependent. If, moreover, one meets them with the weight of power and intimidates them with authority, how can one expect their steadfast loyalty and induce them to devote themselves fully?
Rulers in the closing ages of dynasties have commonly considered themselves worthy and sage, believing that no one in the realm could equal them. Harboring such a disposition, where could they go without making it an occasion for conceit, arrogance, and contempt? Flattery…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
之風因是而生子思之觀衞是已是謂事虛名而忘本務
願治之君何便於此先王之世大臣盡瘁小臣靖恭百工
師師各思自効彼固有以深激之也臣聞之民將窮天下
將多故則府庫必充實何則以君之侈心將生矣天下之
最可憂者國富而君心侈也漢以是而事邊功隋以是而
恣遊幸豈不大可畏哉天下之禍起於有形者可備而藏
於不見者不可得而支也倉廩實府庫充此謂無虞之世
可卧而治者君之欲一動而大亂極壞隨之矣此非無形
之隱禍不可支之至痛與非夫中正撙節之君安能富民
而祈天也是二者有國之恆患也故曰法祖者恭儉盡之
矣夫欲保洪業延永圖則當敬天天命靡常决去留於德
===
之厚薄也然而仁義盡之矣夫仁者行乎天之陽者也義
者立乎天之陰者也天以陽生萬物而以陰成之陰以輔
陽可也陰而勝陽非天道也故義而勝仁非君德也夫聖
人以其不忍之心流溢域中一至於不得已而用刑罰已非
其初意矣而况於敲扑鞭笞流血刻骨之慘哉夫法吏之
酷慢天虐民刀筆筐篋之所為無禮義教化之道而迺寄
民之命於其手或者非天意也甚矣天之愛民之深也豈
其使舞文弄法之吏任情恣意以制其死命也哉此先王
所以恐恐焉不觀於天命而觀於民心之去留也故法吏
者先王之大忌也故曰敬天者仁義盡之矣夫欲民得以
遂生物得以適所則當務於勤民之要然不過命吏教養

其初意矣而況於敲朴鞭笞流血刻骨之慘哉夫法吏之
酷慢天下民刀筆篋櫝之所為無禮義教化之道而徒寄
民之命於其手或者非天意也甚矣天之愛民之深也豈
其使舞文弄法之吏任情恣意以制其死命也哉此先王
所以恐恐焉不觀於天命而觀於民心之去留也故法吏
者先王之大忌也故曰敬天者仁義盡之矣夫欲民得以
遂生物得以適所則當務於勤民之要然不過命吏教養
punctuated:
之風因是而生，子思之觀衞是已。是謂事虛名而忘本務，願治之君何便於此？先王之世，大臣盡瘁，小臣靖恭，百工師師，各思自効，彼固有以深激之也。臣聞之：民將窮，天下將多故，則府庫必充實。何則？以君之侈心將生矣。天下之最可憂者，國富而君心侈也。漢以是而事邊功，隋以是而恣遊幸，豈不大可畏哉？天下之禍，起於有形者可備，而藏於不見者不可得而支也。倉廩實，府庫充，此謂無虞之世，可卧而治者；君之欲一動，而大亂極壞隨之矣。此非無形之隱禍、不可支之至痛與？非夫中正撙節之君，安能富民而祈天也？是二者，有國之恆患也。故曰：法祖者，恭儉盡之矣。
夫欲保洪業，延永圖，則當敬天。天命靡常，决去留於德之厚薄也。然而仁義盡之矣。夫仁者，行乎天之陽者也；義者，立乎天之陰者也。天以陽生萬物，而以陰成之。陰以輔陽可也，陰而勝陽非天道也。故義而勝仁，非君德也。夫聖人以其不忍之心流溢域中，一至於不得已而用刑罰，已非其初意矣，而况於敲扑鞭笞、流血刻骨之慘哉？夫法吏之酷，慢天虐民，刀筆筐篋之所為，無禮義教化之道，而迺寄民之命於其手，或者非天意也。甚矣，天之愛民之深也！豈其使舞文弄法之吏任情恣意，以制其死命也哉？此先王所以恐恐焉，不觀於天命，而觀於民心之去留也。故法吏者，先王之大忌也。故曰：敬天者，仁義盡之矣。
夫欲民得以遂生，物得以適所，則當務於勤民之要，然不過命吏教養
translation_en:
…the climate of flattery arises from this; what Zisi observed in Wei was precisely such a case. This is called pursuing an empty reputation while forgetting fundamental duties. What advantage can a ruler who desires good government find in this? In the age of the former kings, great ministers exhausted themselves in service, lesser ministers were conscientious and reverent, and the various officials urged one another on, each intent on giving his utmost. Those kings certainly had ways of profoundly inspiring them. Your servant has heard this: when the people are about to become impoverished and the realm beset by troubles, the treasuries and storehouses are sure to be full. Why? Because the ruler’s appetite for extravagance is about to arise. The most worrying situation in the realm is a wealthy state whose ruler has an extravagant heart. Because of this, the Han pursued military achievements on the frontiers, and the Sui indulged in imperial pleasure tours. Is this not greatly to be feared? Calamities in the realm that arise in visible form can be guarded against, but those concealed from sight cannot be held off. When granaries are full and treasuries well stocked, this is called an age free from anxiety, one in which the ruler may govern at his ease. Yet once his desires stir, great disorder and utter ruin follow. Is this not a hidden, formless calamity, an unbearable affliction that cannot be checked? Without a ruler who is upright, balanced, restrained, and frugal, how can the people be enriched and Heaven’s blessings sought? These two matters are constant sources of danger to those who possess a state. Thus I say: emulating one’s ancestors is fully encompassed by reverence and frugality.
To preserve the great imperial undertaking and extend its enduring designs, one must revere Heaven. Heaven’s Mandate is not constant: whether it departs or remains is determined by the depth or shallowness of virtue. Yet benevolence and righteousness fully encompass this reverence. Benevolence operates through Heaven’s yang; righteousness is established through Heaven’s yin. Heaven uses yang to bring the myriad things to life and yin to bring them to completion. It is fitting for yin to assist yang; for yin to overcome yang is contrary to Heaven’s Way. Thus, for righteousness to overcome benevolence is contrary to a ruler’s virtue. The sage allows his heart, which cannot bear others’ suffering, to overflow throughout the realm. If he ever reaches the point of having no choice but to employ punishments, this already runs counter to his original intention. How much more so the horrors of beating and flogging, shedding blood and cutting to the bone! The cruelty of judicial functionaries shows contempt for Heaven and abuses the people. Their work is confined to clerical instruments and document boxes, without any way of transforming the people through ritual propriety, righteousness, and instruction. Yet the people’s lives are entrusted to their hands. Perhaps this is not Heaven’s intention. How profoundly Heaven loves the people! Would it allow functionaries who manipulate documents and play tricks with the law to follow their own impulses and indulge their whims in deciding the people’s fate? This is why the former kings were so apprehensive, looking not to Heaven’s Mandate itself but to whether the people’s allegiance departed or remained. Judicial functionaries were therefore a foremost object of concern for the former kings. Thus I say: revering Heaven is fully encompassed by benevolence and righteousness.
To enable the people to live out their lives and all things to find their proper place, one must attend to the essentials of diligent care for the people. Yet this amounts simply to ordering officials to instruct and nurture…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
之而已也臣觀三代以還願治之主嘉謀之士皆能隨世
以就功名其於民之務不可謂無意矣然未有能躋之仁
壽之域天下咸稱曰治安何王道之難行與臣嘗稽之往
古驗之時務念此至熟也三代之時分土而治故地近而
化易及分民而治故勢接而情易通分田而耕故業嘗定
而俗易成此先王維繫聯固可久之道坐而運天下之術
也夫三代之世雖暴君汚吏亦不敢甚虐用其民何則以
民者已之資籍也甚則方伯問之天子誅之故民之勢常
重時則各遂其生各適其所無有大盜崛起土崩之患以
先王有以深結之也夫天樹后王君公承以大夫師長不
唯逸豫惟以亂民俗吏苦不知務唯簿書期會之為急大
吏一出黔首相與易宅繡衣擁騶從盛廩餼飾傳舍而勞
之大吏之威如神如帝足以震耳目而耀於閭市其至與
民情邈不相及也大吏已去而民之室已嘗索然泯泯棼
棼民實勞止唯恐其再至矣受長牧之責任民社之寄者
固當如此乎人方相安以為常曰是固然也小吏以為榮
迺私心嘗竊願之以大吏之足以制其命也故厚遺而餽
賂之不給則急取諸民夫小吏之禄毎薄也內有溪壑之
欲而窘於薄禄而重以醜遺之不及則其取於民也有既
乎甚哉吏之巧於取民如捕蟬者夜爇薪而振其樹也其
闒茸熟爛自棄之輩知已之無能為也方且飽吞厚啗曰
攘民而奪之金不耻也受親民之任承流而宣化者固當

之而已也。臣觀三代以還，願治之主、嘉謀之士，皆能隨世以就功名，其於民之務，不可謂無意矣。然未有能躋之仁壽之域，天下咸稱曰治安，何王道之難行與？臣嘗稽之往古，驗之時務，念此至熟也。三代之時，分土而治，故地近而化易及；分民而治，故勢接而情易通；分田而耕，故業嘗定而俗易成。此先王維繫聯固可久之道，坐而運天下之術也。夫三代之世，雖暴君汚吏，亦不敢甚虐用其民。何則？以民者已之資籍也。甚則方伯問之，天子誅之，故民之勢常重。時則各遂其生，各適其所，無有大盜崛起土崩之患，以先王有以深結之也。
夫天樹后王君公，承以大夫師長，不唯逸豫，惟以亂民。俗吏苦不知務，唯簿書期會之為急。大吏一出，黔首相與易宅，繡衣擁騶從，盛廩餼，飾傳舍而勞之。大吏之威，如神如帝，足以震耳目而耀於閭市，其至與民情邈不相及也。大吏已去，而民之室已嘗索然。泯泯棼棼，民實勞止，唯恐其再至矣。受長牧之責、任民社之寄者，固當如此乎？人方相安以為常，曰：「是固然也。」小吏以為榮，迺私心嘗竊願之，以大吏之足以制其命也。故厚遺而餽賂之，不給則急取諸民。夫小吏之禄毎薄也，內有溪壑之欲，而窘於薄禄，而重以醜遺之不及，則其取於民也有既乎？甚哉！吏之巧於取民，如捕蟬者夜爇薪而振其樹也。其闒茸熟爛自棄之輩，知已之無能為也，方且飽吞厚啗，曰：「攘民而奪之金，不耻也。」受親民之任、承流而宣化者，固當
translation_en:
…them, and that is all. Your servant observes that, from the Three Dynasties onward, rulers who desired good government and men of sound counsel have all been able to adapt to their times and achieve distinction. They cannot be said to have been indifferent to the people's affairs. Yet none has been able to bring the people into a realm of benevolence and longevity, with all under Heaven proclaiming that order and peace prevail. Why is the Kingly Way so difficult to practice? Your servant has examined antiquity, tested it against present affairs, and reflected on this most thoroughly. During the Three Dynasties, territory was divided for government, so the lands were close at hand and moral transformation could easily reach them; the people were divided for government, so rulers and ruled were in close contact and their circumstances and feelings could readily be communicated; fields were divided for cultivation, so livelihoods were settled and good customs could readily take shape. This was the former kings' enduring method of binding the realm together securely, their art of directing all under Heaven while seated. Even tyrannical rulers and corrupt officials in the age of the Three Dynasties did not dare to maltreat and exploit their people excessively. Why? Because the people were the resources upon which they themselves depended. If their abuses became extreme, the Regional Earl would call them to account and the Son of Heaven would punish them. Thus the people's position always carried weight. In those times, each could sustain a livelihood and find a fitting place. There was no danger of great bandit leaders rising up and the realm collapsing, because the former kings had bound the people closely to them.
Heaven established sovereigns, kings, lords, and dukes, supported by grandees and leaders, not merely for their ease and pleasure, but to govern the people. Ordinary officials are woefully ignorant of their proper duties, treating only registers, documents, deadlines, and official meetings as urgent. Whenever a high official travels, the common people must move out of their homes. The embroidered-robed official is surrounded by mounted attendants; ample provisions are furnished and relay lodgings adorned to receive him. His imposing authority, like that of a spirit or a celestial sovereign, overwhelms the senses and dazzles the neighborhoods and marketplaces. Yet his arrival brings him nowhere near an understanding of the people's circumstances. By the time he has departed, their homes have already been stripped bare. Amid bewilderment and turmoil, the people are truly worn out and fear only that he will come again. Should those charged with leading and tending the people, entrusted with the people and the altars of the soil, really behave like this? People accept it complacently as normal, saying, “This is simply how things are.” Lesser officials regard it as an honor and privately long for it, since the high official has the power to determine their fate. Accordingly, they offer lavish gifts and bribes; when their means fall short, they urgently exact more from the people. Lesser officials' salaries are generally meager. Within them are desires as bottomless as ravines, yet they are constrained by their small salaries and further burdened by their inability to provide disreputable gifts in sufficient measure. Can their exactions from the people ever end? How terrible is their ingenuity in extracting wealth from the people! They are like men catching cicadas by burning firewood at night and shaking the trees. Those base, thoroughly corrupt men who have abandoned all self-respect know that they can accomplish nothing. They simply gorge themselves, saying, “There is no shame in plundering the people and seizing their money.” Should those entrusted with direct responsibility for the people, charged with carrying forward imperial influence and spreading moral transformation, really…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
如此乎如是而欲民各遂其生物各適其所難矣哉往者
陛下以民之饑寒為憂加意農桑之務勤民之意至懇切也然
久未獲其效者吏不廉平不能奉
明詔也誠能一重吏責則科指條授而化行裨海之外可筭
計課効期日而得也何憚而久不為此夫天下之士方安
於苟且自利之計聞
陛下核實刻意期於惠民則亦爭自砥礪切磋以功名自期待
矣人得自効務可稱述而良法善政彬彬洋洋相浹洽也
臣又聞之吏有良者而急奪之民置之散處此與不得良
吏同也夫賢者已去方來者未必賢是天下終不得被賢
者之惠也畫策者欲重祿秩而久其任此亦計之得者不
===
可不察也故曰欲民得以遂生物得以適所亦重夫吏責
而已矣凡是數者皆臣就
明詔所及者而演之耳若所謂良法要道善守善終之術臣
敢不竭其愚臣又觀自周以來上下二千餘年之間天下
一統者僅七八百年而止耳其間禍亂時時間作皆由於
勢已移而機不持時已過而志不逮是以國祚天命未之
能延而保業之君終使成王高宗獨美於其前也今
陛下策臣以良法法之良豈良於能運天下之勢策臣以要道
道之要豈要於能握天下之機臣所謂天下勢者何也以
一人而運天下如臂之使手手之使指者是也不得此勢
則猶瘡痏蠹而不可動也臣何以謂運勢者機也今天下

punctuated:
如此乎？如是而欲民各遂其生，物各適其所，難矣哉！往者，陛下以民之饑寒為憂，加意農桑之務，勤民之意至懇切也。然久未獲其效者，吏不廉平，不能奉明詔也。誠能一重吏責，則科指條授，而化行裨海之外，可筭計課効，期日而得也。何憚而久不為此？夫天下之士方安於苟且自利之計，聞陛下核實刻意，期於惠民，則亦爭自砥礪切磋，以功名自期待矣。人得自効，務可稱述，而良法善政彬彬洋洋，相浹洽也。臣又聞之，吏有良者，而急奪之民，置之散處，此與不得良吏同也。夫賢者已去，方來者未必賢，是天下終不得被賢者之惠也。畫策者欲重祿秩而久其任，此亦計之得者，不可不察也。故曰：欲民得以遂生，物得以適所，亦重夫吏責而已矣。

凡是數者，皆臣就明詔所及者而演之耳。若所謂良法要道、善守善終之術，臣敢不竭其愚？臣又觀自周以來，上下二千餘年之間，天下一統者僅七八百年而止耳。其間禍亂時時間作，皆由於勢已移而機不持，時已過而志不逮。是以國祚天命未之能延，而保業之君終使成王、高宗獨美於其前也。今陛下策臣以良法，法之良豈良於能運天下之勢？策臣以要道，道之要豈要於能握天下之機？臣所謂天下勢者何也？以一人而運天下，如臂之使手、手之使指者是也。不得此勢，則猶瘡痏蠹而不可動也。臣何以謂運勢者機也？今天下
translation_en:
…act thus? With things as they are, how difficult it is to enable every person to secure a livelihood and every thing to find its proper place! Previously, Your Majesty, concerned about the people's hunger and cold, gave particular attention to farming and sericulture. Your intention to care for the people was most earnest. Yet these efforts have long failed to bear fruit because officials are neither incorruptible nor impartial and cannot carry out your enlightened edict. If only officials' responsibilities were given greater weight, instructions could be specified by category and issued article by article, and your transforming influence would extend beyond the surrounding seas. Results could be calculated and assessed, and attained within a fixed time. What is there to fear, that this has so long been left undone? The scholars of the realm are now content with expedient schemes for their own advantage. Once they hear that Your Majesty is scrutinizing actual performance and firmly resolved to benefit the people, they too will compete to discipline and improve themselves, aspiring to achievement and renown. Each will be able to demonstrate his abilities, their work will merit praise, and sound laws and good government will flourish abundantly in harmony with one another. Your servant has also heard that when a good official is hastily taken away from the people and placed in an unimportant post, this is no different from their having no good official at all. Once a worthy man has departed, his successor may not be worthy; thus the people of the realm ultimately fail to receive the benefits of worthy government. Those who devise policy propose increasing officials' salaries and ranks and extending their tenure. This too is a sound proposal and must be examined. Thus I say: to enable the people to secure their livelihoods and all things to find their proper places requires only that greater weight be given to officials' responsibilities.

All these points are merely your servant's elaborations on matters raised in your enlightened edict. As for what you call sound laws, essential principles, and methods of preserving your achievements well and bringing them to a good conclusion, how could your servant dare not exhaust his humble understanding? Your servant further observes that, in the more than two thousand years since the Zhou, the realm has been unified for only seven or eight hundred years in all. During that span, calamity and disorder repeatedly arose, all because the balance of power had already shifted while the crucial means of control were not held fast, and the proper moment had already passed while resolve failed to keep pace. Thus the dynasties' allotted fortunes and Heaven's mandate could not be prolonged, and rulers charged with preserving their inherited achievements ultimately left King Cheng and King Gaozong alone in the glory of their earlier examples. Now Your Majesty questions your servant about sound laws: what excellence in law could surpass the ability to direct the configuration of power throughout the realm? You question your servant about essential principles: what principle could be more essential than the ability to grasp the pivotal means of controlling the realm? 之士日趨於浮薄而無實用也農日趨於困屈而不能自
存也工日趨於奇技淫巧而傷天下之財也商日趨於操
柄富貴而侔天下之利也官師日趨於巧宦銳進而不顧
天下之大計也黃緇之流日趨於自便自利而不顧衣食
之原也東南財賦百倍其力而後致之也西北戎馬萬全
其策而後安之也邊鄙日竭而告不給矣夷狄日横而憂
不備矣
宗藩日息而禄不充矣馬政徭役軍伍將吏可謂月異而嵗

機而轉移之耳
今天下雖未極治亦可謂少安矣然而天下方訽訽然若有隱

時自奮於功名之途此士之罪也然而或出於創懲之過

translation_en:
…the realm’s scholars grow daily more frivolous and shallow, lacking practical usefulness; farmers grow daily more impoverished and distressed, unable to sustain themselves; artisans turn increasingly to outlandish techniques and extravagant workmanship, wasting the realm’s wealth; merchants increasingly manipulate power, wealth, and rank, competing for the realm’s profits. Officials increasingly pursue advancement through cunning and aggressive ambition, disregarding the realm’s great concerns. Daoists and Buddhists increasingly seek their own convenience and advantage, disregarding the sources of clothing and food. Tax revenues from the southeast can be delivered only with a hundredfold expenditure of effort; military affairs in the northwest can be brought under control only through wholly secure plans. The borderlands are daily more depleted and report that their supplies are insufficient; the foreign peoples grow daily more overbearing, and we fear that our defenses are inadequate. The imperial clan’s princely branches multiply daily, and their stipends are insufficient. Horse administration, corvée labor, military units, and their commanders and officers may indeed be said to change from month to month and differ from year to year. In its fluctuations, this configuration of forces may likewise be said to have become somewhat unbalanced. What matters is simply to grasp its pivotal mechanism and thereby redirect it.
Although the realm has not yet attained perfect order, it may be called somewhat peaceful. Yet people throughout the realm are now murmuring anxiously [?], as though harboring concealed anxieties or fearing other calamities. This is the consequence of failing to win the people’s hearts. When the circumstances and sentiments of the realm can readily be communicated, the people’s hearts are won. Your servant, while living outside official service, has heard that today’s remonstrance officials have somewhat failed in their duties. This is a major instance of mishandling that pivotal mechanism. Scholars lack substantive learning and constantly wish to accomplish the realm’s affairs merely by coughing and spitting out words. Thus they produce abundant discussion but few practical achievements, and it is fitting that they should receive a salutary chastisement. Yet once the desire to preserve themselves and protect their wives and children arises, they cease to care even about incurring blame [?]. If scholars fail to seize the moment and exert themselves in pursuit of achievement and distinction, that is their fault. But if this should arise from excessive chastisement, would it not be deeply regrettable? How then could one direct the forces of the realm with strength to spare? Thus, among sound methods for preserving the realm, none surpasses this one pivotal mechanism.
Why did your servant previously say that resolve is what enables one to grasp this mechanism? Your foolish servant ventures the opinion that Your Majesty possesses the virtues of enlightened discernment and life-giving nurture, and encounters the destined opportunity for resurgence after more than a hundred and sixty years. This is precisely a time when great things can be accomplished. Yet now people’s expectations have reached their height, while results remain unseen. Might this also be because…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
陛下或於所謂志者未甚切與臣請演志之說以終焉夫志者
心之精神也心之精神聖之帡幪神之底裏也古人之治
天下取之精神心術之際而優為之矣今夫古人之所以
治天下者可得而見也其所以存之而神動之而化鼓舞
之而民宜而天下不倦者此不可得而見也盖可得而見
者聖人之應迹也至退藏宥密神明之此豈流俗故常然
哉是道也刋落枝柯根原見矣培養既至端倪生矣濙泊
既融素質露矣堯得之而無名舜得之而盡善禹得之而
無間文得之而為至德高宗得之而為恭默
陛下得之而為敬一也盖敬則神一則精精神之極與天地流
通天下之事為之則必能勝行之則必能至可以永年可
===
以延世可以保民可以育物可以光
祖宗底來裔也但恐勢尊位極之地所以曠然以觀寂然以省
事克已之力求定性之方致合一之功收一原之効者有
未至耳是平天下之要道無踰此一志也臣何以謂建志
者時也方今勢雖低昂而未去機雖參差而未離如上所
陳者失此不為必為痼疾起而圖之良法要道取之在我
是天命維新萬世之一時也語云難得者時也臣故曰時
也者事之會也聖人之所競也惟聖人能速赴時以成天
下之務而天下之勢嘗固而不離也唯
陛下始終留覽無失此大有為之時天下幸甚臣謹對

punctuated:
陛下或於所謂志者未甚切與？臣請演志之說以終焉。夫志者，心之精神也。心之精神，聖之帡幪，神之底裏也。古人之治天下，取之精神心術之際，而優為之矣。今夫古人之所以治天下者，可得而見也；其所以存之而神，動之而化，鼓舞之而民宜，而天下不倦者，此不可得而見也。盖可得而見者，聖人之應迹也。至退藏宥密，神明之，此豈流俗故常然哉？是道也，刋落枝柯，根原見矣；培養既至，端倪生矣；濙泊既融，素質露矣。堯得之而無名，舜得之而盡善，禹得之而無間，文得之而為至德，高宗得之而為恭默，陛下得之而為敬一也。盖敬則神，一則精，精神之極，與天地流通。天下之事，為之則必能勝，行之則必能至，可以永年，可以延世，可以保民，可以育物，可以光祖宗，底來裔也。但恐勢尊位極之地，所以曠然以觀、寂然以省、事克已之力、求定性之方、致合一之功、收一原之効者，有未至耳。是平天下之要道，無踰此一志也。
臣何以謂建志者時也？方今勢雖低昂而未去，機雖參差而未離。如上所陳者，失此不為，必為痼疾；起而圖之，良法要道，取之在我。是天命維新，萬世之一時也。語云：「難得者，時也。」臣故曰：「時也者，事之會也，聖人之所競也。」惟聖人能速赴時，以成天下之務，而天下之勢嘗固而不離也。唯陛下始終留覽，無失此大有為之時，天下幸甚。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…has Your Majesty perhaps not yet applied yourself earnestly enough to what I call resolve? Your servant asks leave to conclude by elaborating on resolve. Resolve is the vital essence and spiritual power of the mind. This essence and power are the shelter of sagehood and the inner foundation of spiritual efficacy. In governing All-under-Heaven, the ancients drew upon this realm of vital spirit and the workings of the mind, and accomplished their task with ease. Now, the means by which the ancients governed All-under-Heaven can be observed. But how they preserved this within themselves with spiritual efficacy, set it in motion with transforming power, and inspired the people so that they lived fittingly and All-under-Heaven never wearied—this cannot be observed. What can be observed is merely the outward trace of the sage’s responses. As for withdrawing into hidden depths and working with spiritual illumination, how could this be a matter of vulgar habits and established routines? In this Way, when branches are cut away, the root becomes visible; when cultivation reaches its fullness, the first signs emerge; when tranquil detachment has become fully integrated [?], the unadorned substance is revealed. Yao attained it, and his achievement defied naming; Shun attained it and achieved perfect goodness; Yu attained it and was beyond reproach; King Wen attained it and embodied supreme virtue; Gaozong attained it and was reverent and silent. Your Majesty attains it through reverence and unity. Reverence brings spiritual efficacy, and unity brings purity of essence. At their utmost, this essence and spiritual power circulate freely with Heaven and Earth. In the affairs of All-under-Heaven, whatever you undertake you will surely be able to accomplish, and whatever you pursue you will surely bring to fruition. Thus you may prolong your years, perpetuate your dynasty, protect the people, nurture all beings, bring glory to your ancestors, and extend these blessings to future descendants. My only fear is that, in your position of exalted power and supreme rank, something may still be lacking in the means by which you observe with an open mind, reflect in stillness, exert yourself in self-mastery, seek a method for stabilizing your nature, accomplish unity, and reap the effects of a single source. As the essential Way for bringing peace to All-under-Heaven, nothing surpasses this one resolve.
Why does your servant say that the time is what establishes resolve? At present, although the configuration of affairs has its highs and lows, it has not slipped away; although the pivotal opportunities are uneven, they have not escaped us. If the matters set forth above are left unaddressed at this moment, they will surely become chronic maladies. If we rise to deal with them, sound methods and the essential Way lie within our own power to obtain. This is a moment when Heaven’s Mandate is renewed, a moment that comes but once in ten thousand ages. As the saying goes, “What is hard to obtain is the right time.” Thus your servant says, “The right time is the convergence of affairs; it is what the sage strives to seize.” Only the sage can hasten to meet the moment and thereby accomplish the tasks of All-under-Heaven, so that its configuration of affairs remains continually secure and does not fall apart. May Your Majesty attend to these words from beginning to end and not let slip this time for great accomplishment. All-under-Heaven would be most fortunate. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
臣敖銑
臣對臣聞聖王之於天下其得之也以仁其保之也亦以
仁夫仁者天地好生之德也天惟仁故能生萬物而無一
物不被其澤聖人惟仁故能生萬民而無一夫不獲其所
夫能使天下無一夫不獲其所雖欲不王天下其可得乎
何則天能生物不能自理而命之聖人聖人盡撙節愛養
之宜極財成輔相之道是能以天地之心為心自不能不
以之為子矣民生有欲不能自遂而望於聖人聖人所欲
與聚所惡勿施是能以父母之心為心自不能不戴之以
為君矣是故自古得天下者未有不本於此而能建可久
可大之業以詒諸子孫者也保天下者亦未有不由於此
===
而能盡善繼善述之實以光其祖宗者也何也天人一理
創守一道均之以為民而已然則守成之道又豈外於仁
哉孟軻氏曰三代之得天下也以仁其失天下也以不仁
知所以失之則知所以保之矣恭惟
皇帝陛下
大孝格
天至仁育物十四年來民安物阜雖三代之治亦不過此然而
策士於廷猶皇皇焉欲保
祖宗之業遂民物之安思得良法要道以補所未照臣雖至愚
敢不奮發激昻以對揚於萬一乎臣惟天下之治二國勢
也人心也所以維持乎國勢者非法度乎所以固結乎人

punctuated:
臣敖銑。
臣對：臣聞聖王之於天下，其得之也以仁，其保之也亦以仁。夫仁者，天地好生之德也。天惟仁，故能生萬物，而無一物不被其澤；聖人惟仁，故能生萬民，而無一夫不獲其所。夫能使天下無一夫不獲其所，雖欲不王天下，其可得乎？何則？天能生物，不能自理，而命之聖人。聖人盡撙節愛養之宜，極財成輔相之道，是能以天地之心為心，自不能不以之為子矣。民生有欲，不能自遂，而望於聖人。聖人所欲與聚，所惡勿施，是能以父母之心為心，自不能不戴之以為君矣。是故自古得天下者，未有不本於此而能建可久可大之業以詒諸子孫者也；保天下者，亦未有不由於此而能盡善繼善述之實以光其祖宗者也。何也？天人一理，創守一道，均之以為民而已。然則守成之道，又豈外於仁哉？孟軻氏曰：「三代之得天下也以仁，其失天下也以不仁。」知所以失之，則知所以保之矣。
恭惟皇帝陛下，大孝格天，至仁育物。十四年來，民安物阜，雖三代之治，亦不過此。然而策士於廷，猶皇皇焉欲保祖宗之業，遂民物之安，思得良法要道以補所未照。臣雖至愚，敢不奮發激昻以對揚於萬一乎？臣惟天下之治二：國勢也，人心也。所以維持乎國勢者，非法度乎？所以固結乎人
translation_en:
Your servant Ao Xian.

Your servant replies: I have heard that sage kings gain All under Heaven through benevolence and preserve it likewise through benevolence. Benevolence is Heaven and Earth’s virtue of cherishing life. Because Heaven is benevolent, it brings forth the myriad things, and none fails to receive its bounty. Because the sage is benevolent, he nurtures the myriad people, and not a single person fails to find his proper place. If he can ensure that not one person in All under Heaven fails to find his proper place, could he avoid becoming its king even if he wished to?

Why is this? Heaven can bring things forth but cannot itself put them in order, and so entrusts this task to the sage. The sage fully observes the proper measures of restraint, care, and nurture, and carries to perfection the way of ordering and assisting the processes of Heaven and Earth. Thus he makes the heart of Heaven and Earth his own, and Heaven cannot but regard him as its son. People are born with desires but cannot fulfill them unaided, and so look to the sage. The sage gathers for them what they desire and does not impose upon them what they dislike. Thus he makes the heart of a parent his own, and the people cannot but uphold him as their ruler.

Therefore, since antiquity, none who gained All under Heaven has been able to establish an enduring and great enterprise to bequeath to his descendants without taking this as his foundation. Nor has anyone who preserved All under Heaven been able truly to carry forward his predecessors’ purposes and undertakings, thereby bringing glory to his ancestors, without following this path. Why? Heaven and humanity share one principle; founding a dynasty and preserving it follow one way. Both are simply for the sake of the people. How, then, could the way of preserving an established realm lie outside benevolence? Meng Ke said: “The Three Dynasties gained All under Heaven through benevolence and lost it through lack of benevolence.” To know how it was lost is to know how it may be preserved.

I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor moves Heaven with your great filial devotion and nurtures all things with your utmost benevolence. For fourteen years, the people have lived in peace and all things have flourished. Even the government of the Three Dynasties did not surpass this. Yet, in putting policy questions to scholars at court, you remain deeply concerned to preserve your ancestors’ enterprise and secure the well-being of the people and all things. You seek sound institutions and essential principles of governance to supplement what your discernment has not yet illuminated. Though your servant is exceedingly foolish, dare I fail to rouse myself with fervor and respond to your charge, however little I may contribute?

Your servant considers that the governance of All under Heaven has two aspects: the strength of the state and the hearts of the people. Is it not laws and institutions that sustain the strength of the state? As for what firmly binds the hearts of the people …

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
心者非德澤乎法度立則人知所畏而不敢背德澤施則
人知所愛而不忍背是故享國長久之道無有喻於此者
然必人心固而後國勢安德澤深而後法度行何也德澤
者本也法度者末也譬諸草木德澤者其根也根深矣又
從而沃之培之則其根益深譬諸居室德澤者其基也基
固矣又從而拓之築之則其基益固臣嘗觀諸三代禹有
天下弼成五服有典則以詒子孫矣湯有天下肇脩人紀
制風愆以儆有位矣至於周六卿分職五等建邦九一世
祿之制黨庠術序之教良法要道至詳至備然後世語三
代之治者不曰禹湯文武之法而曰禹湯文武之仁何則
仁其本也況禹之後如啟如少康皆能敬承禹道是故有
===
四百年之夏也湯之後如太甲武丁六七君皆能保乂有
殷是故有六百年之商也文武之後如成康宣王皆能繼續
光明文武之業是故有八百年之周也故曰有夏服天
命惟有歷年殷受天命惟有歷年而周家卜世卜年實過
其歷是則三代有道之長所以亘古今而獨盛者有由然
也嗣是而後漢則高祖以寬仁開之文帝以仁厚培之光
武明章以寬大煦嫗之厥享國四百年唐則太宗以仁義
啟之玄宗憲宗以經制維之厥享國三百年宋則前有太
祖建隆之治後有仁宗皇祐之化厥享國亦三百年其視
秦隋以下或百年或五六十年或僅止於一身者固不侔
矣然究其心則皆假仁者也夫假仁者猶可以延曆永祚

四百年之夏也湯之後如大甲武丁六七君皆能保又有

也嗣是而後漢則高祖以寬仁開之文帝以仁厚培之光

矣然究其心則皆假仁者也夫假仁者猶可以延曆永祚
punctuated:
心者，非德澤乎？法度立，則人知所畏而不敢背；德澤施，則人知所愛而不忍背。是故享國長久之道，無有喻於此者。然必人心固而後國勢安，德澤深而後法度行。何也？德澤者，本也；法度者，末也。譬諸草木，德澤者其根也。根深矣，又從而沃之培之，則其根益深。譬諸居室，德澤者其基也。基固矣，又從而拓之築之，則其基益固。
臣嘗觀諸三代：禹有天下，弼成五服，有典則以詒子孫矣；湯有天下，肇脩人紀，制風愆以儆有位矣。至於周，六卿分職，五等建邦，九一世祿之制，黨庠術序之教，良法要道，至詳至備。然後世語三代之治者，不曰禹湯文武之法，而曰禹湯文武之仁。何則？仁其本也。況禹之後，如啟如少康，皆能敬承禹道，是故有四百年之夏也；湯之後，如太甲武丁六七君，皆能保乂有殷，是故有六百年之商也；文武之後，如成康宣王，皆能繼續光明文武之業，是故有八百年之周也。故曰：「有夏服天命，惟有歷年；殷受天命，惟有歷年。」而周家卜世卜年，實過其歷。是則三代有道之長，所以亘古今而獨盛者，有由然也。
嗣是而後，漢則高祖以寬仁開之，文帝以仁厚培之，光武明章以寬大煦嫗之，厥享國四百年；唐則太宗以仁義啟之，玄宗憲宗以經制維之，厥享國三百年；宋則前有太祖建隆之治，後有仁宗皇祐之化，厥享國亦三百年。其視秦隋以下，或百年，或五六十年，或僅止於一身者，固不侔矣。然究其心，則皆假仁者也。夫假仁者猶可以延曆永祚
translation_en:
…hearts of the people—is it not beneficent bounty? When laws and institutions are established, people know what to fear and dare not turn against the ruler; when beneficent bounty is bestowed, people know what to love and cannot bear to turn against him. Thus, no means of ensuring a dynasty’s long endurance surpasses this. Yet only when the people’s hearts are steadfast is the state secure, and only when beneficent bounty is profound can laws and institutions take effect. Why? Beneficent bounty is the root; laws and institutions are the branches. To compare it to plants and trees, beneficent bounty is their root. Once the root is deep, further watering and tending make it deeper still. To compare it to a dwelling, beneficent bounty is its foundation. Once the foundation is firm, further extending and building make it firmer still.
Your servant has examined the Three Dynasties. When Yu possessed All under Heaven, he brought the five service zones to completion and left statutes and standards to his descendants. When Tang possessed All under Heaven, he first set human relationships in order and established prohibitions against corrupt practices and transgressions to admonish those in office. Under the Zhou, the six ministers divided their duties, and the five ranks of nobility established their states. There were institutions for taking one ninth of agricultural produce and granting hereditary stipends, and instruction in district and local schools. Sound laws and essential principles were supremely detailed and complete. Yet when later generations speak of the government of the Three Dynasties, they speak not of the laws of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, but of their benevolence. Why? Benevolence was their foundation. Moreover, among Yu’s successors, rulers such as Qi and Shaokang could all reverently carry on Yu’s way; hence the Xia endured for four hundred years. Among Tang’s successors, six or seven rulers, including Taijia and Wuding, could all preserve and govern Yin; hence the Shang endured for six hundred years. Among Wen and Wu’s successors, Kings Cheng, Kang, and Xuan could all continue and illuminate the achievements of Wen and Wu; hence the Zhou endured for eight hundred years. Thus it is said: “The Xia obeyed Heaven’s mandate and endured for many years; the Yin received Heaven’s mandate and endured for many years.” The house of Zhou, moreover, actually exceeded the span foretold by divination concerning its generations and years. There was thus a reason why the Three Dynasties’ long possession of the Way made them uniquely flourishing throughout history.
Thereafter, in the Han, Gaozu founded the dynasty through generosity and benevolence, Emperor Wen nurtured it through benevolence and kindness, and Guangwu, Ming, and Zhang fostered it through magnanimity; the dynasty endured for four hundred years. In the Tang, Taizong inaugurated it through benevolence and righteousness, and Xuanzong and Xianzong sustained it through established institutions; the dynasty endured for three hundred years. In the Song, there was first the good government of Taizu’s Jianlong era, and later the transforming influence of Renzong’s Huangyou era; that dynasty likewise endured for three hundred years. These were certainly unequalled by the Qin, Sui, and lesser dynasties, some of which lasted a hundred years, some fifty or sixty, and some only a single ruler’s lifetime. Yet if we examine their hearts, they were all merely borrowing benevolence for their purposes. If even those who borrowed benevolence could prolong their allotted years and perpetuate their dynastic blessings…

punctuated:
庶幾三代。則夫超軼漢唐宋之治，而上繼乎夏商周之盛者，當何如哉？洪惟太祖高皇帝迅掃胡元，肇造華夏，明物察倫，達乎天德，執象率物，根于至誠。其所建立，皆取法於帝王，求端於天地，德合覆載之大，明並日月之光，可謂兼創守而盡之矣。太宗文皇帝載靖內難，奄定兩京，聖德神功，昭布海宇。列聖相承，鑒于成憲，益隆弗替。是以百六十年于茲，仁風翔洽，德澤汪濊。陛下又以堯舜之資，入繼大統，臨御以來，蠲租以阜民財，賑貸以周民急，恤刑以蘇民命，天下之至仁也。是以內則百僚效職，以熙於庶績；外則夷狄向風，以輸於職貢。赫然中興之盛，豈徒曰守成而已哉！

夫何邇年災異頻仍，旱潦相繼？是豈天心仁愛陛下，以為修省之地耶？抑豈陛下之仁有所未純耶？臣請推廣仁之說焉。夫仁，人心也。心存則仁存，然人君每患於不存者，失在於自私而用智爾。自私則不能以有為為應迹，用智則不能以明覺為自然。一膜之外，視為胡越，是故天地自天地，民物自民物，吾身自吾身矣。大惟無私則公，公則廓然而無我；不用智則虛，虛
translation_en:
…approaching the Three Dynasties. What, then, would it take to surpass the governance of the Han, Tang, and Song and carry forward the flourishing rule of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou?

We reverently reflect that Taizu, the Gao Emperor, swiftly swept away the Mongol Yuan and founded anew the realm of Huaxia. He understood things and discerned human relationships, attaining Heaven’s virtue; he upheld the great exemplar and guided all beings, grounding himself in utmost sincerity. Everything he established took the sage emperors and kings as its models and sought its origins in Heaven and Earth. His virtue matched the greatness of Heaven’s sheltering and Earth’s sustaining embrace; his illumination equaled the radiance of sun and moon. He may be said to have fully accomplished both founding a dynasty and preserving it. Taizong, the Wen Emperor, then quelled internal troubles and secured the two capitals. His sagely virtue and divine achievements shone throughout the realm. The successive sage emperors took the established institutions as their guide, further enhancing them without allowing them to lapse. Thus, for the 160 years down to the present, the influence of benevolence has spread everywhere, and the beneficence of virtue has flowed abundantly.

Your Majesty, moreover, with the innate qualities of Yao and Shun, succeeded to the imperial line. Since ascending the throne, you have remitted taxes to enrich the people, provided relief and loans to meet their urgent needs, and exercised compassion in punishments to preserve their lives. This is the utmost benevolence under Heaven. Consequently, within the realm the officials discharge their duties, bringing all undertakings to fruition; beyond it, the Yi and Di peoples turn toward your civilizing influence and deliver their due tribute. Such is the resplendent flourishing of this dynastic resurgence! How could it be called merely preserving what was achieved before?

Why, then, have disasters and anomalies occurred repeatedly in recent years, with droughts and floods following one another? Could it be that Heaven, in its benevolent love for Your Majesty, is providing an occasion for self-cultivation and reflection? Or could Your Majesty’s benevolence still fall short of complete purity? Your servant begs leave to elaborate upon benevolence.

Benevolence is the human heart. When the heart is preserved, benevolence is preserved. Yet rulers frequently suffer from failing to preserve it; their fault lies simply in selfishness and calculated cleverness. Selfishness prevents them from making their actions responses to circumstances; calculated cleverness prevents their lucid awareness from operating naturally. Whatever lies beyond the membrane of their own bodies they regard as alien as the Hu and Yue. Thus Heaven and Earth remain merely Heaven and Earth, the people and other beings remain merely the people and other beings, and one’s own person remains merely one’s own person. Only [?] through freedom from selfishness does one become impartial; through impartiality one becomes expansive and free of self. By dispensing with calculated cleverness, one becomes empty and receptive; being empty and receptive…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
則物来而順應真見夫天地萬物本吾一體故不以天地
視天地而以吾身視天地不以萬物視萬物而以吾身四
肢百骸視萬物夫人之視四肢百骸寧有弗愛者哉視四
肢百骸而不愛者非仁也故一手足之痿痺一耳目之聵
盲一髮膚之疴癢心不與知是豈得為仁乎是故聖人通
天下為一身者也天下之飢者寒者疲癃殘疾困窮而拂
鬱者皆吾手足耳目髮膚之毀傷也思吾身之飢則必食
之矣思吾身之寒則必衣之矣思吾身之疲癃殘疾困窮
拂鬱則必維持調護之矣今者自朝廷以至百官自百官
以至萬民
陛下果能視之如吾一身否耶水旱蝗蝻無歲無之老弱轉死
===
===
於溝壑少壯流移於四方
陛下果能視之如吾手足耳目髮膚之毀傷否耶
陛下於此反之於心有一之未盡是
陛下一念之仁有未純也一念之仁未純則與天地不相似而
仁道或幾乎息矣欲望氣化大和民物阜安也不亦難乎
雖然帝王之治本於仁帝王之仁根於心然所以養其心
者豈有他哉亦惟在於崇敬畏戒逸欲親君子遠小人而
已矣臣見
陛下敬一之箴五箴之註
經筵罔間於寒暑儆戒不忘於燕閒所以養其心者固無有
弗純矣臣獨懼夫用人行政之道猶有所未盡也何則論

則物来而順應，真見夫天地萬物本吾一體，故不以天地視天地，而以吾身視天地；不以萬物視萬物，而以吾身四肢百骸視萬物。夫人之視四肢百骸，寧有弗愛者哉？視四肢百骸而不愛者，非仁也。故一手足之痿痺，一耳目之聵盲，一髮膚之疴癢，心不與知，是豈得為仁乎？是故聖人通天下為一身者也。天下之飢者、寒者、疲癃殘疾、困窮而拂鬱者，皆吾手足耳目髮膚之毀傷也。思吾身之飢，則必食之矣；思吾身之寒，則必衣之矣；思吾身之疲癃殘疾、困窮拂鬱，則必維持調護之矣。今者，自朝廷以至百官，自百官以至萬民，陛下果能視之如吾一身否耶？水旱蝗蝻，無歲無之，老弱轉死於溝壑，少壯流移於四方，陛下果能視之如吾手足耳目髮膚之毀傷否耶？陛下於此反之於心，有一之未盡，是陛下一念之仁有未純也。一念之仁未純，則與天地不相似，而仁道或幾乎息矣。欲望氣化大和、民物阜安也，不亦難乎？

雖然，帝王之治本於仁，帝王之仁根於心，然所以養其心者，豈有他哉？亦惟在於崇敬畏、戒逸欲、親君子、遠小人而已矣。臣見陛下敬一之箴、五箴之註，經筵罔間於寒暑，儆戒不忘於燕閒，所以養其心者，固無有弗純矣。臣獨懼夫用人行政之道猶有所未盡也。何則？論
translation_en:
…then, as things come, one responds to them fittingly, truly perceiving that Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things are fundamentally one body with oneself. Thus one regards Heaven and Earth as one’s own body, rather than as Heaven and Earth alone; one regards the myriad things as the limbs and bones of one’s own body, rather than as the myriad things alone. When people regard their own limbs and bones, could they fail to cherish them? To regard one’s limbs and bones without cherishing them is to lack benevolence. Thus, if a hand or foot becomes paralyzed or numb, an ear deaf or an eye blind, or any part of the hair or skin afflicted or itching, and the heart takes no cognizance of it, how could this count as benevolence? Accordingly, the sage embraces all under Heaven as one body. Those throughout the realm who are hungry or cold, infirm or disabled, impoverished or frustrated—all are injuries to our own hands, feet, ears, eyes, hair, and skin. When we consider our own body’s hunger, we surely feed it; when we consider its cold, we surely clothe it; when we consider its infirmity, disability, poverty, or frustration, we surely sustain and tend it. Now, from the court to the hundred officials, and from the hundred officials to the myriad people, can Your Majesty truly regard them as your own body? Floods, droughts, and locusts, both mature and young, occur every year. The old and weak perish in ditches and gullies, while the young and strong wander in all directions. Can Your Majesty truly regard this as injury to your own hands, feet, ears, eyes, hair, and skin? If Your Majesty examines your heart in these matters and finds even one respect in which you have fallen short, then the benevolence of your thought is not yet pure. If benevolence is impure in even a single thought, one ceases to accord with Heaven and Earth, and the Way of benevolence may almost come to an end. Would it not then be difficult to hope for supreme harmony in the transformations of vital energy, and for prosperity and peace among the people and all things?

Nevertheless, the government of emperors and kings is founded upon benevolence, and their benevolence is rooted in the heart. Is there any other means of nourishing that heart? It lies simply in upholding reverence and awe, guarding against indolence and desire, drawing close to noble men, and keeping petty men at a distance. Your servant has seen Your Majesty’s Admonition on Reverent Unity and your commentaries on the Five Admonitions. Your Classics Colloquia continue without interruption through cold and heat, and even in private leisure you do not forget vigilance and self-admonition. Surely there is nothing impure in the means by which you nourish your heart. My sole fear is that something remains unfulfilled in the way you employ men and conduct government. Why is this? Consider…

陛下能盡罷之乎横賜濫賞耗吾仁者也

punctuated: 夫壬人，害吾仁者也，陛下能盡去之乎？聲色貨利，誘吾仁者也，陛下能盡遠之乎？土木甲兵，妨吾仁者也，陛下能盡罷之乎？横賜濫賞，耗吾仁者也，陛下能盡革之乎？盖人之常情，務内者或遺乎外，謹始者多忽其終。臣願陛下終始此心，内外無間，體驗於深宫獨行之時，致審於刑賞舉措之際，則心日益存，仁日益熟，天德可全，而王道可終矣。所以永宗社萬禩之固，保家國千世之傳者，端不外此。尚何患災沴之不消，民物之不得其所哉？臣不勝惓惓仰望之至，謹對。
translation_en: …As for treacherous men, they injure one’s benevolence: can Your Majesty dismiss them all? Music, sensual pleasures, wealth, and profit tempt one away from benevolence: can Your Majesty keep them all at a distance? Construction projects and military undertakings obstruct one’s benevolence: can Your Majesty halt them all? Unwarranted gifts and indiscriminate rewards deplete one’s benevolence: can Your Majesty abolish them all? It is common human nature that those who attend to the inward sometimes neglect the outward, and those who are careful at the beginning often become heedless at the end. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would preserve this heart from beginning to end, allowing no division between the inward and the outward, personally putting it into practice when acting alone in the secluded palace, and exercising the utmost discernment when imposing punishments, granting rewards, and taking action. Then this heart will be increasingly preserved and benevolence increasingly perfected; the virtue of Heaven can be made complete, and the Kingly Way carried through to the end. The means of securing the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain for ten thousand years, and ensuring that the ruling house and state are transmitted for a thousand generations, lie wholly in this. Why then worry that calamities and baleful influences will not disappear, or that the people and all living things will not find their proper places? Your servant cannot contain his earnest hopes as he looks up to Your Majesty. Respectfully submitted in reply.

text:
臣郭朴
臣對臣聞人君建國家之業于無疆者有經國之規模有
植國之根本經國之規模存乎法植國之根本存乎仁創

規模也深仁厚澤真德實意使一世之心固結而不可解
者植國之根本也法制定則國賴之以立德澤深則民賴
之以生自古享國長久之道不外是二者向使一於法而
仁不足是謂徒法徒法不能以自行矣一於仁而法不周
是謂徒善徒善不足以為政矣創立之也無其本推行之
也無其具其何以底烝民之生若萬物之性以綿國家之

臣郭朴。

臣對：臣聞人君建國家之業于無疆者，有經國之規模，有植國之根本。經國之規模存乎法，植國之根本存乎仁。創法定制，立綱陳紀，使一代之法整肅而不可易者，經國之規模也；深仁厚澤，真德實意，使一世之心固結而不可解者，植國之根本也。法制定，則國賴之以立；德澤深，則民賴之以生。自古享國長久之道，不外是二者。向使一於法而仁不足，是謂徒法，徒法不能以自行矣；一於仁而法不周，是謂徒善，徒善不足以為政矣。創立之也無其本，推行之也無其具，其何以底烝民之生，若萬物之性，以綿國家之祚於泰山□□？

皇帝陛下中和建極，仁孝格天，聖神之化徧於海宇，寬仁之德洽於民心。纘祖宗之洪猷，剃朝野之積弊，帝王雍熙之盛、宗社悠久之休，在今日矣。乃不自滿假，進臣等于廷，策以永祚保邦之道，欲使民安物阜，以隆嘉靖之治。臣有以仰見皇上望道未見、求治若渴之盛心也。臣疎庸，不足以對揚明詔，敢不叅之史傳，酌之時宜，攄愚見以為
translation_en:
Your servant Guo Pu.

Your servant replies: I have heard that a ruler who establishes the enterprise of his state and ruling house for an unlimited duration must possess both a framework for governing the state and a foundation upon which to establish it. The framework for governing the state lies in laws; the foundation upon which to establish it lies in benevolence. To create laws and establish institutions, set out guiding principles and lay down regulations, so that the laws of a dynasty are orderly, rigorous, and unalterable: this is the framework for governing the state. To show profound benevolence and abundant kindness, genuine virtue and sincere intent, so that the hearts of an entire age are firmly bound together and cannot be sundered: this is the foundation upon which to establish the state. Once laws and institutions are settled, the state relies upon them for its establishment; when virtue and beneficence are profound, the people rely upon them for their livelihood. Since antiquity, the way to preserve a dynasty for a long time has extended no further than these two things. If one were to rely exclusively on laws while lacking sufficient benevolence, this would be called mere law, and mere law cannot put itself into effect. If one were to rely exclusively on benevolence while laws were incomplete, this would be called mere goodness, and mere goodness is insufficient for government. If establishment lacks its foundation and implementation lacks its instruments, how could one secure the livelihood of the multitude, accord with the nature of all things, and prolong the fortunes of the state and ruling house in relation to Mount Tai [two illegible characters; sense uncertain]?

Your Majesty the Emperor establishes the supreme standard through centrality and harmony, and your benevolence and filial piety reach Heaven. Your sagely and numinous transforming influence pervades all within the seas, and your magnanimity and benevolence suffuse the people's hearts. You carry forward the grand designs of your ancestors and remove [?] the accumulated abuses within the court and beyond it. The flourishing concord of emperors and kings, and the enduring blessings of the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain, are realized today. Yet you do not consider yourself fully accomplished. You have summoned us, your servants, to court and posed a policy question concerning the way to perpetuate dynastic fortunes and preserve the realm, wishing to bring peace to the people and abundance to all things, and thereby enhance the governance of the Jiajing reign. Through this, I reverently perceive Your Majesty's exalted resolve: you look toward the Way as though you had not yet seen it, and seek good government as one thirsting seeks water. Your servant is unlearned and mediocre, unworthy to respond to and extol your enlightened edict. How could I dare fail to consult the histories, weigh what suits the present circumstances, and set forth my humble views as…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
陛下獻乎今夫立國之道二心與政而已矣未有心弗達諸政
政弗本諸心者也歷觀前代之君其先世之創業後嗣之
纘承歷年歷世之永久靡不由茲是故方懋厥德下車泣
罪禹之仁也而其經國也有典有則以貽子孫焉關石和
鈞王府則有焉繼之者有若啟有若少康仁益深于民所
以衍而為四百年之夏也克寬克仁彰信兆民湯之仁也
而其經國也旁求俊彥啟迪後人焉三風十愆儆于有位
焉繼之者賢聖迭興仁益深于民所以衍而為六百年之
商也懷保惠鮮伐暴救民文武之仁也而其經綸之迹以
天保以上治內焉采薇以下治外焉嗣之者又有成康宣
王之君仁益深于民所以衍為八百年之周也故曰有夏
===
服天命惟有歷年有殷受天命惟有歷年而周家卜年卜
世寔過其歷是雖當太和之運亨豫之期而法制之維持
德澤之優渥亦不可誣也由周而來得國之正者莫如漢
唐宋漢高之寬明仁恕大綱以正足以延漢祚矣承之者
有若七制之主而文景之德澤尤深其有四百年之漢宜
也唐太宗之納諫愛民萬目以舉足以永唐祚矣承之者
有若三宗之君而開元之初政尤善其有三百年之唐宜
也藝祖之寬仁好生法制明肅其延宋祚有道矣繼之者
世有賢君而仁宗四十年恭儉之澤尤長其有三百年之
宋亦宜也是雖漢唐宋之治不足以擬夏商周之盛然所
以保民物而延國祚者孰不基于仁心仁政之兼備乎由

宋亦宜也是雖漢唐宋之治不足以擬夏商周之盛然所
以保民物而延國祚者孰不基于仁心仁政之兼備乎由
punctuated:
陛下獻乎？今夫立國之道二：心與政而已矣。未有心弗達諸政、政弗本諸心者也。歷觀前代之君，其先世之創業、後嗣之纘承，歷年歷世之永久，靡不由茲。是故方懋厥德，下車泣罪，禹之仁也；而其經國也，有典有則，以貽子孫焉；關石和鈞，王府則有焉。繼之者有若啟、有若少康，仁益深于民，所以衍而為四百年之夏也。克寬克仁，彰信兆民，湯之仁也；而其經國也，旁求俊彥，啟迪後人焉；三風十愆，儆于有位焉。繼之者賢聖迭興，仁益深于民，所以衍而為六百年之商也。懷保惠鮮，伐暴救民，文武之仁也；而其經綸之迹，以《天保》以上治內焉，《采薇》以下治外焉。嗣之者又有成、康、宣王之君，仁益深于民，所以衍為八百年之周也。故曰：「有夏服天命，惟有歷年；有殷受天命，惟有歷年。」而周家卜年卜世，寔過其歷。是雖當太和之運、亨豫之期，而法制之維持、德澤之優渥，亦不可誣也。

由周而來，得國之正者莫如漢、唐、宋。漢高之寬明仁恕，大綱以正，足以延漢祚矣。承之者有若七制之主，而文景之德澤尤深，其有四百年之漢宜也。唐太宗之納諫愛民，萬目以舉，足以永唐祚矣。承之者有若三宗之君，而開元之初政尤善，其有三百年之唐宜也。藝祖之寬仁好生，法制明肅，其延宋祚有道矣。繼之者世有賢君，而仁宗四十年恭儉之澤尤長，其有三百年之宋亦宜也。是雖漢、唐、宋之治不足以擬夏、商、周之盛，然所以保民物而延國祚者，孰不基于仁心仁政之兼備乎？由
translation_en:
…to offer to Your Majesty? Now, there are two essentials to establishing a state: the heart and government, and nothing more. Never is the heart without expression in government, nor government without its foundation in the heart. Surveying the rulers of former ages—the founding achievements of their ancestors, their successors’ continuation of those achievements, and the endurance of their states through years and generations—we find that none failed to depend upon these two essentials. Thus, diligently cultivating his virtue and descending from his carriage to weep over an offender expressed Yu’s benevolence. In ordering his state, he provided statutes and standards to bequeath to his descendants; the royal treasury maintained uniform weights and measures. His successors, such as Qi and Shaokang, extended benevolence ever more deeply among the people, thereby perpetuating the Xia dynasty for four hundred years. Being magnanimous and benevolent, and making his trustworthiness manifest to the myriad people, expressed Tang’s benevolence. In ordering his state, he sought outstanding men far and wide to guide later generations, and warned those holding office against the three pernicious habits and ten transgressions. Among his successors, worthy and sage rulers arose in succession, extending benevolence ever more deeply among the people and thereby perpetuating the Shang dynasty for six hundred years. Cherishing and protecting the people, showing kindness to those in distress, attacking tyrants, and rescuing the people expressed the benevolence of Kings Wen and Wu. As for their measures of government, the poems through “Heaven Protects” (Tianbao) concerned ordering internal affairs, while those from “Gathering Bracken” (Caiwei) onward concerned ordering external affairs. Their successors included Kings Cheng, Kang, and Xuan, who extended benevolence ever more deeply among the people, thereby perpetuating the Zhou dynasty for eight hundred years. Hence it is said: “The Xia bore Heaven’s mandate and endured for many years; the Yin received Heaven’s mandate and endured for many years.” The Zhou house, however, divined the years and generations of its rule and in fact exceeded their duration. Although these dynasties enjoyed an age of supreme harmony and a time of prosperity and ease, the sustaining force of their laws and institutions and the abundance of their beneficent influence cannot be denied.

Since the Zhou, no dynasties have equaled the Han, Tang, and Song in the legitimacy with which they acquired the realm. Gaozu of Han was magnanimous, discerning, benevolent, and forbearing; through these qualities the great guiding principles were set right, sufficiently to prolong the Han’s dynastic fortunes. His successors included the rulers of the seven distinguished reigns, and the beneficent influence of Emperors Wen and Jing was especially profound. It was fitting that the Han should endure for four hundred years. Taizong of Tang accepted remonstrance and cherished the people; through these qualities all the detailed affairs of government were attended to, sufficiently to perpetuate the Tang’s dynastic fortunes. His successors included the three revered emperors, and the government of the early Kaiyuan era was especially good. It was fitting that the Tang should endure for three hundred years. The founding emperor of Song was magnanimous and benevolent, cherished life, and maintained clear and strict laws and institutions: he possessed the means to prolong the Song’s dynastic fortunes. Worthy rulers succeeded him generation after generation, and the beneficent influence of Renzong’s forty years of reverence and frugality was especially lasting. It was likewise fitting that the Song should endure for three hundred years. Although the government of the Han, Tang, and Song could not match the flourishing rule of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou, which of their means of protecting the people and all living things and prolonging their dynastic fortunes was not founded upon the union of a benevolent heart and benevolent government? 績三考黜陟幽明言久任也今之任人或一歲而遷選或
未考而再調雖有惠愛之實莫究其施臣願復久任之法
可乎其二曰閱軍伍之實以飭武備臣聞詩云靺鞈有奭
以作六師言講武也今之武備行伍虛于老弱節制疎于
訓練設有征討之舉莫得其用臣願重閱實之令可乎其
三曰清賦役以恤民臣聞
陛下屢有蠲貸之詔而民不得蒙實惠者有司沮格之過也臣
願
陛下申戒百司務以愛民為心弛額外之徵省無名之賦蠲其
逋負寛其力役其不能宣
德意者黜之則民隱其少恤乎其四曰謹貯蓄以防歉臣聞
===
陛下嘗有積穀之令而不待收實效者有司奉行者之失也臣
願
陛下嚴飭所司專以養民為務省冗食之流節濫用之費謹其
出納防其侵漁而擾民廢事者罰之則荒政其少修乎夫
久任恤民則民蒙至治之澤而得以享樂利之休飭武備
荒則政無廢弛之弊而足以弭意外之變此即夏書之所
謂民惟邦本本固邦寧者也即周雅之所謂君子萬年保
其家邦者也今日之務莫急于此而王政之大端亦孰有
外于此哉
陛下留神弊政加志窮民不棄芻蕘不罪疎陋采臣之說下之
所司議其可行者行之則

績，三考黜陟幽明。」言久任也。今之任人，或一歲而遷選，或未考而再調，雖有惠愛之實，莫究其施。臣願復久任之法，可乎？

其二曰：閱軍伍之實以飭武備。臣聞《詩》云：「靺鞈有奭，以作六師。」言講武也。今之武備，行伍虛于老弱，節制疎于訓練，設有征討之舉，莫得其用。臣願重閱實之令，可乎？

其三曰：清賦役以恤民。臣聞陛下屢有蠲貸之詔，而民不得蒙實惠者，有司沮格之過也。臣願陛下申戒百司，務以愛民為心，弛額外之徵，省無名之賦，蠲其逋負，寛其力役。其不能宣德意者黜之，則民隱其少恤乎？

其四曰：謹貯蓄以防歉。臣聞陛下嘗有積穀之令，而不待收實效者，有司奉行者之失也。臣願陛下嚴飭所司，專以養民為務，省冗食之流，節濫用之費，謹其出納，防其侵漁，而擾民廢事者罰之，則荒政其少修乎？夫久任恤民，則民蒙至治之澤，而得以享樂利之休；飭武備荒，則政無廢弛之弊，而足以弭意外之變。此即《夏書》之所謂「民惟邦本，本固邦寧」者也，即《周雅》之所謂「君子萬年，保其家邦」者也。今日之務，莫急于此，而王政之大端，亦孰有外于此哉？陛下留神弊政，加志窮民，不棄芻蕘，不罪疎陋，采臣之說，下之所司，議其可行者行之，則
translation_en:
…performance; after three assessments, demote the obscure and promote the illustrious.” This speaks of keeping officials long in office. In appointments today, some are selected for promotion after a single year, while others are transferred again before even being assessed. Though they may have genuinely benefited and cared for the people, they cannot carry their work through. Might Your Majesty restore the practice of long tenure in office?

The second proposal is to inspect the actual condition of the military ranks in order to put military preparedness in order. Your servant has heard that the Book of Odes says: “Their leather ceremonial aprons glow crimson, as they rouse the six armies.” This speaks of military training. In military preparedness today, the ranks are depleted through age and infirmity, and command and discipline are lax for want of training. Should a campaign become necessary, these forces could not be put to effective use. Might Your Majesty give renewed weight to the order for inspections of actual conditions?

The third proposal is to put taxes and labor services in order so as to relieve the people. Your servant has heard that Your Majesty has repeatedly issued edicts granting remissions and relief. That the people have been unable to receive tangible benefits is the fault of the responsible officials, who obstruct their implementation. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would renew your admonitions to all offices, requiring them to make care for the people their guiding concern: abolish levies beyond the prescribed quotas, reduce taxes imposed without legitimate grounds, remit arrears, and lighten compulsory labor services. Dismiss those unable to carry out your benevolent intentions. Would this not bring some relief to the people's suffering?

The fourth proposal is to attend carefully to stockpiling in order to guard against poor harvests. Your servant has heard that Your Majesty previously ordered the accumulation of grain, yet tangible results have not been awaited [?]; this is a failing of the officials charged with implementation. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would strictly instruct the responsible offices to devote themselves to sustaining the people: reduce the number of superfluous dependents maintained at public expense, curtail extravagant expenditure, carefully manage receipts and disbursements, and prevent embezzlement and exploitation. Punish those who harass the people and neglect their duties. Would this not bring some improvement to famine administration?

With long official tenures and relief for the people, the people would receive the blessings of excellent government and enjoy happiness and prosperity. With military affairs put in order and preparations made against famine, government would be free from neglect and laxity and could quell unforeseen disturbances. This is precisely what the Documents of Xia means by “The people are the foundation of the state; when the foundation is firm, the state is at peace.” It is also what the Court Hymns of Zhou means by “May the lord live ten thousand years, preserving his house and state.” Among today's affairs, none is more urgent than these; and what major principle of kingly government lies beyond them? If Your Majesty attends to defective administration, gives thought to the impoverished people, does not discard the counsel of grass cutters and wood gatherers or condemn my ignorance and inadequacy, accepts your servant's proposals, and refers them to the responsible offices to deliberate upon and implement those that are practicable, then…

皇仁以沛，國脉以滋，邦本以培，王靈以振，黎民樂於變之治，萬物遂咸若之性矣。
抑臣猶有說焉。臣聞帝王之治本於道，帝王之道本於心，帝王之心純於敬，帝王之敬精於學。要之，心者，聖學之要、天德之基、王道之本也。是故學所以養此也，敬所以存此也，道所以達此也，治所以成此也。以育民物，以立綱紀，以覆天下，以澤後世，孰非此心之用哉？况夫人主之心，攻之甚衆，而保之甚難，使非純一之至，何以達之治而詣其極耶？
陛下謙虛望道，宵旰圖基命，邃其學矣；執中協一，法祖憲天，懋其敬矣；明倫盡制，尊親廣孝，順其道矣；秉憲貞度，禮賢愛民，隆其治矣。凡此謂不由於聖心之純哉？臣愚杞人之懷，惟願陛下存之不息，保之有終，不移于紛華波蕩之中，不奪於外誘物欲之感，則純一不已之施設、至誠無息之功用，上以昭

…imperial benevolence will flow abundantly, the lifeblood of the state will be nourished, the foundations of the realm will be strengthened, and royal authority will be invigorated. The common people will rejoice in a government that transforms them, and all things will fulfill their natures in universal harmony.
Yet your servant has something further to say. Your servant has heard that the government of emperors and kings is rooted in the Way; their Way is rooted in the heart; their hearts are purified through reverence; and their reverence is refined through learning. In sum, the heart is the essential element of sagely learning, the foundation of heavenly virtue, and the root of the Kingly Way. Thus learning nurtures this heart, reverence preserves it, the Way gives it expression, and government brings it to fulfillment. To nurture the people and all living things, establish the guiding principles and ordering bonds, shelter all under Heaven, and bestow blessings upon later generations—which of these is not a function of this heart? Moreover, the ruler’s heart faces exceedingly many assaults and is exceedingly difficult to safeguard. Unless it attains the utmost purity and singleness, how can it find expression in government and bring that government to perfection?
Your Majesty humbly aspires to the Way, laboring from before dawn until late at night to secure the foundations of the heavenly mandate, and has thereby deepened your learning. By holding fast to the Mean, achieving unity, taking your ancestors as models, and following Heaven, you have strengthened your reverence. By clarifying human relationships and fully establishing their regulations [?], honoring your parents and extending filial piety, you have followed the Way. By upholding established norms and maintaining correct standards, honoring the worthy and loving the people, you have brought your government to flourishing excellence. Can any of this be said not to arise from the purity of your sagely heart? Your foolish servant harbors the apprehensions of the man of Qi who feared that the sky would fall. I wish only that Your Majesty preserve this heart without ceasing and safeguard it to the end, neither swayed amid the tumultuous currents of worldly splendor nor overcome by the influence of external temptations and material desires. Then the measures arising from unceasing purity and singleness, and the achievements of utmost sincerity that never rests, will serve, above, to make manifest…

punctuated: 祖宗之烈，下以永國家之傳，而經國之規模、植國之根本，有隆而無替矣。臣草茅下士，不識忌諱，冒瀆天威，無任隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en: …the glorious achievements of Your Majesty’s ancestors, and below, perpetuate the succession of the state. Thus the grand framework for governing the state and the foundations on which it stands will flourish without decline. Your servant, a humble scholar from the countryside, ignorant of what must not be said, has rashly offended Your Majesty’s awe-inspiring dignity and is overwhelmed with utmost dread. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
臣任瀛
臣對臣聞帝王以仁心而肇鴻龐之業以仁政而保隆平
之治夫仁者人心之生理也天地之所以生育長養萬物
者在於仁人君之所以代天理物者亦在於仁心者政之
本也而政者所以推此心之仁以達之天下也大哉仁之
為用乎斂之無所不具充之無所不周至哉仁之為德乎
推之而無不準動之而無不化故創業不以仁草昧之初
何以收拾其渙散之心守成不以仁承平之日何以固結
其綏服之念有仁以遂其欲則愛之也如父母而歸之也
如流水民將懷之而不能舍矣有仁以厚其澤則浹於肌
膚淪於骨髓民將依之而不忍去矣夫君人者繼天立極
===
固將以為民也眾非元后何戴后非眾罔與守邦民懷之
而不能舍則有元后之戴而無仇讎之心也民依之而不
忍去則有盤石之固而無瓦解之勢也取之以仁守之以
仁心政兼備本末具舉享國長久之道在是矣三代所以
歷年多享國久者政以能盡是道我
國家仁厚一脉而歷年之多享國之久將與天壤相為無窮
遠過三代之歷矣下此而漢唐宋又何足言哉欽惟
皇帝陛下以剛健純粹之資緝熈光明之學
駿德貫於天地偉畧超乎古今
勵精化理
光濟前休深仁厚澤丕冒群生

勵精化理
光浙前休深仁厚澤丕冒群生
punctuated:
臣任瀛。
臣對：臣聞帝王以仁心而肇鴻龐之業，以仁政而保隆平之治。夫仁者，人心之生理也。天地之所以生育長養萬物者，在於仁；人君之所以代天理物者，亦在於仁。心者，政之本也；而政者，所以推此心之仁以達之天下也。大哉，仁之為用乎！斂之無所不具，充之無所不周。至哉，仁之為德乎！推之而無不準，動之而無不化。故創業不以仁，草昧之初，何以收拾其渙散之心？守成不以仁，承平之日，何以固結其綏服之念？有仁以遂其欲，則愛之也如父母，而歸之也如流水，民將懷之而不能舍矣。有仁以厚其澤，則浹於肌膚，淪於骨髓，民將依之而不忍去矣。夫君人者繼天立極，固將以為民也。眾非元后何戴？后非眾罔與守邦。民懷之而不能舍，則有元后之戴，而無仇讎之心也；民依之而不忍去，則有盤石之固，而無瓦解之勢也。取之以仁，守之以仁，心政兼備，本末具舉，享國長久之道在是矣。三代所以歷年多、享國久者，政以能盡是道。我國家仁厚一脉，而歷年之多、享國之久，將與天壤相為無窮，遠過三代之歷矣。下此而漢唐宋，又何足言哉！欽惟皇帝陛下，以剛健純粹之資、緝熈光明之學，駿德貫於天地，偉畧超乎古今，勵精化理，光濟前休，深仁厚澤，丕冒群生。
translation_en:
Your servant, Ren Ying.

Your servant replies: I have heard that emperors and kings establish their grand enterprises through benevolent hearts and preserve flourishing, peaceful rule through benevolent government. Benevolence is the life-giving principle of the human heart. It is through benevolence that Heaven and Earth bring forth and nurture the myriad things; it is likewise through benevolence that the ruler governs all things on Heaven’s behalf. The heart is the foundation of government, and government is the means of extending the benevolence of this heart throughout the world. How great is the efficacy of benevolence! Gathered within, it contains everything; expanded outward, it reaches everywhere. How perfect is benevolence as a virtue! Applied, it accords with every circumstance; set in motion, it transforms everything. Thus, if a dynasty is founded without benevolence, how can the scattered hearts of the people be brought together in the initial age of disorder? If an established dynasty is maintained without benevolence, how can the people’s peaceful allegiance be secured in times of lasting peace? When benevolence fulfills their desires, they love their ruler as their parents and turn to him as water flows onward: the people will cherish him and be unable to forsake him. When benevolence makes his beneficence abundant, it penetrates their flesh and sinks into their bones and marrow: the people will depend upon him and be unwilling to leave.

The ruler of men succeeds Heaven and establishes the supreme standard, surely for the people’s sake. Without a sovereign, whom would the multitude uphold? Without the multitude, the sovereign would have none with whom to defend the state. When the people cherish him and cannot forsake him, they uphold him as sovereign and harbor no enmity. When the people depend upon him and cannot bear to leave, his rule is as firm as a great rock and faces no prospect of disintegration. To acquire the realm through benevolence and preserve it through benevolence, with both the heart and government fully cultivated, and both foundation and consequences attended to: herein lies the way to enduring possession of the realm. The Three Dynasties endured for so many years and possessed their realms so long precisely because they fully realized this way. Our dynasty has maintained an unbroken tradition of benevolence and generosity. Its years and its possession of the realm will endure without limit alongside Heaven and Earth, far surpassing the duration of the Three Dynasties. As for the lesser Han, Tang, and Song dynasties, what need is there even to speak of them?

I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor possesses a firm, vigorous, pure disposition and learning continually cultivated toward illumination. Your great virtue pervades Heaven and Earth, and your magnificent designs surpass those of antiquity and the present. You devote your energies to transforming and governing the people, gloriously carrying forward the splendid achievements of your predecessors. Your profound benevolence and abundant beneficence extend broadly over all living beings…

text:

宗社億萬年靈長之祚端在是矣然且
既聖而不自聖已安而不自安乃於
萬幾之暇進臣等於
廷發
德音下
明詔此即唐堯稽衆舍已之意虞舜好問好察之心也顧以
臣之謭陋何足以仰承休德
少裨
聖政之萬一乎伏念臣草茅賤士一旦遭際若此豈敢隱默不
言以負
===
陛下今日策士之意哉臣惟天生民有欲無主乃亂故必有出
類之才起而君長之治之而爭奪息導之而生養遂教之
而倫理明立君以安民者天之心也易曰天地之大德曰
生聖人之大寶曰位何以守位曰仁以仁厚立國者帝王
君天下之道也故必存於內者有不忍人之心而後發於
外者有不忍人之政既不失之徒善又不失之徒法帝王
立國之規模保治之要道不越乎此自古歷年之多享國
長久以三代為稱首求其所以如禹之乘四載而抑洪水
勞八年而粒黎民祗台德先而下車泣辜地平天成而萬
世永賴何莫而非仁也及啓又能敬承繼禹之道孰非以
仁守之乎此有夏所以享國四百年之多也成湯祝網以

punctuated:
恩澤及於庶物，聲教洽於于玆，宗社億萬年靈長之祚端在是矣。然且既聖而不自聖，已安而不自安，乃於萬幾之暇，進臣等於廷，發德音，下明詔。此即唐堯稽衆舍已之意，虞舜好問好察之心也。顧以臣之謭陋，何足以仰承休德，少裨聖政之萬一乎？伏念臣草茅賤士，一旦遭際若此，豈敢隱默不言，以負陛下今日策士之意哉？
臣惟天生民有欲，無主乃亂，故必有出類之才，起而君長之，治之而爭奪息，導之而生養遂，教之而倫理明。立君以安民者，天之心也。《易》曰：「天地之大德曰生，聖人之大寶曰位。何以守位？曰仁。」以仁厚立國者，帝王君天下之道也。故必存於內者有不忍人之心，而後發於外者有不忍人之政，既不失之徒善，又不失之徒法。帝王立國之規模，保治之要道，不越乎此。自古歷年之多、享國長久，以三代為稱首。求其所以，如禹之乘四載而抑洪水，勞八年而粒黎民，祗台德先而下車泣辜，地平天成而萬世永賴，何莫而非仁也？及啓又能敬承繼禹之道，孰非以仁守之乎？此有夏所以享國四百年之多也。成湯祝網以
translation_en:
…Your beneficence reaches all things, and your moral influence and instruction spread everywhere [?]. Herein lies the enduring blessing of the imperial ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain for countless ages. Yet, though already sage, Your Majesty does not regard yourself as sage; though already secure, you do not rest in security. Amid the countless affairs of government, you have found time to summon us, your servants, to court, utter your gracious words, and issue your enlightened edict. This embodies Tang Yao’s resolve to consult the multitude and set aside his own views, and Yu Shun’s disposition to inquire eagerly and examine closely. But how could someone as shallow and ignorant as your servant adequately respond to your excellent virtue or contribute even the slightest assistance to your sagely government? I humbly reflect that I am a lowly scholar from the countryside, suddenly granted such an opportunity. How could I dare remain silent and betray Your Majesty’s purpose in examining scholars with policy questions today?
Your servant considers that Heaven gives birth to the people with desires; without a ruler, disorder ensues. Thus someone of outstanding ability must arise to rule and lead them. By governing them, he ends contention and seizure; by guiding them, he enables them to live and sustain themselves; by teaching them, he makes human relationships and moral principles clear. To establish a ruler so that the people may live in peace is Heaven’s intention. The Book of Changes says: “The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life; the great treasure of the sage is called position. By what is position maintained? By benevolence.” To found a state upon benevolence and generosity is the way by which emperors and kings rule all under Heaven. They must first harbor within themselves a heart that cannot bear others’ suffering; only then can they manifest outwardly a government that cannot bear others’ suffering. Thus they avoid both the failing of mere good intentions and the failing of mere laws. The pattern by which emperors and kings found states, and the essential means by which they preserve good government, extend no further than this. Since antiquity, the Three Dynasties have been foremost in the number of years and the length of time they held their realms. Consider the reasons for this. Yu traveled by four modes of conveyance to subdue the floods, labored for eight years to provide the common people with grain, reverently put his own virtue first, and descended from his carriage to weep over an offender. The earth was brought to order and Heaven’s work accomplished, with benefits upon which all later generations would forever depend. Which of these acts was not benevolent? When Qi in turn reverently carried on Yu’s way, was this not preserving the realm through benevolence? This is why the Xia held their realm for fully four hundred years. title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
懷群動禱旱以康兆民代虐以寬而子惠困窮推亡固存
而表正萬邦何莫非仁也太甲克終允德盤庚訓民遷國
高宗嘉靖殷邦小大罔怨孰非以仁守之乎此有商所以
享國六百載之久也至於有周文王之惠鮮懷保而澤及
枯骨明德慎罰而咸和萬民武王之惇信明義而重民五
教勝殷遏劉而永清四海何莫而非仁也逮乎成王禮樂
大備刑措不用康王率循大卞對揚光訓守之以仁如此
此所以永定郟鄏之鼎卜年八百而又過其曆焉自是而
降漢有天下四百年若高帝鏖秦誅項蕩滌八荒約法三
章與民更始寬仁大度者也繼以文帝恭脩玄默景帝恭
儉愛民光武除莽苛政總攬權綱才明勇畧同符高祖者
===
也繼以明帝法令分明幽枉必達章帝平徭簡賦事從寬
厚唐有天下三百年若高祖起自晉陽以除隋亂太宗擒
充戮竇掃滅群雄致治之美庶幾成康後世識度弘遠英
武果斷有如玄宗英睿有謀仁愛孝友有如肅宗志平僭
叛能用忠謀有如憲宗至於宋興合數世之瓜分削百年
之根據豁達大度愛養民力而仁義之風無讓漢唐者太
祖也洞察隱微日用儉素而於文籍尤所篤好者太宗也
深仁厚澤而培植國本者仁宗也繼體守文而中興王業
者高宗也肆宋享國亦三百年惟漢唐宋施仁有廣狹淺
深之不同故國祚亦因之而有脩短之殊雖其君德有純
駁心有誠偽政雜王伯而要之仁厚一念以為立國之規

punctuated:
懷群動，禱旱以康兆民，代虐以寬而子惠困窮，推亡固存而表正萬邦，何莫非仁也？太甲克終允德，盤庚訓民遷國，高宗嘉靖殷邦，小大罔怨，孰非以仁守之乎？此有商所以享國六百載之久也。至於有周，文王之惠鮮懷保而澤及枯骨，明德慎罰而咸和萬民；武王之惇信明義而重民五教，勝殷遏劉而永清四海，何莫而非仁也？逮乎成王，禮樂大備，刑措不用；康王率循大卞，對揚光訓，守之以仁如此。此所以永定郟鄏之鼎，卜年八百，而又過其曆焉。

自是而降，漢有天下四百年。若高帝鏖秦誅項，蕩滌八荒，約法三章，與民更始，寬仁大度者也。繼以文帝恭脩玄默，景帝恭儉愛民，光武除莽苛政，總攬權綱，才明勇畧同符高祖者也。繼以明帝法令分明，幽枉必達，章帝平徭簡賦，事從寬厚。唐有天下三百年。若高祖起自晉陽，以除隋亂；太宗擒充戮竇，掃滅群雄，致治之美，庶幾成康。後世識度弘遠、英武果斷有如玄宗，英睿有謀、仁愛孝友有如肅宗，志平僭叛、能用忠謀有如憲宗。至於宋興，合數世之瓜分，削百年之根據，豁達大度，愛養民力，而仁義之風無讓漢唐者，太祖也；洞察隱微，日用儉素，而於文籍尤所篤好者，太宗也；深仁厚澤而培植國本者，仁宗也；繼體守文而中興王業者，高宗也。肆宋享國亦三百年。惟漢唐宋施仁有廣狹淺深之不同，故國祚亦因之而有脩短之殊。雖其君德有純駁，心有誠偽，政雜王伯，而要之，仁厚一念以為立國之規
translation_en:
…to cherish all living creatures, prayed during drought to bring well-being to the multitudes, replaced cruelty with leniency and cared like a father for those in distress and poverty, overthrew those destined to perish and secured those fit to endure, and set a corrective example for the myriad states: which of these acts was not benevolence? Tai Jia maintained true virtue to the end; Pan Geng instructed the people and relocated the capital; Gaozong brought good order and peace to Yin, so that neither great nor small harbored resentment. Which of them did not preserve his realm through benevolence? This is why the Shang dynasty enjoyed its dominion for six hundred years. Coming to the Zhou, King Wen showed kindness to the bereft and cherished and protected the people, his beneficence extending even to dry bones; he made virtue manifest and exercised caution in punishment, bringing harmony to all the people. King Wu upheld trustworthiness and made righteousness clear, attaching importance to the people's instruction in the five moral relationships; he conquered Yin and stopped the slaughter, securing lasting peace throughout the world. Which of these acts was not benevolence? Under King Cheng, rites and music were fully established, and punishments were set aside, unused. King Kang followed the great laws and reverently upheld the illustrious instructions. Such was their preservation of the realm through benevolence. This is why the dynastic tripods were firmly established at Jiaru: divination foretold eight hundred years, and the dynasty lasted even beyond that allotted span.

Thereafter, the Han possessed the empire for four hundred years. Emperor Gao fought fiercely against Qin and executed Xiang Yu, swept clean the eight reaches of the world, reduced the laws to three articles, and made a fresh beginning with the people: he was lenient, benevolent, and magnanimous. He was succeeded by Emperor Wen, who reverently cultivated profound tranquility, and Emperor Jing, who was respectful and frugal and loved the people. Guangwu abolished Wang Mang's harsh government and took firm command of sovereign authority; in talent, discernment, courage, and strategic ability, he matched Gaozu. He was followed by Emperor Ming, whose laws and commands were clear and under whom even hidden grievances were sure to reach the throne, and Emperor Zhang, who equalized labor service, reduced taxation, and conducted affairs with leniency and generosity. The Tang possessed the empire for three hundred years. Gaozu rose from Jinyang to put an end to the disorder under the Sui. Taizong captured Wang Shichong and executed Dou Jiande, swept away the contending warlords, and achieved a quality of government approaching that of Kings Cheng and Kang. Among later rulers, Xuanzong possessed broad and far-reaching judgment, martial prowess, and decisiveness; Suzong was perceptive and resourceful, benevolent and loving, filial and devoted to his brothers; Xianzong was intent on suppressing usurpers and rebels and could employ loyal counsel. When the Song arose, it reunited territories fragmented for generations and eliminated entrenched powers of a hundred years' standing. It was Taizu who was open-minded and magnanimous, cherished and nurtured the people's resources, and fostered a spirit of benevolence and righteousness that yielded nothing to the Han and Tang. It was Taizong who discerned the hidden and subtle, lived frugally and simply, and was particularly devoted to books. It was Renzong who, through profound benevolence and abundant beneficence, nourished the foundations of the state. It was Gaozong who inherited the throne, preserved the established institutions, and revived the royal enterprise. Thus the Song, too, enjoyed its dominion for three hundred years. Yet the benevolence practiced by the Han, Tang, and Song differed in breadth and depth, and their dynastic lifespans accordingly differed in length. Although their rulers' virtue varied in purity, their intentions in sincerity, and their government mingled the ways of the true king and the hegemon, nevertheless, their commitment to benevolence and generosity served as the framework for founding the state…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
模斷斷乎不可誣也
聖制所謂基之於先王德洽於民心亦繼之以嗣王能盡持盈
慎滿之道是已洪惟我
太祖高皇帝憫元政之不綱慨生民之無主躬提師旅誓清四
海自起義臨濠即拳拳以安養生息百姓為己任命將征
伐每以毋妄殺毋焚掠為戒平武昌以來即議定律雖當
草創之初而投戈講藝息馬論道納不嗜殺人之說焚錦
衣衛之刑具惟欲拯斯民於塗炭躋天下於衽席其生萬
民之心即天地生萬物之心也逮天下既定於是事為之
制曲為之防凡所以維持天下左右斯民者無所不用其
至稽六典以建官列藩省以制外重
===
親藩之封廣衛兵之設有
大誥三編以訓戒臣民有卧碑監規以教育生徒於萬民也
有種桑之令有給鹽之惠於軍士也有月粮之給衣物之
賜而減租之
詔賑恤之令無歲不下
宮中無事誦論語節用愛人之言嘆為格言見晁錯論富壽安
逸之旨而嘆其切志趣定矣秦皇漢武好尚神仙以求長
生則深論其非宋真宗信天書喜祥瑞則厭惡其事好尚
端矣戒嗜慾則毀縷金床碎水精宮刻漏節財用則宮室
但取朴素宮中隙地惟用種蔬命牛諒定禮命陶凱定樂
而中和之用著鄉飲有讀法高年有賜爵而風動之化成

有種桑之令有給鹽之惠於軍士也有月糧之給衣物之
賜而减租之
詔賑恤之令無歲不下
宮中無事誦論語節用愛人之言嘆爲格言見晁錯論富壽安
逸之旨而嘆其切志趣定矣秦皇漢武好尚神仙以求長
生則深論其非宋真宗信天書言祥瑞則厭惡其事好尚
端矣戒嗜慾則毀鏤金床碎水精宮刻漏節財用則宮室
