而中和之用著鄉飲有讀法高年有賜爵而風動之化成
punctuated:
模，斷斷乎不可誣也。聖制所謂「基之於先王，德洽於民心，亦繼之以嗣王能盡持盈慎滿之道」，是已。
洪惟我太祖高皇帝，憫元政之不綱，慨生民之無主，躬提師旅，誓清四海。自起義臨濠，即拳拳以安養生息百姓為己任。命將征伐，每以毋妄殺、毋焚掠為戒。平武昌以來，即議定律。雖當草創之初，而投戈講藝，息馬論道，納不嗜殺人之說，焚錦衣衛之刑具，惟欲拯斯民於塗炭，躋天下於衽席。其生萬民之心，即天地生萬物之心也。逮天下既定，於是事為之制，曲為之防，凡所以維持天下、左右斯民者，無所不用其至。稽六典以建官，列藩省以制外，重親藩之封，廣衛兵之設。有《大誥》三編以訓戒臣民，有卧碑、監規以教育生徒。於萬民也，有種桑之令，有給鹽之惠；於軍士也，有月粮之給、衣物之賜。而減租之詔、賑恤之令，無歲不下。
宮中無事，誦《論語》節用愛人之言，嘆為格言；見晁錯論富壽安逸之旨，而嘆其切，志趣定矣。秦皇、漢武好尚神仙以求長生，則深論其非；宋真宗信天書、喜祥瑞，則厭惡其事，好尚端矣。戒嗜慾，則毀縷金床，碎水精宮刻漏；節財用，則宮室但取朴素，宮中隙地惟用種蔬。命牛諒定禮，命陶凱定樂，而中和之用著；鄉飲有讀法，高年有賜爵，而風動之化成。
translation_en:
…as a guiding pattern: this most assuredly cannot be denied. This is precisely what Your Majesty’s pronouncement means by saying, “The foundation was laid by former kings, whose virtue permeated the people’s hearts; they were then followed by successor kings who could fully practice the way of preserving fullness and exercising caution amid abundance.”
We reverently reflect that our Taizu, the Exalted Emperor, distressed by the collapse of orderly government under the Yuan and grieved that the people had no sovereign, personally led his armies and vowed to pacify all within the Four Seas. From the time he raised his righteous forces at Linhao, he earnestly took upon himself the responsibility of bringing the common people peace and sustenance and enabling them to recover and prosper. Whenever he ordered generals to undertake campaigns, he admonished them against indiscriminate killing, burning, and plunder. After pacifying Wuchang, he immediately deliberated on establishing a legal code. Even during the dynasty’s founding, he laid aside weapons to discuss the classical arts and rested his horses to discourse on the Way. He accepted the teaching that a ruler should take no pleasure in killing and burned the torture instruments of the Embroidered Uniform Guard. His sole desire was to rescue the people from misery and bring all under Heaven to the ease of resting upon sleeping mats. His concern to sustain the lives of the myriad people was the very concern with which Heaven and Earth give life to all things.
Once the realm had been pacified, he established regulations for every matter and safeguards for every contingency. He exerted himself to the utmost in everything that sustained the realm and aided its people. He consulted the Six Codes to establish offices, arrayed provincial administrations to govern the outlying regions, attached great importance to the enfeoffment of imperial princes, and expanded the establishment of guard troops. There were the three compilations of the Grand Pronouncements to instruct and admonish officials and commoners, and the school admonition tablets and Directorate of Education regulations to educate students. For the common people, there were orders to plant mulberry trees and the benefaction of salt distributions; for soldiers, monthly grain allowances and gifts of clothing. Not a year passed without edicts reducing taxes and orders providing relief.
In leisure moments within the palace, he recited the Analects’ words on being sparing in expenditure and loving the people, admiring them as a guiding maxim. When he read Chao Cuo’s discussion of wealth, longevity, peace, and ease, he admired its pertinence: his aspirations were firmly settled. He strongly condemned the First Emperor of Qin and Emperor Wu of Han for their devotion to immortals in pursuit of everlasting life. He abhorred Emperor Zhenzong of Song’s belief in heavenly writings and delight in auspicious signs: his preferences were upright. To restrain indulgence and desire, he destroyed a bed ornamented with gold thread and smashed a crystal palace-shaped clepsydra. To economize, he required only simplicity in palace buildings and used the vacant ground within the palace solely for growing vegetables. He ordered Niu Liang to establish the rites and Tao Kai to establish the music, thereby manifesting the efficacy of equilibrium and harmony. Laws were read aloud at the community drinking ceremonies, and honorary ranks were granted to the elderly; thus a transforming influence spread like the wind.

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
此所以復帝王所自立之中國正中夏文明之大統儒臣
宋濂所謂功高萬古得國之正獨禀全智敬天勤民家法
之嚴兵政有統是六者亦庶幾鋪張揚厲我
聖祖之功德者哉昔武王之反商政而當時猶謂之於湯有光
況胡元以夷狄入主中國天地於是易位日月於是晦冥
綱常於是淪斁自古以來中國所未有之禍也我
太祖起而驅逐之而廓清之其德業之隆功烈之盛振古之所
無者也又豈漢唐宋區區一時之功業可得而比擬其萬
一也哉是以道洽政治歷年久遠
詒燕翼於萬年
垂鴻休於無疆

此所以復帝王所自立之中國，正中夏文明之大統。儒臣宋濂所謂功高萬古、得國之正、獨禀全智、敬天勤民、家法之嚴、兵政有統，是六者，亦庶幾鋪張揚厲我聖祖之功德者哉！昔武王之反商政，而當時猶謂之於湯有光。況胡元以夷狄入主中國，天地於是易位，日月於是晦冥，綱常於是淪斁，自古以來中國所未有之禍也。我太祖起而驅逐之，而廓清之，其德業之隆、功烈之盛，振古之所無者也。又豈漢唐宋區區一時之功業，可得而比擬其萬一也哉！是以道洽政治，歷年久遠，詒燕翼於萬年，垂鴻休於無疆。
太宗文皇帝中靖家邦，纂述大統，潤色洪業。列聖相承，守而弗替，百六十餘年來，率皆以大聖之德而行至仁之化，以純王之心而施純王之政。創業守成，盡善盡美，聖子神孫所當遵行體念，永永不可忘焉者也。
恭惟陛下自臨御以來，圖治，宵旰不暇，意禮文，留心聖學，明作，功惇大之治，兼舉無弊，大化流行於宇宙，至仁丕冒於軒堯，薫蒸透徹，融液周遍，仁厚之風將增光祖宗，超三代而上之矣。方且
translation_en:
This was how he restored the China established by the ancient emperors and kings themselves and rectified the great line of succession of the civilization of the Central Lands. The Confucian courtier Song Lian spoke of six things: achievements surpassing all antiquity, the legitimacy of his acquisition of the realm, his uniquely complete wisdom, his reverence for Heaven and diligence for the people, the strictness of his household rules, and the orderly direction of military administration. Might these six points adequately celebrate and proclaim the achievements and virtue of our sagely founder? In former times, King Wu reversed the policies of the Shang, yet his contemporaries still said that he brought glory to Tang. How much more does this apply to the alien Yuan, who entered China as barbarians and became its rulers! Heaven and earth thereby exchanged places, the sun and moon grew dark, and the cardinal bonds and constant moral principles fell into ruin. This was a calamity such as China had never experienced since antiquity. Our Taizu arose, drove them out, and swept the realm clear. The grandeur of his virtuous undertakings and the magnificence of his achievements were unprecedented in all antiquity. How could the limited achievements of the Han, Tang, and Song, each confined to its own time, compare with even one ten-thousandth of his? Thus the Way pervaded the realm, government was well ordered, and the dynasty endured for many years, bequeathing plans for the security of his descendants for ten thousand years and transmitting boundless blessings.
Emperor Wen, Taizong, pacified the imperial house and realm from within, carried forward the great succession, and embellished the mighty undertaking. The successive sage emperors maintained it without allowing it to lapse. For more than a hundred and sixty years, all have exercised the transforming influence of utmost benevolence through the virtue of great sages, and administered the government of true kings with the hearts of true kings. Both the founding and the preservation of the dynasty have been supremely good and perfect. These are things that their sagely sons and divine grandsons should follow, embody, and keep in mind, never forgetting them for all eternity.
I reverently reflect that, since Your Majesty ascended the throne, you have sought good government, laboring from before dawn until late at night without respite, attending to ritual forms [?], and devoting yourself to sagely learning. Through enlightened action and achievement [?], you have established generous and expansive government, undertaking all measures together without ill effect. Your great transforming influence flows throughout the universe; your utmost benevolence abundantly extends over Xuanyuan and Yao [?]. It permeates everything like a warming fragrance, penetrating thoroughly, diffusing and circulating everywhere. This spirit of benevolence and generosity will bring added glory to your ancestors and surpass even the Three Dynasties. And now you are also…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
體道謙冲以思
祖宗創造萬艱惕然悚懼為言又諄諄以民得以遂生物得以
適所為問即此
一念所以永
宗社萬禩之固保家國千載之傳胥此在矣而又何以他求為
哉盖繼世之君不知創業之艱難則無以體此仁不知斯
民之休戚則無以施此仁
陛下既知此而念此矣臣有以知
陛下能盡善繼善述之道而得祈天永命之理無疑也然
今日之所當積累力行而不懈者亦惟以仁而已矣所謂仁
者非徒然姑息之謂煦煦小惠而已必也以聖人之訓為
===
必可信以帝王之道為必可行一話一言遵
祖訓而不失一政一令率
舊章而不愆喜怒以天不以人賞罰以公不以私慎刑憲之
科去煩苛之條所以盡此仁廣忠讜之路開不諱之門所
以廣此仁定上下之分以振紀綱停不急之務以節財用
仁之實也親君子遠小人進忠直退邪佞以法
祖奉親為要務以敬
天勤民為大本仁之綱也覩玉食之珎奇而憂民之無食服錦
衣之輕煖而憂民之無衣處
九重之壯麗而憂民之無居仁之事也遠聲色為斧斤戒晏
安為鴆毒不惑於異端之荒唐不錮於祥瑞之蒙蔽不役

祖訓而不失一政一令率
舊章而不愆喜怒以天不以人賞罰以公不以私慎刑憲之
科去煩苛之條所以盡此仁廣忠讜之路開不諱之門所
以廣此仁定上下之分以振紀綱停不急之務以節財用
仁之實也親君子遠小人進忠直退邪佞以法
祖奉親爲要務以敬
天勤民爲大本仁之綱也覩玉食之珍奇而憂民之無食服錦
衣之輕煖而憂民之無衣處
九重之壯麗而憂民之無居仁之事也遠聲色爲斧斤戒晏
安爲鴆毒不惑於異端之荒唐不錮於祥瑞之蒙蔽不役
punctuated:
體道謙冲，以思祖宗創造萬艱，惕然悚懼為言，又諄諄以民得以遂生、物得以適所為問。即此一念，所以永宗社萬禩之固、保家國千載之傳，胥此在矣，而又何以他求為哉？盖繼世之君，不知創業之艱難，則無以體此仁；不知斯民之休戚，則無以施此仁。陛下既知此而念此矣，臣有以知陛下能盡善繼善述之道，而得祈天永命之理，無疑也。
然今日之所當積累力行而不懈者，亦惟以仁而已矣。所謂仁者，非徒然姑息之謂、煦煦小惠而已。必也以聖人之訓為必可信，以帝王之道為必可行。一話一言，遵祖訓而不失；一政一令，率舊章而不愆。喜怒以天，不以人；賞罰以公，不以私。慎刑憲之科，去煩苛之條，所以盡此仁；廣忠讜之路，開不諱之門，所以廣此仁。定上下之分以振紀綱，停不急之務以節財用，仁之實也。親君子，遠小人，進忠直，退邪佞，以法祖奉親為要務，以敬天勤民為大本，仁之綱也。覩玉食之珎奇而憂民之無食，服錦衣之輕煖而憂民之無衣，處九重之壯麗而憂民之無居，仁之事也。遠聲色為斧斤，戒晏安為鴆毒，不惑於異端之荒唐，不錮於祥瑞之蒙蔽，不役
translation_en:
…embodying the Way in humility, reflecting on the countless hardships your ancestors endured in founding the dynasty, and speaking with trembling apprehension. You also earnestly ask how the people may fulfill their lives and all things find their proper places. In this single concern lies everything needed to secure the ancestral temples and altars of state for ten thousand years and preserve the transmission of the ruling house and realm for a thousand generations. Why seek anything elsewhere? For a ruler who inherits the throne, ignorance of the hardships of founding the dynasty leaves him unable to embody this benevolence; ignorance of the people's well-being and suffering leaves him unable to put it into practice. Your Majesty already understands and bears these things in mind. Your servant therefore knows without doubt that Your Majesty can fully realize the Way of worthily continuing your predecessors' undertakings and carrying out their intentions, and grasp the principle of praying to Heaven for an enduring Mandate.
Yet what must now be steadily cultivated and vigorously practiced without flagging is simply benevolence. By benevolence I do not mean mere indulgence or petty, solicitous favors. One must regard the sages' teachings as assuredly trustworthy and the Way of the sage emperors and kings as assuredly practicable. In every utterance and every word, follow the ancestral instructions without deviation; in every policy and every command, adhere to established statutes without transgression. Let joy and anger accord with Heaven, rather than human impulses; let rewards and punishments proceed from impartiality, rather than private interests. Exercise care in the provisions of penal law and remove vexatious and harsh regulations: these are means of fully realizing this benevolence. Broaden the avenues for loyal, forthright counsel and open the door to speech without taboo: these are means of extending this benevolence. Establish the distinctions between superior and inferior to invigorate the governing order, and suspend nonessential undertakings to economize on expenditure: these are the substance of benevolence. Draw near to exemplary men and keep petty men at a distance; advance the loyal and upright and dismiss the wicked and sycophantic. Make emulating your ancestors and serving your parents essential duties, and revering Heaven and diligently caring for the people the great foundation: these are the guiding principles of benevolence. When viewing the rare delicacies of the imperial table, worry that the people lack food; when wearing light, warm brocade robes, worry that the people lack clothing; when dwelling amid the splendor of the palace's ninefold enclosures, worry that the people lack shelter: these are the acts of benevolence. Shun music and sensual pleasures as destructive axes; guard against idle ease as deadly poison. Do not be deluded by the absurdities of heterodox teachings, nor imprisoned by the deception of auspicious omens, nor enslaved …

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
於耳目之新奇抑奔競以端士習擇將帥以詰戎兵仁之
發也不寶遠物慮開貢獻之門以蕩此仁不輕改作慮作
聰明之漸以蠹此仁
日新聖學以涵養之親近儒臣以講明之將見
聖心虛明而靜一蘊於內者皆忠厚惻怛之充周發於外者皆
溥博公平之洋溢由是大化神明而鴻恩博洽民無不遂
其生日月貞明而雨暘時若無物不適其所
國祚靈長雍熈泰和之盛殆與天地相為終始矣然此非臣
之臆說也孟軻氏嘗曰三代之得天下也以仁其失天下
也以不仁孔子繫易之乾曰元者善之長也夫乾者君之
象也元即仁也而仁者德之聚也其行之之端惟其擴充
===
而已矣子思致曲之云孟子善推所為之說皆擴充之旨
也此固
陛下所以行而臣愚猶惓惓言之者欲
陛下持不息之誠為克終之圖永保
今日之仁於悠久焉耳我
太祖嘗曰日月之能久照萬世不改其明堯舜之道不息萬世
不改其行三代因時損益者其小過不及耳若一代定法
不可輕改後世子孫當思敬守祖法臣愚請以
聖祖之訓為
陛下今日行仁之本臣干冒
天威無任惶懼隕越之至臣謹對

於耳目之新奇，抑奔競以端士習，擇將帥以詰戎兵，仁之發也。不寶遠物，慮開貢獻之門以蕩此仁；不輕改作，慮作聰明之漸以蠹此仁。日新聖學以涵養之，親近儒臣以講明之，將見聖心虛明而靜一，蘊於內者皆忠厚惻怛之充周，發於外者皆溥博公平之洋溢。由是大化神明，而鴻恩博洽，民無不遂其生；日月貞明，而雨暘時若，無物不適其所。國祚靈長，雍熈泰和之盛，殆與天地相為終始矣。
然此非臣之臆說也。孟軻氏嘗曰：「三代之得天下也以仁，其失天下也以不仁。」孔子繫《易》之乾曰：「元者，善之長也。」夫乾者，君之象也；元即仁也，而仁者，德之聚也。其行之之端，惟其擴充而已矣。子思致曲之云，孟子善推所為之說，皆擴充之旨也。此固陛下所以行，而臣愚猶惓惓言之者，欲陛下持不息之誠，為克終之圖，永保今日之仁於悠久焉耳。
我太祖嘗曰：「日月之能久照，萬世不改其明；堯舜之道不息，萬世不改其行。三代因時損益者，其小過不及耳。若一代定法，不可輕改。後世子孫，當思敬守祖法。」臣愚請以聖祖之訓為陛下今日行仁之本。臣干冒天威，無任惶懼隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…by novelties that delight the ears and eyes; restraining the scramble for advancement to rectify the habits of scholars, and selecting generals to put the armed forces in order—these are manifestations of benevolence. Do not treasure exotic objects from distant lands, lest opening the door to tribute offerings dissipate this benevolence. Do not lightly institute changes, lest the beginnings of a display of cleverness corrode this benevolence. Daily renew Your Majesty’s sagely learning to nurture it, and draw close to Confucian ministers to elucidate it. Then Your Majesty’s mind will become receptive and clear, tranquil and unified: what is stored within will be a fullness of loyalty, generosity, and compassion; what issues outward will be an overflowing of breadth, fairness, and impartiality. Thus your great transforming influence will work with spiritual efficacy, and your vast beneficence will reach everywhere, so that all the people may fulfill their lives. The sun and moon will shine with constancy, rain and sunshine will come in their proper seasons, and all things will find their fitting places. The dynasty’s blessed tenure will endure, and its flourishing concord, prosperity, and supreme harmony will last virtually as long as Heaven and Earth themselves.
Yet these are not your servant’s conjectures. Meng Ke once said: “The Three Dynasties gained the realm through benevolence; they lost the realm through a lack of benevolence.” In his appended explanation of the Qian hexagram in the Book of Changes, Confucius said: “The primal is the foremost of goodness.” Qian is the image of the ruler; the primal is benevolence, and benevolence is the gathering of virtues. The essential means of practicing it lies simply in extending it to the fullest. Zisi’s words about bringing even partial goodness to its fullest realization, and Mengzi’s teaching about skillfully extending what one already does, both express this principle of expansion. This is indeed what Your Majesty practices. If your foolish servant nevertheless speaks of it so earnestly, it is only because I wish Your Majesty to maintain unceasing sincerity, plan to carry the undertaking through to its conclusion, and preserve today’s benevolence forever.
Our Taizu once said: “The sun and moon can shine enduringly because through myriad ages they do not alter their brightness. The Way of Yao and Shun never ceases because through myriad ages its practice does not change. What the Three Dynasties added or removed in accordance with their times concerned only minor excesses and deficiencies. As for a dynasty’s established laws, these must not lightly be changed. Descendants in later generations should resolve to uphold the ancestral laws reverently.” Your foolish servant begs that the sacred ancestor’s instructions serve as the foundation for Your Majesty’s practice of benevolence today. Having presumed to offend Your Majesty’s heavenly authority, your servant is overcome with fear and trembling, utterly apprehensive lest he fall into error. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
臣沈宏
臣對臣聞帝王繼述之道内存乎祈天永命之心而外弘
其御世酬物之政夫心者政之本也無是心則政不立政
者心之推也無是政則心弗弘政之不立是謂徒善徒善
則天下之化泥矣心之弗弘是謂徒法徒法則天下之治
敝矣泥且敝皆帝王之所弗為也帝王之道有要焉亦曰
敬而已矣盖敬也者徹内徹外之道也成始成終之道也
所以祈天永命者在是所以御世酬物者在是是故以之
創業則足以伐暴救民而貽燕翼之謀以之守成則足以
興滯補敝而盡繼述之善古之久安長治者罔不繇此矣
此所謂創守無二道祖宗無二心者也君人者將欲綿其
運祚而壽其國脉豈不在於一敬之作所哉臣伏草茅歷
觀往古有見於廢興存亡之故而未嘗不三復於斯也今
日恭遇
皇帝陛下於萬幾之暇特進臣等而
清問及焉得非臣愚可言之時乎然觀乎時勢而究其本指
以廣德業以裨弘深則臣非其人也而竊有志焉臣伏讀
制策有曰三代以来惟周之歷世最多且久盖由先王德澤洽
於民心亦繼之以嗣王能盡持盈慎滿之道者也繼而先
之以
皇祖高皇帝之創業次之以
太宗文皇帝之繼述又次之以

皇祖高皇帝之創業次之以
太宗文皇帝之繼述又次之以
punctuated:
臣沈宏

臣對：臣聞帝王繼述之道，内存乎祈天永命之心，而外弘其御世酬物之政。夫心者，政之本也；無是心，則政不立。政者，心之推也；無是政，則心弗弘。政之不立，是謂徒善；徒善，則天下之化泥矣。心之弗弘，是謂徒法；徒法，則天下之治敝矣。泥且敝，皆帝王之所弗為也。帝王之道有要焉，亦曰敬而已矣。盖敬也者，徹内徹外之道也，成始成終之道也。所以祈天永命者在是，所以御世酬物者在是。是故以之創業，則足以伐暴救民，而貽燕翼之謀；以之守成，則足以興滯補敝，而盡繼述之善。古之久安長治者，罔不繇此矣。此所謂創守無二道，祖宗無二心者也。君人者將欲綿其運祚，而壽其國脉，豈不在於一敬之作所哉？臣伏草茅，歷觀往古，有見於廢興存亡之故，而未嘗不三復於斯也。今日恭遇皇帝陛下於萬幾之暇，特進臣等，而清問及焉，得非臣愚可言之時乎？然觀乎時勢，而究其本指，以廣德業，以裨弘深，則臣非其人也，而竊有志焉。

臣伏讀制策有曰：「三代以来，惟周之歷世最多且久，盖由先王德澤洽於民心，亦繼之以嗣王能盡持盈慎滿之道者也。」繼而先之以皇祖高皇帝之創業，次之以太宗文皇帝之繼述，又次之以
translation_en:
Your servant, Shen Hong.

Your servant replies: I have heard that the way in which emperors and kings carry forward their predecessors’ work consists inwardly in preserving the resolve to pray to Heaven for an enduring mandate, and outwardly in extending their governance to rule the world and respond to its affairs. The heart is the foundation of governance: without such a heart, governance cannot be established. Governance is the extension of the heart: without such governance, the heart cannot find full expression. When governance is not established, this is called goodness alone; with goodness alone, the moral transformation of the realm becomes obstructed. When the heart does not find full expression, this is called laws alone; with laws alone, the government of the realm falls into decay. Obstruction and decay are both things that emperors and kings refuse to bring about. The way of emperors and kings has an essential principle: it is simply reverence. Reverence is the way that penetrates both the inner and the outer, the way that brings both beginning and end to completion. Herein lies the means of praying to Heaven for an enduring mandate; herein lies the means of ruling the world and responding to its affairs. Thus, when employed in founding a dynasty, it suffices to punish the violent and rescue the people, and to bequeath plans for the peace and protection of one’s descendants. When employed in preserving an established dynasty, it suffices to revive what has languished and remedy what has decayed, and fully to realize the excellence of carrying forward one’s predecessors’ work. All who achieved lasting peace and enduring good government in antiquity followed this path. This is what is meant by saying that founding and preserving a dynasty have no two different ways, and that founders and succeeding ancestors have no two different hearts. If a ruler wishes to prolong his dynasty’s allotted fortune and extend the life of his state, must this not depend upon making reverence alone his abiding place [?]? Living in humble obscurity, I have surveyed antiquity, gained some understanding of the causes of decline and flourishing, survival and destruction, and never ceased to ponder this repeatedly. Today I have respectfully had the opportunity to encounter Your Imperial Majesty, who, amid the countless affairs of government, has specially summoned us into your presence and addressed your august questions to us. Is this not the moment when even an ignorant servant such as I may speak? Yet as for examining present circumstances and probing their underlying purport, so as to enlarge your virtuous achievements and contribute to their breadth and depth, I am not equal to the task, though I privately aspire to it.

I have reverently read the imperial policy question, which says: “Since the Three Dynasties, Zhou alone lasted for the greatest number of generations and the longest time. This was because the virtue and beneficence of its former kings thoroughly reached the people’s hearts, and because succeeding kings followed them who could fully practice the way of sustaining fullness and exercising caution amid abundance.” It then proceeds first to the founding achievements of your imperial ancestor, Emperor Gao; next to the continuation of that work by Taizong, Emperor Wen; and then to…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
列聖之遵承而思慕其良法要道此有以見
陛下嘉樂之意謙恭之德真得祈天永命之心直欲追殷周而
上之以綿
宗社于萬年無疆之休者也臣敢不對揚
休命於萬一乎竊惟自古帝王之治天下有德以基化本有
功以綏太平德存乎心政之所以立也功顯乎外心之所
以形也唐虞以往尚矣今自三代論之祗台德先不距朕
行禹之所以立政也九功惟叙九叙惟歌禹之所以弘心
也矧其繼之則有敬承之啓興復之仲康而夏之所以創
守者可見矣聖敬日躋昭假遲遲湯之所以立政也布昭
聖武子惠困窮湯之所以弘心也矧其繼之則有克終允
德之太甲祇慎天命之太戊嘉靖殷邦之高宗而商之所
以創守者可見矣若夫周也文武開之於前成康繼之於
後歷世三十歷年八百世祚之多且久誠有以出夏商之
右矣然揆其所自則緝熈敬止世德作求天保以上治内
采薇以下治外而文武之功德盛矣基命宥密夙夜弗康
對揚文武率循大卞而成康之功德盛矣至於宣王繼厲
之烈猶能赫然中興以後文武之舊可見德澤之在人心
者誠深洽矣使繼世者皆若成康皆若宣王焉則周雖至
今存可也嗣是而下其創業者漢有高帝唐有文皇宋有
藝祖而開國之道擬之先王未備也其繼體者漢有文宣
唐有玄憲宋有仁宗而承家之道擬之先王未備也是故

行禹之所以立政也九功惟叙九叙惟歌禹之所以弘心
也矧其繼之則有敬承之啓興復之仲康而夏之所以創
守者可見矣聖敬日躋昭假遲遲湯之所以立政也布昭
聖武子惠困窮湯之所以弘心也矧其繼之則有克終允
===
德之太甲祇慎天命之太戊嘉靖殷邦之高宗而商之所
以創守者可見矣若夫周也文武開之於前成康繼之於
後歷世三十歷年八百世祚之多且久誠有以出夏商之
右矣然揆其所自則緝熙敬止世德作求天保以上治內
采薇以下治外而文武之功德盛矣基命宥密夙夜帝康
對揚文武率循大卞而成康之功德盛矣至於宣王繼厲
之烈猶能赫然中興以復文武之舊可見德澤之在人心
者誠深洽矣使繼世者皆若成康皆若宣王焉則周雖至
今存可也嗣是而下其創業者漢有高帝唐有文皇宋有
藝祖而開國之道擬之先王未備也其繼體者漢有文宣
唐有玄憲宋有仁宗而承家之道擬之先王未備也是故
punctuated:
列聖之遵承，而思慕其良法要道。此有以見陛下嘉樂之意、謙恭之德，真得祈天永命之心，直欲追殷周而上之，以綿宗社于萬年無疆之休者也。臣敢不對揚休命於萬一乎？
竊惟自古帝王之治天下，有德以基化本，有功以綏太平。德存乎心，政之所以立也；功顯乎外，心之所以形也。唐虞以往尚矣，今自三代論之：「祗台德先，不距朕行」，禹之所以立政也；「九功惟叙，九叙惟歌」，禹之所以弘心也。矧其繼之，則有敬承之啓、興復之仲康，而夏之所以創守者可見矣。「聖敬日躋，昭假遲遲」，湯之所以立政也；「布昭聖武，子惠困窮」，湯之所以弘心也。矧其繼之，則有克終允德之太甲、祇慎天命之太戊、嘉靖殷邦之高宗，而商之所以創守者可見矣。
若夫周也，文武開之於前，成康繼之於後，歷世三十，歷年八百，世祚之多且久，誠有以出夏商之右矣。然揆其所自，則「緝熈敬止」、「世德作求」，《天保》以上治内，《采薇》以下治外，而文武之功德盛矣。「基命宥密」、「夙夜弗康」、「對揚文武」、「率循大卞」，而成康之功德盛矣。至於宣王繼厲之烈，猶能赫然中興，以後文武之舊，可見德澤之在人心者誠深洽矣。使繼世者皆若成康，皆若宣王焉，則周雖至今存可也。
嗣是而下，其創業者，漢有高帝，唐有文皇，宋有藝祖，而開國之道，擬之先王未備也。其繼體者，漢有文宣，唐有玄憲，宋有仁宗，而承家之道，擬之先王未備也。是故
translation_en:
…the successive sage emperors’ faithful continuation of that legacy, and Your Majesty’s longing for their excellent institutions and essential principles. Here we can see Your Majesty’s appreciative delight and humble reverence: you have truly grasped the spirit of praying to Heaven for an enduring mandate, desiring to emulate Yin and Zhou and surpass them, thereby extending the blessings of the ancestral temples and altars of state without limit for ten thousand years. Dare your servant fail to acknowledge and extol even a ten-thousandth part of your gracious command?
I humbly consider that, from antiquity, emperors and kings have governed All under Heaven through virtue, which establishes the foundation of moral transformation, and achievement, which secures great peace. Virtue resides in the heart and is the means by which government is established; achievement manifests itself outwardly and is the means by which the heart takes visible form. The ages of Tang Yao and Yu Shun and earlier are remote indeed. Let us therefore discuss the Three Dynasties. “Reverently place my virtue first, and do not oppose my conduct”: this was how Yu established his government. “The nine achievements are duly ordered; the nine orders are celebrated in song”: this was how Yu extended the purposes of his heart. Moreover, among his successors were Qi, who reverently carried on his work, and Zhongkang, who restored it. Thus we can see how the Xia dynasty was founded and preserved. “His sagely reverence advanced daily, and his radiant influence reached far and endured”: this was how Tang established his government. “He displayed his sagely martial might, and cherished the distressed and impoverished as his children”: this was how Tang extended the purposes of his heart. Moreover, among his successors were Taijia, who maintained sincere virtue to the end; Taiwu, who reverently heeded Heaven’s mandate; and Gaozong, who brought good order and peace to the state of Yin. Thus we can see how the Shang dynasty was founded and preserved.
As for Zhou, Wen and Wu founded it at the beginning, and Cheng and Kang succeeded them afterward. It lasted thirty generations and eight hundred years; in the number of generations and duration of its dynastic rule, it truly surpassed Xia and Shang. Yet, examining the source of this success, we find “continuing in brightness and abiding in reverence” and “seeking to fulfill the virtue of successive generations.” The poems through “Heaven Protects” (Tian bao) concern governing within; those from “Gathering Vetch” (Cai wei) onward concern governing beyond. Thus abundant were the achievements and virtues of Wen and Wu. “Establishing the mandate with broad and quiet resolve,” “taking no ease morning or night,” “acknowledging and extolling Wen and Wu,” and “following the great laws”: thus abundant were the achievements and virtues of Cheng and Kang. Even King Xuan, succeeding to the baleful legacy of King Li, could still bring about a brilliant restoration and carry forward the old legacy of Wen and Wu [?]. This shows how profoundly their virtuous beneficence had permeated the people’s hearts. Had all succeeding rulers been like Cheng and Kang, or like King Xuan, Zhou might well have survived even to the present day.
Thereafter, among dynastic founders, Han had Emperor Gao, Tang had Emperor Wen, and Song had Yizu. Yet their ways of founding a state were incomplete when measured against those of the ancient kings. Among succeeding rulers, Han had Wen and Xuan, Tang had Xuan and Xian, and Song had Renzong. Yet their ways of carrying on the dynastic house were incomplete when measured against those of the ancient kings. Therefore…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
享祚之久比之後世則有餘而擬之三代則未及盖有由
矣洪惟我
皇祖高皇帝聖哲開運純敬格天駿德神功巍巍蕩蕩有以迥
出千古之上矣迨
太宗文皇帝益弘繼述之謨
列聖相承世培熈洽之運莫非本之於心為要道推之於外為
良法則
國祚綿延歴于無疆固其所也兹幸伏遇
陛下以不世出之資持不自滿之志踐祚以來興道致治有加
於昔矣而又以未盡繼述之道為慮臣知
陛下此心即古之聖王兢兢業業所其無逸之心也是心也蘊
===
===
於內則為祈天永命之本達於外則為御世酬物之政持
盈慎滿之道莫過於此矣臣嘗伏讀
聖製敬一箴及五箴之解未嘗不仰而嘆曰堯舜禹湯文武之
心在是矣今日之對臣復何言哉臣聞人主坐法宫之中
若甚隱也而風聲美惡鼓動天下則甚顯也慎獨之功豈
非持敬之所當勉者乎中庸曰知遠之近知風之自知微
之顯詩曰相在爾室尚不愧於屋漏盖言幾之當審獨之
當慎也今
陛下欲恒敬一之德以為國家無窮之福則不可以不慎其獨
欲慎其獨則不可以不審其幾夫審之慎之者無他惟
陛下試省焉耳或者大庭此心而深宫時有不然者乎萬幾此

陛下此心即古之聖王兢兢業業所其無逸之心也是心也藴
於内則爲祈天永命之本達於外則爲御世酧物之政持

之顯詩曰相在爾室尚不愧於屋漏盖言幾之當審獨之
當慎也今

欲慎其獨則不可以不審其幾夫審之慎之者無他惟
陛下試省焉耳或者大庭此心而深宫時有不然者乎萬幾此
punctuated:
享祚之久，比之後世則有餘，而擬之三代則未及，盖有由矣。洪惟我皇祖高皇帝，聖哲開運，純敬格天，駿德神功，巍巍蕩蕩，有以迥出千古之上矣。迨太宗文皇帝，益弘繼述之謨。列聖相承，世培熈洽之運，莫非本之於心為要道，推之於外為良法，則國祚綿延，歴于無疆，固其所也。兹幸伏遇陛下，以不世出之資，持不自滿之志，踐祚以來，興道致治，有加於昔矣。而又以未盡繼述之道為慮，臣知陛下此心，即古之聖王兢兢業業、所其無逸之心也。是心也，蘊於內則為祈天永命之本，達於外則為御世酬物之政，持盈慎滿之道，莫過於此矣。
臣嘗伏讀聖製《敬一箴》及五箴之解，未嘗不仰而嘆曰：「堯舜禹湯文武之心在是矣！」今日之對，臣復何言哉？臣聞人主坐法宫之中，若甚隱也，而風聲美惡，鼓動天下，則甚顯也。慎獨之功，豈非持敬之所當勉者乎？《中庸》曰：「知遠之近，知風之自，知微之顯。」《詩》曰：「相在爾室，尚不愧於屋漏。」盖言幾之當審、獨之當慎也。今陛下欲恒敬一之德，以為國家無窮之福，則不可以不慎其獨；欲慎其獨，則不可以不審其幾。夫審之慎之者無他，惟陛下試省焉耳。或者大庭此心，而深宫時有不然者乎？萬幾此
translation_en:
…There is indeed a reason why the duration of their dynastic rule exceeded that of later ages, yet fell short of the Three Dynasties. We reverently reflect upon our imperial ancestor, Emperor Gao: with sagely wisdom he inaugurated the dynasty’s fortune, and with pure reverence he reached Heaven. His magnificent virtue and wondrous achievements were so lofty and vast that he surpassed all preceding ages. When Emperor Wen, Taizong, succeeded, he further enlarged the plans for carrying on and fulfilling his predecessor’s work. The succeeding sage emperors, generation after generation, nurtured an age of flourishing harmony. All took what was rooted in the heart as the essential Way and extended it outward as sound institutions. That the dynasty’s good fortune should continue without limit is therefore only fitting. Now we have the good fortune to encounter Your Majesty, who possesses gifts rarely seen in any age while maintaining a resolve never to be self-satisfied. Since ascending the throne, you have promoted the Way and achieved good government to a degree surpassing the past. Yet you remain concerned that you have not fully fulfilled the Way of carrying on your predecessors’ work. Your servant knows that this disposition of Your Majesty is precisely that of the sage kings of antiquity, who were ever vigilant and made freedom from idle ease their abiding concern. Stored within, this disposition is the foundation for seeking Heaven’s enduring mandate; expressed outwardly, it becomes the governance by which one rules the world and responds to affairs. There is no better way to sustain prosperity and remain cautious at its height.
Your servant has reverently read the imperially composed Admonition on Reverent Single-mindedness and the explanations of the Five Admonitions. I have never failed to look up in admiration and exclaim: “Here are the hearts of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu!” What more can your servant say in today’s response? Your servant has heard that when a ruler sits within his palace, he seems deeply hidden; yet the influence of his conduct, whether good or bad, stirs all under Heaven and is thus exceedingly manifest. Is not vigilance when alone a practice in which one must exert oneself to maintain reverence? The Doctrine of the Mean says: “Know how the distant is near, know whence influence comes, and know how the subtle becomes manifest.” The Book of Odes says: “Observe yourself within your chamber; may you be without shame even in its secluded corner.” These passages mean that one must scrutinize the first stirrings of thought and remain vigilant when alone. Now, if Your Majesty wishes to sustain the virtue of reverent single-mindedness and thereby bring endless blessings to the state, you must be vigilant when alone. If you wish to be vigilant when alone, you must scrutinize those first stirrings. Such scrutiny and vigilance require nothing other than that Your Majesty undertake self-examination. Might you maintain this disposition in the great court, yet sometimes fail to do so deep within the palace? Amid the myriad affairs of government, this…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
心而暇逸時有不然者乎惟嚴惟翼勿貳勿參必湛然於
無感之時而洞然於有感之際至明以察之至健以决之
而後可以為之審而後可以為之慎此心既存則蘊之為
本達之為用良法要道有不合德於
祖宗匹休於先王豈理也哉
制策又曰爾多士蘊持既久素閑王政宜悉所知以告朕朕將
采擇而勉之此有以見
陛下不棄芻蕘之賤而使之盡言如此臣愚承問而可復諱乎
今畧舉為政之實以對惟
陛下試采擇焉其一曰務出治之實以立紀綱夫國家安危之
形在天下而本原之地在朝廷君人者如一元上運大同
===
其德以從人公卿有司者如五氣順成各致其能以相濟
故元首明而股肱良則庶事以之而康矣元首叢脞而股
肱惰則庶事以之而隳矣在昔帝王君臣相得都俞吁咈
天下不以為諛且戾也今或不然無乃
陛下接之不以其時訪之不以其情乎夫朝廷者四方之極所
為而是雖立斷之不為過所為而非雖屢更之不為病故
萬全而無弊者帝王之治也臣願
陛下念手足腹心一體之義虛心延訪推誠任人一有所為必
反覆辯論以求至當之歸果見其有利於民有利於國然
後斷然行之而無疑也如此則政無因循朝無曠位而明
良喜起之風君臣同遊之盛於是復見矣紀綱其有不立

無感之時而洞然於有感之際至明以察之至健以決之
而後可以爲之審而後可以爲之慎此心既存則緼之爲

祖宗匹休於先王豈理也哉

采擇而勉之此有以見
陛下不棄芻蕘之賤而使之盡言如此〔臣〕愚承問而可復諱乎
今畧舉爲政之實以對惟
陛下試采擇焉其一曰務出治之實以立紀綱夫國家安危之
形在天下而本原之地在朝廷君人者如一元上運大同
===
其德以從人公卿有司者如五氣順成各致其能以相濟
故元首明而股肱良則庶事以之而康矣元首叢脞而股
肱惰則庶事以之而隳矣在昔帝王君臣相得都俞吁咈
天下不以爲諛且戾也今或不然無乃
陛下接之不以其時訪之不以其情乎夫朝廷者四方之極所
爲而是雖立斷之不爲過所爲而非雖屢更之不爲病故
萬全而無弊者帝王之治也〔臣〕願
陛下念手足腹心一體之義虛心延訪推誠任人一有所爲必
反覆辯論以求至當之歸果見其有利於民有利於國然
後斷然行之而無疑也如此則政無因循朝無曠位而明
良喜起之風君臣同遊之盛於是復見矣紀綱其有不立
punctuated:
心，而暇逸時有不然者乎？惟嚴惟翼，勿貳勿參，必湛然於無感之時，而洞然於有感之際，至明以察之，至健以决之，而後可以為之審，而後可以為之慎。此心既存，則蘊之為本，達之為用，良法要道，有不合德於祖宗、匹休於先王，豈理也哉？

制策又曰：「爾多士蘊持既久，素閑王政，宜悉所知以告朕，朕將采擇而勉之。」此有以見陛下不棄芻蕘之賤，而使之盡言如此。臣愚承問，而可復諱乎？今畧舉為政之實以對，惟陛下試采擇焉。

其一曰：務出治之實，以立紀綱。夫國家安危之形在天下，而本原之地在朝廷。君人者，如一元上運，大同其德以從人；公卿有司者，如五氣順成，各致其能以相濟。故元首明而股肱良，則庶事以之而康矣；元首叢脞而股肱惰，則庶事以之而隳矣。在昔帝王君臣相得，都俞吁咈，天下不以為諛且戾也。今或不然，無乃陛下接之不以其時，訪之不以其情乎？夫朝廷者，四方之極。所為而是，雖立斷之不為過；所為而非，雖屢更之不為病。故萬全而無弊者，帝王之治也。臣願陛下念手足腹心一體之義，虛心延訪，推誠任人。一有所為，必反覆辯論，以求至當之歸。果見其有利於民，有利於國，然後斷然行之而無疑也。如此，則政無因循，朝無曠位，而明良喜起之風、君臣同遊之盛，於是復見矣。紀綱其有不立
translation_en:
…this same mind, yet at times fail to do so during leisure and ease? Be solemn and reverent, allowing neither division nor distraction. The mind must be serene when nothing stirs it and lucid when things move it. Examine these stirrings with the utmost clarity and decide upon them with the utmost firmness; only then can one scrutinize them and exercise vigilance over them. Once this mind is preserved, what is stored within becomes the foundation, and what is expressed outwardly becomes its practical operation. Could sound laws and essential principles then fail to accord in virtue with your imperial ancestors and match the glory of the former kings? How could that be reasonable?

The imperial policy question further states: “You scholars have long cultivated and maintained your learning and are well versed in royal government. You should tell Us all that you know. We shall select from it and strive to put it into practice.” This shows how Your Majesty does not disdain even the lowliness of grass-cutters and wood-gatherers, but allows them to speak fully. Having received your inquiry, how could your foolish servant still hold anything back? I shall now briefly set forth concrete matters of government in reply, asking only that Your Majesty consider and select from them.

The first is to strive for substance in the conduct of government, thereby establishing its guiding principles and discipline. The manifestations of the state’s security or peril appear throughout the realm, but their source lies at court. The ruler is like the primal force moving above, broadly harmonizing his virtue to accord with others [?]; the dukes, ministers, and responsible officials are like the five vital forces bringing things to completion in due order, each contributing its capacity to assist the others. Thus, when the head is enlightened and the limbs are good, all affairs prosper through them; when the head is preoccupied with petty details and the limbs are idle, all affairs fall into ruin through them. In antiquity, rulers and ministers understood one another. Whether they voiced approval or objection, the realm did not regard them as flattering or contrary. Today this may not be so. Could it be that Your Majesty does not receive them at the proper times or consult them in a way that elicits their true views?

The court is the standard for the four quarters. If what it does is right, even an immediate decision is no fault; if what it does is wrong, even repeated revision is no defect. Thus, the government of sage emperors and kings is thoroughly sound and free of abuses. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would bear in mind the principle that hands, feet, belly, and heart form a single body: invite consultation with an open mind, extend your sincerity, and entrust responsibilities to others. Whenever anything is to be undertaken, it must be debated repeatedly so as to reach the most fitting conclusion. Once it is clear that it benefits the people and the state, carry it out decisively and without hesitation. In this way, government will not merely follow established routines, and no office at court will lack someone fulfilling its duties. The spirit in which an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers gladly rouse one another to action, and the flourishing harmony in which ruler and ministers move together, will then be seen again. Could the guiding principles and discipline fail to be established…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
天下其有不治也哉其二曰務恤民之實以若天鑒臣聞
之書曰天視自我民視天聽自我民聽民心之欣戚天心
因之以為喜怒者也故一婦負屈三年致旱一夫號寃六
月飛霜況四海之廣兆民之衆無辜籲天天變之多豈無
自耶臣觀今之民生可謂困矣西成之收不足以償東作

于民也
===
陛下果能惓惓此心加意于民則雖不免災害之見而民不爲
災矣其三曰務納諫之實以行直道臣聞巽悅順從者耳

帝王所以和顏遜志助之以勞來之勤勸賞之渥所以來
punctuated:
天下其有不治也哉？其二曰：務恤民之實，以若天鑒。臣聞之，《書》曰：「天視自我民視，天聽自我民聽。」民心之欣戚，天心因之以為喜怒者也。故一婦負屈，三年致旱；一夫號寃，六月飛霜。況四海之廣，兆民之衆，無辜籲天，天變之多，豈無自耶？臣觀今之民生，可謂困矣。西成之收不足以償東作之貸，地之所出不足以償賦之所入。冬煖號寒，年豐啼飢，流離載道，十室九空矣。況又加之以水旱蟲蝗之為災，徭役差遣之為虐，如之何不夫鬻其妻，父棄其子，強則為盜賊，弱則填溝壑而止也？臣願陛下急求所以恤民之道而行之，大要在於重守令而節財賦，省力役而斥異端。夫守令不重，則好民所惡，惡民所好，由是訟獄繁而盜賊起矣。財賦不節，則一以科百，十以科千，由是貪黷橫而刑罰苛矣。力役省，則力本者得以自盡，而民之衣食有所出；異端斥，則左道者不能惑衆，而民之衣食無所耗。慎此四者，而尤願加之意焉。《春秋》于僖公而屢書不雨，見其有志於民也；于文公而一書不雨，見其無志于民也。陛下果能惓惓此心，加意于民，則雖不免災害之見，而民不為災矣。

其三曰：務納諫之實，以行直道。臣聞柔悅順從者，耳目之娛，心腹之害也，雖芟夷之，而常患其有餘；剛方讜直者，一時之忤，無窮之利也，雖長養之，而常患其不足。古之帝王所以和顏遜志，助之以勞來之勤、勸賞之渥，所以來
translation_en:
…could the realm fail to be well governed? My second point is this: earnestly put care for the people into practice, to accord with Heaven’s scrutiny. Your servant has heard these words in the Book of Documents: “Heaven sees through what our people see; Heaven hears through what our people hear.” Heaven’s pleasure and anger follow the joy and sorrow in the people’s hearts. Thus, one woman’s unjust suffering brought three years of drought; one man’s cry against injustice brought frost in the sixth month. How much more must this hold across the vast lands within the Four Seas, with their multitudes of people! When the innocent appeal to Heaven, can the many portents in Heaven be without cause? Your servant observes that the people’s livelihood today is truly distressed. The autumn harvest cannot repay the loans taken out for spring cultivation; what the land produces cannot meet the taxes demanded. In warm winters they cry out from cold; in abundant years they weep from hunger. Displaced people fill the roads, and nine households in ten stand empty. On top of this come the calamities of floods, droughts, insects, and locusts, and the oppression of labor services and compulsory assignments. How could husbands avoid selling their wives and fathers abandoning their children, with the strong becoming bandits and the weak ending up dead in ditches and gullies? Your servant wishes Your Majesty urgently to seek and implement ways to care for the people. The essentials are to give due weight to prefects and magistrates, restrain fiscal exactions, reduce compulsory labor, and reject heterodox teachings. If prefects and magistrates are not given due weight, they favor what the people hate and hate what the people favor; lawsuits then multiply and bandits arise. If fiscal exactions are not restrained, a levy of one becomes a hundred, and one of ten becomes a thousand; corruption then runs rampant and punishments become harsh. If compulsory labor is reduced, those engaged in agriculture can devote themselves fully to it, providing a source of clothing and food for the people. If heterodox teachings are rejected, practitioners of deviant ways cannot delude the multitude, and the people’s resources for clothing and food will not be depleted. Attend carefully to these four matters; above all, I wish that you would devote your concern to the people. The Spring and Autumn Annals repeatedly records the absence of rain under Duke Xi, showing his concern for the people; under Duke Wen it records the absence of rain only once, showing his lack of concern for them. If Your Majesty can indeed sustain this earnest concern and give the people greater attention, then, although calamities may still occur, the people will not suffer disaster.

My third point is this: earnestly put acceptance of remonstrance into practice, to pursue the upright Way. Your servant has heard that pliant, ingratiating, and compliant men delight the eyes and ears but do harm to the heart and vitals. Even when they are cut away, one constantly fears that too many remain. Firm, principled, and forthright men cause momentary displeasure but bring inexhaustible benefit. Even when they are nurtured, one constantly fears that there are too few. This is why the emperors and kings of antiquity adopted a kindly expression and a receptive disposition, supporting such men with diligent encouragement and generous rewards, in order to draw forth…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
公論而錫天下之福也臣伏見
陛下之所以為直道計者非不至矣日有輪劄是以直道望諫
官也時御
經筵是以直道望輔臣也五策大對是以直道望諸生也燭
幽昭隱天下以此咸服
陛下之明納污藏疾天下以此咸服
陛下之量而直道至今尤未盡行者何也無乃為之臣者一有
所懲則以言為戒謀國之心皆轉而為自全之計其風漸
長非國之福也臣願
陛下無渝初心益弘其量凡以進言得罪者悉優容而假借之
則直道無弗行矣何者盖聞人君之尊天也其威雷霆也
===
人臣以卑微之身而欲犯尊觸威亦難矣故臣子之有志
於盡職納忠者惟恃人主之善聽焉耳夫聽言之道非仁
不容非明不察非武不斷人君三德此尤不可少者此堯
舜之聖所以開衢室好問察而至今頌之不衰也其四曰
務教化之實以端士習臣聞窮之所養達之所施幼之所
學壯之所行也古之識治體者未嘗不以厚士習為先務
夫今之士習亦甚薄矣凡有子而教之者方其幼也授之
句讀即擇其可合於有司者俾誦習焉及其長也連篇累
牘持之以要科目以媒青紫至於人倫之大行檢之實則
漫不加意何也盖父兄所教師友所傳利而已矣其習已
久恬不為非以之領郡邑如之何責其為龔黃卓魯以之

於盡職納忠者惟恃人主之善聽焉耳夫聽言之道非仁
不容非明不察非武不斷人君三德此尤不可少者也堯

學壯之所行也古之識治體者未嘗不以厚士習爲先務

句讀即擇其可合於有司者俾誦習焉及其長也連篇累
牘持之以要科目以媒青紫至於人倫之大行檢之實則
漫不加意何也蓋父兄所教師友所傳利而已矣其習已
久恬不爲非以之領郡邑如之何責其爲龔黃卓魯以之
punctuated:
公論而錫天下之福也。臣伏見陛下之所以為直道計者，非不至矣。日有輪劄，是以直道望諫官也；時御經筵，是以直道望輔臣也；五策大對，是以直道望諸生也。燭幽昭隱，天下以此咸服陛下之明；納污藏疾，天下以此咸服陛下之量。而直道至今尤未盡行者，何也？無乃為之臣者一有所懲，則以言為戒，謀國之心皆轉而為自全之計？其風漸長，非國之福也。臣願陛下無渝初心，益弘其量，凡以進言得罪者，悉優容而假借之，則直道無弗行矣。何者？盖聞人君之尊，天也；其威，雷霆也。人臣以卑微之身而欲犯尊觸威，亦難矣。故臣子之有志於盡職納忠者，惟恃人主之善聽焉耳。夫聽言之道，非仁不容，非明不察，非武不斷。人君三德，此尤不可少者。此堯舜之聖所以開衢室、好問察，而至今頌之不衰也。

其四曰：務教化之實，以端士習。臣聞窮之所養，達之所施；幼之所學，壯之所行也。古之識治體者，未嘗不以厚士習為先務。夫今之士習，亦甚薄矣。凡有子而教之者，方其幼也，授之句讀，即擇其可合於有司者，俾誦習焉；及其長也，連篇累牘，持之以要科目，以媒青紫。至於人倫之大、行檢之實，則漫不加意，何也？盖父兄所教、師友所傳，利而已矣。其習已久，恬不為非。以之領郡邑，如之何責其為龔黃卓魯？以之
translation_en:
…to invite public-minded counsel and bestow blessings upon the realm. Your servant humbly observes that Your Majesty’s efforts to promote upright conduct have indeed been most thorough. Each day there are memorials submitted in rotation: thus you expect uprightness from the remonstrance officials. From time to time you attend the Classics Colloquium: thus you expect uprightness from your chief ministers. In the formal responses to the five policy questions, you likewise expect uprightness from the candidates. You illuminate what is obscure and bring hidden matters to light; for this, all under Heaven admire Your Majesty’s discernment. You tolerate faults and accommodate shortcomings; for this, all under Heaven admire Your Majesty’s magnanimity. Why, then, has upright conduct still not been fully put into practice? Might it be that, once your ministers have suffered some chastisement, they become wary of speaking, and their concern for the state turns entirely into calculations for their own preservation? This tendency is gradually growing, to the detriment of the state. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would remain true to your original purpose and further enlarge your magnanimity, treating all who have incurred punishment for offering counsel with indulgence and forbearance. Upright conduct would then prevail everywhere. Why is this so? I have heard that a ruler’s exalted position is like Heaven, and his awesome power like thunder. For a minister, in his lowly station, to challenge that exalted position and brave that power is indeed difficult. Thus ministers who aspire to fulfill their duties and offer loyal counsel rely solely upon their sovereign’s willingness to listen. In listening to counsel, without benevolence one cannot accommodate it; without discernment one cannot examine it; without resolve one cannot decide upon it. These three virtues are especially indispensable to a ruler. This is why the sage rulers Yao and Shun opened a hall at the crossroads to receive counsel and delighted in questioning and examining, and why praise of them has continued unabated to this day.

The fourth point is: pursue the substance of moral instruction in order to rectify the habits of scholars. Your servant has heard that what one cultivates while obscure is what one puts into practice upon attaining office, and what one learns in youth is what one carries out in maturity. Those in antiquity who understood the essentials of governance invariably made fostering sound habits among scholars their first priority. Yet the habits of scholars today have become exceedingly shallow. Anyone educating a son, while the boy is still young and being taught to distinguish phrases and sentences, immediately selects passages likely to meet the approval of the examining officials and has him recite and study them. When he grows older, he produces compositions filling page after page, using them to secure success in the examinations and gain the blue and purple robes of office. As for the great principles of human relationships and the substance of moral conduct, he pays them no heed. Why is this? Because what fathers and elder brothers teach, and what teachers and friends transmit, is nothing but personal advantage. These habits have persisted so long that people accept them complacently and see nothing wrong in them. If such men are put in charge of prefectures and counties, how can one demand that they emulate Gong, Huang, Zhuo, and Lu? If they are employed to…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
列朝宁如之何望其為韓范歐富士習之薄此風俗之所
以日偷也臣願
陛下重師儒之官嚴風紀之司抑奔競之風夫師儒不重則模
範不端風紀不嚴則行檢不飭奔競不抑則廉耻道喪慎
此三者而又範之以
皇極鼓之以神化又何憂乎人才之不輩出匹休於三代也哉
夫出治也恤民也納諫也教化也四者之敝敝之大者此
至治之所以未臻而有來
當宁之憂也雖然主張之權在上不在下運旋之術在內不
在外故臣愚始終以為言者惟以主敬之道為
陛下獻夫無逸一書周公所以告成王者其意亦不過曰久此
===
===
敬耳中庸曰不息則久久則徵易曰聖人久於其道而天
下化成臣願
陛下敬德不息久而益盛永惟無逸以體大易中庸之義則德
無不徵化無不成以之出治則所謂一人元良萬邦以貞
也以之恤民則所謂豈弟君子民之父母也以之聽納則
所謂明四目達四聰也以之教化則所謂成人有德小子
有造也是故一敬立而天下之治從之矣以言乎內則萬
邦作孚也以言乎外則四夷來王也其大至於位天地育
萬物召禎祥而為盛德自然之應理之所必至者豈不螽
斯蟄蟄遐壽無期亦如堯舜禹湯文武也哉
聖念及此

===
下化成臣願
陛下敬德不息久而益盛永惟無逸以體大易中庸之義則德
無不徵化無不成以之出治則所謂一人元良萬邦以貞
也以之恤民則所謂豈弟君子民之父母也以之聽納則
所謂明四目達四聰也以之教化則所謂成人有德小子
有造也是故一敬立而天下之治從之矣以言乎內則萬
邦作孚也以言乎外則四夷來王也其大至於位天地育
萬物召禎祥而爲盛德自然之應理之所必至者豈不益
斯熱遐壽無期亦如堯舜禹湯文武也哉
聖念及此
punctuated:
列朝宁，如之何望其為韓范歐富？士習之薄，此風俗之所以日偷也。臣願陛下重師儒之官，嚴風紀之司，抑奔競之風。夫師儒不重，則模範不端；風紀不嚴，則行檢不飭；奔競不抑，則廉耻道喪。慎此三者，而又範之以皇極，鼓之以神化，又何憂乎人才之不輩出，匹休於三代也哉！
夫出治也，恤民也，納諫也，教化也，四者之敝，敝之大者。此至治之所以未臻，而有來當宁之憂也。雖然，主張之權在上不在下，運旋之術在內不在外。故臣愚始終以為言者，惟以主敬之道為陛下獻。夫《無逸》一書，周公所以告成王者，其意亦不過曰久此敬耳。《中庸》曰：「不息則久，久則徵。」《易》曰：「聖人久於其道，而天下化成。」臣願陛下敬德不息，久而益盛，永惟無逸，以體《大易》《中庸》之義，則德無不徵，化無不成。以之出治，則所謂「一人元良，萬邦以貞」也；以之恤民，則所謂「豈弟君子，民之父母」也；以之聽納，則所謂「明四目，達四聰」也；以之教化，則所謂「成人有德，小子有造」也。是故一敬立，而天下之治從之矣。以言乎內，則萬邦作孚也；以言乎外，則四夷來王也。其大至於位天地，育萬物，召禎祥而為盛德自然之應，理之所必至者，豈不螽斯蟄蟄，遐壽無期，亦如堯舜禹湯文武也哉！聖念及此，
translation_en:
…when they take their places at court, how can we expect them to become men like Han, Fan, Ou, and Fu? This deterioration in scholars’ conduct is why public customs grow daily more lax. Your servant wishes Your Majesty to give greater weight to educational officials, enforce rigor in the offices charged with maintaining discipline, and curb the pursuit of advancement through competition for favor. If educational officials are not esteemed, the models they provide will not be upright; if discipline is not strict, conduct will not be regulated; if competition for advancement is not restrained, the way of integrity and shame will be lost. Attend carefully to these three matters, and further mold men through the sovereign’s supreme standard and inspire them through your wondrous transforming influence: why then worry that talented men will not emerge in succession, matching the excellence of the Three Dynasties?
The failings in these four matters—governing, caring for the people, accepting remonstrance, and moral instruction—are the gravest of failings. They are why perfect government has not yet been attained and why anxiety has been brought upon Your Majesty on the throne. Nevertheless, the authority to direct affairs lies above, not below; the means of turning affairs around lie within, not without. Thus what your foolish servant has urged throughout is solely to offer Your Majesty the way of making reverent attentiveness your guiding principle. As for the text Against Ease (Wuyi), through which the Duke of Zhou admonished King Cheng, its purport is no more than to say that this reverent attentiveness must endure. The Doctrine of the Mean says: “Without ceasing, it endures; enduring, it becomes manifest.” The Book of Changes says: “The sage endures in his way, and the transformation of all under Heaven is accomplished.” Your servant wishes Your Majesty to revere virtue without ceasing, growing ever more flourishing with time, and always to keep freedom from idle ease in mind, thereby embodying the meaning of the great Book of Changes and the Doctrine of the Mean. Then your virtue will invariably become manifest, and your transforming influence will invariably achieve its effect. Applied to governing, this is what is meant by “The one man is supremely good, and the myriad states are thereby set right.” Applied to caring for the people, it is what is meant by “The gracious and amiable gentleman is the father and mother of the people.” Applied to hearing and accepting counsel, it is what is meant by “Opening the eyes to the four quarters and clearing the hearing toward the four quarters.” Applied to moral instruction, it is what is meant by “Adults possess virtue, and the young attain accomplishment.” Thus, once reverent attentiveness is established, orderly government throughout the realm follows. Speaking of affairs within, the myriad states will place their trust in you; speaking of affairs beyond, the peoples of the four quarters will come to acknowledge your kingship. Its greatness extends to setting Heaven and Earth in their proper places, nurturing the myriad things, and calling forth auspicious signs as the natural response to abundant virtue—the inevitable outcome of principle. Would you not then have descendants as numerous as swarming locusts and longevity without limit, just like Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu? If Your Majesty’s sagely thoughts reach this point…

text:
天地神人之福也久安長治之道端在於定而漢唐宋之諸君
皆不足以望下風矣臣愚不識忌諱干冒
天威臣不勝戰慄隕越之至臣謹對

translation_en: …is a blessing for Heaven and Earth, spirits and men. The way to lasting peace and enduring good government lies precisely in stability; the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song could not even hope to approach such an achievement. Your foolish servant, ignorant of taboos, has offended Your Majesty’s heavenly authority. I am overwhelmed by trembling and dread of falling into disgrace. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
臣駱文盛
臣對臣聞古之帝王所以爲創守之道仁與敬而已矣仁
以結斯民之心敬以承先世之志結民心則國本以固承
先志則善政弗忘若是乎創守之道胥得之矣其所以垂
至治之休所以衍無疆之慶外此豈有他術哉臣智識愚
昧竊不自量亦嘗諺觀于天下之勢而得其先後緩急之
宜矣顧披瀝無由徒懷耿耿今幸進之
大廷仰承
清問惓惓於我
祖宗之功德而欲長保弘業于無窮臣有以知
陛下高駕遠詣之志豈不以仁厚立洪基則當爲文武禮樂興
===
太平則當爲成康其於夏商之盛且無論矣而况於漢唐
宋之有可議者乎然夏商周之所以得與夫漢唐宋之所
以失典冊具存
陛下既已稔聞之矣今臣復敢勦說雷同上瀆
宸聰獨以其至近至切者爲
陛下陳之惟不以其庸常爲可厭不以其淺易爲可忽而試垂
省覽焉欽惟我
皇祖高皇帝功德之隆前代莫及其在宋濂之序曰曆有曰功
高萬古也曰得國之正也曰獨稟全智也曰敬天勤民也
曰家法之嚴也曰軍政有統也而其恢弘一時者固可槩
見至求其所以爲創造之基則惟仁民而已矣觀夫

punctuated:
臣駱文盛。

臣對：臣聞古之帝王所以爲創守之道，仁與敬而已矣。仁以結斯民之心，敬以承先世之志。結民心則國本以固，承先志則善政弗忘。若是乎，創守之道胥得之矣。其所以垂至治之休，所以衍無疆之慶，外此豈有他術哉？臣智識愚昧，竊不自量，亦嘗諺觀于天下之勢，而得其先後緩急之宜矣。顧披瀝無由，徒懷耿耿。今幸進之大廷，仰承清問，惓惓於我祖宗之功德，而欲長保弘業于無窮。臣有以知陛下高駕遠詣之志，豈不以仁厚立洪基，則當爲文武；禮樂興太平，則當爲成康？其於夏商之盛，且無論矣，而况於漢唐宋之有可議者乎？然夏商周之所以得，與夫漢唐宋之所以失，典冊具存，陛下既已稔聞之矣。今臣復敢勦說雷同，上瀆宸聰？獨以其至近至切者爲陛下陳之，惟不以其庸常爲可厭，不以其淺易爲可忽，而試垂省覽焉。

欽惟我皇祖高皇帝功德之隆，前代莫及。其在宋濂之序曰曆，有曰功高萬古也，曰得國之正也，曰獨稟全智也，曰敬天勤民也，曰家法之嚴也，曰軍政有統也。而其恢弘一時者，固可槩見。至求其所以爲創造之基，則惟仁民而已矣。觀夫
translation_en:
Your servant Luo Wensheng.

Your servant replies: I have heard that the way by which the emperors and kings of antiquity founded their realms and preserved their inheritance consisted simply of benevolence and reverence. Through benevolence they bound the people's hearts to themselves; through reverence they carried forward the intentions of earlier generations. When the people's hearts are bound to the ruler, the foundations of the state are secure; when the intentions of his predecessors are carried forward, their good government is not forgotten. Thus both founding and preserving are properly accomplished. Could there be any other means of handing down the blessings of consummate government and extending good fortune without limit?

My understanding is ignorant and benighted, yet, presumptuously exceeding my capacity, I have attempted to examine [?] the circumstances of the realm and discern the proper order of priorities and degrees of urgency. But I had no means of laying bare my thoughts and could only cherish my earnest concern. Now, fortunately, I have advanced to the great court and respectfully received Your Majesty's august question. It expresses profound concern for the achievements and virtue of our dynastic ancestors and the desire to preserve their magnificent enterprise forever. From this I recognize Your Majesty's lofty and far-reaching aspirations. Surely, in laying great foundations through benevolence and generosity, you would emulate Kings Wen and Wu; in bringing about supreme peace through rites and music, you would emulate Kings Cheng and Kang. Even the flourishing ages of Xia and Shang need not be discussed, much less those aspects of Han, Tang, and Song that invite criticism. Yet the reasons for the successes of Xia, Shang, and Zhou, and for the failures of Han, Tang, and Song, are all preserved in the historical records, and Your Majesty is already thoroughly familiar with them. Would I now dare merely to repeat borrowed opinions and conventional views, troubling your august hearing? I shall set before Your Majesty only what is most immediate and most pressing. I ask only that you not find it tiresome because it is commonplace, or dismiss it because it is simple, but deign to consider it.

I reverently reflect that the greatness of the achievements and virtue of our imperial ancestor, Emperor Gao, was unmatched in earlier dynasties. In Song Lian's preface [the following wording is garbled: ?], it is said that his achievements surpassed all antiquity; that his acquisition of the realm was rightful; that he alone was endowed with complete wisdom; that he revered Heaven and labored for the people; that his dynastic household rules were strict; and that his military administration had a unified command. These statements give a general view of the greatness he displayed in his age. But if we seek what constituted the foundation of his establishment of the dynasty, it was simply benevolence toward the people. Consider…

text:
諭諸臣之辭有曰人民凋弊失業者多有曰所業有限供需百
出有曰憂人者常體其心愛人者每惜其力蓋未嘗不以
民命為重至其政之所施亦無非矜恤元元之實是故刑
獄以寬厚為本宮室以綺麗為戒定賦以節用而民力以
□□步以憫農而末作有禁歲事有種桑之法凝寒有給
□之惠釋費震之罪以勸良吏停開封之役以惜農時所
謂以不忍人之心行不忍人之政者率多類此易曰上以
厚下安宅書曰民惟邦本本固邦寧是可見民苟未安則
天下之事無一可為者我
聖祖之高見遠慮其在是哉自是
太宗繼述於草創之初
===

諭諸臣之辭有曰：「人民凋弊，失業者多。」有曰：「所業有限，供需百出。」有曰：「憂人者常體其心，愛人者每惜其力。」蓋未嘗不以民命為重。至其政之所施，亦無非矜恤元元之實。是故刑獄以寬厚為本，宮室以綺麗為戒；定賦以節用，而民力以□□；步以憫農，而末作有禁；歲事有種桑之法，凝寒有給□之惠。釋費震之罪以勸良吏，停開封之役以惜農時。所謂以不忍人之心行不忍人之政者，率多類此。《易》曰：「上以厚下安宅。」《書》曰：「民惟邦本，本固邦寧。」是可見民苟未安，則天下之事無一可為者。我聖祖之高見遠慮，其在是哉！自是太宗繼述於草創之初，列聖遵承於大定之後，百有六十餘載，傳之於今，有由然也。
茲者伏遇陛下思祖宗創造萬艱，惕然悚懼，訪所謂良法要道，于以永宗社萬禩之固，保家國千世之傳。臣以為此何假於遠求之哉！惟敬承我祖宗仁民之心，而致治之基在是矣。且今天下之民承平日久，謂之未安，則農桑以為業，室家之相保，若無他可言也；謂之已安，則為民病者殆不可勝數。臣未暇舉其詳，且自其最甚者言之：涸澤以漁，傷根而刈，此民之困於賦斂也；時
translation_en:
…Among his admonitions to his ministers were these words: “The people are impoverished and exhausted; many have lost their livelihoods.” Again: “Their means of livelihood are limited, but demands for supplies arise on every side.” Again: “Those who care for others’ troubles always enter into their feelings; those who love others always spare their strength.” He invariably regarded the people’s lives as a matter of utmost importance. His policies, too, were all concrete expressions of compassion for the common people. Thus, leniency and generosity were the foundation of criminal justice, and ornate luxury was something to guard against in palace construction. He fixed taxes with a view to restraining expenditure, and the people’s strength was [text illegible: □□]; a measure concerning “steps” [?] showed compassion for farmers, and secondary occupations were restricted. In the yearly agricultural cycle there were regulations for planting mulberry trees; in freezing weather there was the kindness of distributing □ [illegible]. He pardoned Fei Zhen’s offense to encourage good officials and halted construction work at Kaifeng to spare the agricultural season. These were generally instances of what is called carrying out government that cannot bear to injure others, with a heart that cannot bear their suffering. The Book of Changes says: “Those above enrich those below and thereby secure their dwelling.” The Book of Documents says: “The people are the foundation of the state; when the foundation is firm, the state is at peace.” This shows that if the people are not secure, nothing in the realm can be accomplished. Surely herein lay the lofty insight and far-reaching foresight of our sagely founder! Thereafter, Taizong continued his work in the early days of the dynasty’s establishment, and the successive sagely emperors upheld it after the realm had been firmly settled. There is good reason why it has been transmitted to the present for more than 160 years.
Now Your Majesty, reflecting on the myriad hardships through which your ancestors founded the dynasty, is filled with vigilance and apprehension. You seek what are called sound institutions and essential principles, so as to secure the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain for ten thousand years and ensure the transmission of the dynastic house and state for a thousand generations. Your servant believes there is no need to seek these things far afield! Simply reverently carry forward our ancestors’ benevolent concern for the people: herein lies the foundation for achieving good government. Moreover, the people of the realm have now enjoyed peace for a long time. If one says they are not secure, they have farming and sericulture as their livelihoods, and their households sustain one another; it would seem there is nothing further to say. Yet if one says they are secure, the things that afflict them are almost beyond counting. Your servant has not had time to enumerate them in detail; let me speak first of the most severe. Draining the marsh to catch its fish, cutting plants so as to damage their roots—such is the people’s distress under taxation and exactions. At times …

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
訛舉羸煩勞土厭此民之困於力役也富連阡陌貧無卓
錐此民之困於兼并也巨浸淊天赤土彌望此民之困於
水旱也田廬取償妻子為質此民之困於逋負也一耕十
食一蠶百衣此民之困於游惰也呌囂東西屨突南北此
民之困於吏胥也供給愈難陪償無已此民之困於畜牧
也他如緇黃之蠹貪殘之政婚娶之艱喪葬之費凡民之
所以不安其生者其勢若此謂之厚下謂之本固可乎下
不厚而謂之安宅本不固而謂之邦寧可乎故臣妄謂今
天下之勢譬之人身饑餒已久尪羸已甚雖日以膏粱飫
飲之參苓補助之且不能頓復其元氣使徒被以文繡習
於聲容日從事於詠歌舞蹈之列吾見祗益其患耳烏在
===
其病之能起也耶臣願
陛下審于其勢之所急專意於養民為務選用賢良慎擇守令
凡可以憫民之窮恤民之患者日夕遑遑以為之所如欲
均賦斂則財用之當節欲寬力役則工作之當止欲抑兼
并則限田之議可求欲濟水旱則溝洫之制可講欲甦逋
負則申倍息之禁欲止游惰則重閑民之罰欲懲吏胥則
嚴朘剝之條欲便畜牧則擇閑廄之使其她毀度以滅緇
黃遠斥以乂貪殘論財有戒以便婚娶厚殉有刑以惠喪
葬若是乎病日以去而利日以興民食將於是乎足民生
將於是乎寧國本以之固國脉以之延由是而肅軍令以
重國體可也由是而慎邊防以振國勢可也由是而通河

訛舉羸，煩勞土厭，此民之困於力役也；富連阡陌，貧無卓錐，此民之困於兼并也；巨浸淊天，赤土彌望，此民之困於水旱也；田廬取償，妻子為質，此民之困於逋負也；一耕十食，一蠶百衣，此民之困於游惰也；呌囂東西，屨突南北，此民之困於吏胥也；供給愈難，陪償無已，此民之困於畜牧也。他如緇黃之蠹，貪殘之政，婚娶之艱，喪葬之費，凡民之所以不安其生者，其勢若此。謂之厚下，謂之本固，可乎？下不厚而謂之安宅，本不固而謂之邦寧，可乎？故臣妄謂今天下之勢，譬之人身，饑餒已久，尪羸已甚，雖日以膏粱飫飲之，參苓補助之，且不能頓復其元氣；使徒被以文繡，習於聲容，日從事於詠歌舞蹈之列，吾見祗益其患耳，烏在其病之能起也耶？

臣願陛下審于其勢之所急，專意於養民為務，選用賢良，慎擇守令。凡可以憫民之窮、恤民之患者，日夕遑遑以為之所。如欲均賦斂，則財用之當節；欲寬力役，則工作之當止；欲抑兼并，則限田之議可求；欲濟水旱，則溝洫之制可講；欲甦逋負，則申倍息之禁；欲止游惰，則重閑民之罰；欲懲吏胥，則嚴朘剝之條；欲便畜牧，則擇閑廄之使。其她毀度以滅緇黃，遠斥以乂貪殘，論財有戒以便婚娶，厚殉有刑以惠喪葬。若是乎，病日以去，而利日以興，民食將於是乎足，民生將於是乎寧，國本以之固，國脉以之延。由是而肅軍令以重國體，可也；由是而慎邊防以振國勢，可也；由是而通河
translation_en:
…disordered levies and exhausting labor [?]: these are the people's hardships from corvée service. The rich possess fields stretching across paths and boundaries, while the poor have nowhere even to plant an awl: these are the people's hardships from land engrossment. Vast floods reach the heavens, and parched earth stretches as far as the eye can see: these are the people's hardships from flood and drought. Fields and dwellings are seized in repayment, and wives and children are taken as pledges: these are the people's hardships from unpaid debts. One person tills while ten eat; one person raises silkworms while a hundred wear silk: these are the people's hardships from idleness. Shouting east and west, trampling and barging about north and south [?]: these are the people's hardships from petty officials and clerks. Providing supplies grows ever harder, and compensatory payments never end: these are the people's hardships from livestock rearing. Other burdens include the depredations of Buddhist and Daoist clergy, greedy and cruel administration, the difficulties of marriage, and the expense of funerals and burial. Such are the conditions that prevent the people from living in peace. Can this be called strengthening those below or securing the foundation? When those below are not strengthened, can the dwelling be called secure? When the foundation is insecure, can the realm be called tranquil? Thus your servant ventures to say that the present condition of the realm resembles a human body long starved and severely emaciated. Even if it were fed daily to satiety on rich meats and fine grain, and fortified with ginseng and poria, its vital energy could not be restored at once. If one merely dressed it in embroidered robes, trained it in music and ceremonial deportment, and made it participate daily in singing and dancing, I see only its suffering increasing. How could it recover from its illness?

Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would discern what is most urgent in these circumstances, devote your attention to nourishing the people, appoint worthy and capable men, and carefully select prefects and magistrates. In all matters that could relieve the people's poverty and distress, strive anxiously day and night to make provision for them. If you wish to equalize taxation, expenditure must be restrained; if you wish to ease corvée service, construction projects must be stopped. If you wish to curb land engrossment, proposals to limit landholdings may be sought; if you wish to alleviate flood and drought, systems of drainage and irrigation channels may be examined. If you wish to relieve those burdened by unpaid debts, reaffirm the prohibition on interest amounting to twice the principal [?]; if you wish to stop idleness, increase the penalties for people without an occupation. If you wish to discipline petty officials and clerks, enforce strictly the provisions against extortion; if you wish to facilitate livestock rearing, carefully select the officials responsible for the stables. In other matters, abolish ordination authorizations [?] to eliminate Buddhist and Daoist clergy; dismiss and banish the greedy and cruel to bring them under control; prohibit bargaining over wealth to facilitate marriage; and penalize lavish burial offerings to ease the burdens of funerals and burial. In this way, abuses will diminish daily and benefits will increase daily. The people's food will then become sufficient, and their lives will then become peaceful. The foundation of the state will thereby be secured, and its life sustained. On this basis, it will be possible to enforce military commands strictly and enhance the dignity of the state; on this basis, it will be possible to attend carefully to frontier defenses and strengthen the power of the state; on this basis, it will be possible to open the waterways…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
漕以便國用可也由是而精考課以明國憲可也由是而
重師儒以興學校可也由是而正風俗以息浮薄可也由
是而旌讜直以作士氣可也由是而抑奔競以敦士習可
也由是而嚴祭祀以奉神靈可也由是而定禮樂以致中
和可也所謂持盈慎滿之道莫大乎是而歷世之久歷年
之長亦豈有外於是哉苟徒區區掇拾遺文補葺故事儀
章則欲其備度數則欲其詳而托言於光前啓後之烈是
之謂有法祖之名無法祖之實渾厚之治體既未能敦而
精明之治功亦何以建哉由此觀之可見愛民之仁足以
盡法
祖之敬而仁敬固為一道也與夫愛民法祖之實臣既以陳之
===
===
於前矣至其本原之地則又有在焉古之人曰徒善不足
以為政又曰有內聖之德則有外王之業臣嘗伏讀
陛下之敬一箴與夫五箴之訓深感夫
陛下之學得之極其精
陛下之心養之極其純
陛下之德充之極其盛蓋不必更求之古而有所增益臣亦何
所陳說而冀以裨補于萬一哉但人之恒情言之有餘而
行之或未足始之克謹而終之或不繼臣固不敢以此疑
陛下惟考之實事則若有未盡徵之治効則若有未成如漢文
帝之海內富庶黎民淳厚如唐太宗之斗米三錢外戶不
閉如宋仁宗之恭儉仁恕民物康阜今亦未之見焉又何

盡法
===
祖之敬而仁敬固爲一道也與夫愛民法祖之實臣既以陳之
於前矣至其本原之地則又有在焉古之人曰徒善不足
以爲政又曰有內聖之德則有外王之業臣嘗伏讀
陛下之敬一箴與夫五箴之訓深感夫
陛下之學得之極其精
陛下之心養之極其純
陛下之德充之極其盛蓋不必更求之古而有所增益臣亦何
所陳說而冀以裨補于萬一哉但人之恒情言之有餘而
行之或未足始之克謹而終之或不繼臣固不敢以此疑
陛下惟考之實事則若有未盡徵之治効則若有未成如漢文
帝之海內富庶黎民淳厚如唐太宗之斗米三錢外戶不
閉如宋仁宗之恭儉仁恕民物康阜今亦未之見焉又何
punctuated:
漕以便國用可也。由是而精考課以明國憲可也，由是而重師儒以興學校可也，由是而正風俗以息浮薄可也，由是而旌讜直以作士氣可也，由是而抑奔競以敦士習可也，由是而嚴祭祀以奉神靈可也，由是而定禮樂以致中和可也。所謂持盈慎滿之道，莫大乎是，而歷世之久、歷年之長，亦豈有外於是哉？苟徒區區掇拾遺文，補葺故事，儀章則欲其備，度數則欲其詳，而托言於光前啓後之烈，是之謂有法祖之名，無法祖之實。渾厚之治體既未能敦，而精明之治功亦何以建哉？由此觀之，可見愛民之仁足以盡法祖之敬，而仁敬固為一道也與？夫愛民法祖之實，臣既以陳之於前矣。至其本原之地，則又有在焉。

古之人曰：「徒善不足以為政。」又曰：「有內聖之德，則有外王之業。」臣嘗伏讀陛下之《敬一箴》與夫五箴之訓，深感夫陛下之學，得之極其精；陛下之心，養之極其純；陛下之德，充之極其盛。蓋不必更求之古而有所增益，臣亦何所陳說而冀以裨補于萬一哉？但人之恒情，言之有餘而行之或未足，始之克謹而終之或不繼。臣固不敢以此疑陛下，惟考之實事，則若有未盡；徵之治効，則若有未成。如漢文帝之海內富庶、黎民淳厚，如唐太宗之斗米三錢、外戶不閉，如宋仁宗之恭儉仁恕、民物康阜，今亦未之見焉。又何
translation_en:
…grain transport by canal, thereby facilitating the state's provisioning, would be possible. On this foundation, it would be possible to refine performance evaluations and uphold the state's laws; to honor teachers and Confucian scholars and promote schools; to rectify customs and put an end to frivolity; to commend forthright integrity and invigorate the spirit of scholars; to restrain competitive pursuit of advancement and foster substantial conduct among scholars; to observe sacrifices solemnly and serve the spirits; and to establish rites and music and bring about equilibrium and harmony. Nothing is more important than this in what is called the way of preserving fullness and exercising caution amid abundance. Could the endurance of a dynasty through successive generations and long years depend on anything beyond this? If one merely busies oneself collecting surviving writings and patching together old precedents, seeking completeness in ceremonial forms and meticulous detail in prescribed measures, while claiming achievements that glorify one's predecessors and open the way for one's successors, this is emulating the ancestors in name without doing so in substance. If the substantial and generous foundations of government have not been strengthened, how can achievements of discerning and effective government be established? Viewed in this light, does it not become clear that benevolence in caring for the people suffices to fulfill the reverence required in emulating the ancestors, and that benevolence and reverence are indeed a single way? Your servant has already set forth above the substance of caring for the people and emulating the ancestors. Yet their ultimate source lies elsewhere.

An ancient said: “Good intentions alone are insufficient for governing.” Another saying states: “With the virtue of inward sagehood comes the achievement of outward kingship.” Your servant has reverently read Your Majesty's Admonition on Reverent Single-mindedness (Jingyi zhen), together with the teachings of the Five Admonitions. I am deeply impressed by the utmost refinement of Your Majesty's attainment in learning, the utmost purity with which Your Majesty has nurtured your mind, and the utmost fullness to which Your Majesty has developed your virtue. Surely there is no need to seek further enrichment from antiquity. What could your servant possibly put forward in the hope of contributing even the slightest improvement? Yet it is common human nature for words to be abundant while actions sometimes fall short, and for care at the beginning sometimes to go unsustained at the end. Your servant certainly dares not suspect Your Majesty of this. Only, when I examine actual affairs, something seems not yet fully accomplished; when I assess the results of government, something seems not yet achieved. Under Emperor Wen of Han, the realm was prosperous and populous, and the common people were sincere and substantial in character. Under Emperor Taizong of Tang, a dou of rice cost three cash, and outer doors were left unbarred. Under Emperor Renzong of Song, reverence, frugality, benevolence, and forbearance prevailed, and the people and all things flourished. We have yet to see such conditions today. How much less, then, …

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
有於成周之盛哉又何慊於經制之定禮樂之興哉此臣
之所以不能無疑者也臣願
陛下靜觀而反求之不以臣言為妄於是勉其所不足求其所
未至敬勝夫怠終如其始將見日見之行而煥然百度之
咸熈雖由是而成至治登太和超三軼五將無不可者尚
何民生之有未遂國本之有未植天之眷命有未篤變之
消弭有未盡經制之未可定禮樂之未可興也耶盖至是
而法
祖之敬至矣盡矣一毫無餘憾矣于以作百王之則于以垂萬
世之休極自我建法自我始雖謂之創可也而況於守乎
哉否則道非前定而易窮法以無本而多戾虛文勝而實
===
意衰立志遠而成功少天下後世將以為不世出之
大聖人而治効猶止於此則隆古之化果不可以復見也耶此
臣之所以甚為激切者也惟
陛下矜其愚寬其誅俯賜采納疆勉而行之則天下幸甚萬世
幸甚臣謹對

punctuated: 有於成周之盛哉？又何慊於經制之定、禮樂之興哉？此臣之所以不能無疑者也。臣願陛下靜觀而反求之，不以臣言為妄，於是勉其所不足，求其所未至，敬勝夫怠，終如其始。將見日見之行，而煥然百度之咸熈。雖由是而成至治，登太和，超三軼五，將無不可者。尚何民生之有未遂，國本之有未植，天之眷命有未篤，變之消弭有未盡，經制之未可定，禮樂之未可興也耶？盖至是而法祖之敬至矣，盡矣，一毫無餘憾矣。于以作百王之則，于以垂萬世之休。極自我建，法自我始，雖謂之創可也，而況於守乎哉？否則道非前定而易窮，法以無本而多戾，虛文勝而實意衰，立志遠而成功少。天下後世將以為不世出之大聖人，而治効猶止於此，則隆古之化果不可以復見也耶？此臣之所以甚為激切者也。惟陛下矜其愚，寬其誅，俯賜采納，疆勉而行之，則天下幸甚，萬世幸甚。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…could there be anything to match the flourishing age of Zhou? And how could one feel satisfied with the establishment of enduring institutions and the flourishing of rites and music? This is why your servant cannot be without doubts. I wish that Your Majesty would contemplate this calmly and seek the answer within yourself, without dismissing your servant’s words as groundless. Then exert yourself where your efforts are insufficient and strive for what you have yet to attain. Let reverence overcome indolence, and remain as steadfast at the end as at the beginning. We shall then see this manifested in daily conduct [?], and all the affairs of government will flourish in renewed splendor. From this, even achieving perfect government, attaining supreme harmony, and surpassing the Three Kings and the Five Emperors would all be possible. How could the people’s livelihood still be unfulfilled, the foundations of the state still be unestablished, Heaven’s favor and mandate still lack firmness, or the elimination of calamities still be incomplete? How could enduring institutions remain impossible to establish, or rites and music impossible to bring to flourishing?

For at this point, the reverence expressed in following the ancestors would have reached its utmost and its fulfillment, leaving not the slightest cause for regret. By this, Your Majesty would become a model for all kings and bequeath blessings to ten thousand generations. The supreme standard would be established by Your Majesty, and the laws would originate with Your Majesty. One could even call this founding a new order—how much more, then, would it suffice to preserve the inherited one!

Otherwise, if the Way is not determined beforehand, its application will readily reach an impasse; if laws lack a foundation, they will produce many contradictions. Empty formalities will prevail while sincere purpose declines; aspirations will be lofty, but accomplishments few. The world and later generations will consider Your Majesty a great sage who appears but once in many ages, yet the results of his government will have gone only this far. Can the transforming influence of high antiquity truly never be seen again? This is why your servant speaks with such intense urgency. May Your Majesty pity his ignorance, spare him punishment, graciously accept his words, and exert yourself to put them into practice. Then the world would be most fortunate, and ten thousand generations most fortunate. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
臣尹臺
臣對臣聞帝王所以創守天下者無異道焉存乎心與政
而已矣天下之治其創與守也時殊而理若異致然圖大
保有使上下昭然升于大猷嗣服傳久遠不替則豈獨創
之難守之亦甚難也夫知其難也則凡求之吾心以推之
政事咸覬其無失理者殆不容以易焉為之是心與政相
濟以成治者帝王創守天下所不異也夫心者治之統也
政繫以出矣政者治之紀也心繇以達矣古先帝王其存
於心者既恒恐一民物之闕理遺艱大之疚而政又足以
翼協之苟慕乎心無弗殫乎其政是以當時大治後世誦
聖功德載乎無終凡以創守之謀訏詒於久遠者有此具
===
也後之人君其道鮮備矣心狃於偏私推之政則塞而不
達政崇於虛侈求之心則繆而不合若是而期治國大體
庶幾古帝王什一遺於後世是以章一代創守之迹不其
左乎夫後世治不古侔使天下罕被其澤而靡究乎歷年
之數則蓋有繇然矣臣竊誦詩書所載及上世紀傳所錄
聞恒私歎三代創守之法不可尚以為本諸心政之統紀
者甚著明焉故其享祚久遠亦宜非後世所及至觀我
祖宗創造丕搆於前
列聖紹嗣休服於後所以茂建懿模洪規於億萬年者無不自
其一心達之天下之政然後知三代所以為有道之長誠
不越乎此矣夫帝王之道豈不同條共貫哉臣伏跡草野

列聖紹嗣休服於後所以茂建懿模洪規於億萬年者無不自
其一心達之天下之政然後知三代所以爲有道之長誠
不越乎此矣夫帝王之道豈不同條共貫哉臣伏跡草野
punctuated:
臣尹臺。
臣對：臣聞帝王所以創守天下者，無異道焉，存乎心與政而已矣。天下之治，其創與守也，時殊而理若異致，然圖大保有，使上下昭然升于大猷，嗣服傳久遠不替，則豈獨創之難，守之亦甚難也。夫知其難也，則凡求之吾心以推之政事，咸覬其無失理者，殆不容以易焉為之。是心與政相濟以成治者，帝王創守天下所不異也。夫心者，治之統也，政繫以出矣；政者，治之紀也，心繇以達矣。古先帝王，其存於心者，既恒恐一民物之闕理、遺艱大之疚，而政又足以翼協之，苟慕乎心，無弗殫乎其政。是以當時大治，後世誦聖，功德載乎無終。凡以創守之謀訏詒於久遠者，有此具也。後之人君，其道鮮備矣。心狃於偏私，推之政則塞而不達；政崇於虛侈，求之心則繆而不合。若是而期治國大體，庶幾古帝王什一遺於後世，是以章一代創守之迹，不其左乎？夫後世治不古侔，使天下罕被其澤，而靡究乎歷年之數，則蓋有繇然矣。臣竊誦《詩》《書》所載，及上世紀傳所錄聞，恒私歎三代創守之法不可尚，以為本諸心政之統紀者甚著明焉，故其享祚久遠，亦宜非後世所及。至觀我祖宗創造丕搆於前，列聖紹嗣休服於後，所以茂建懿模洪規於億萬年者，無不自其一心達之天下之政，然後知三代所以為有道之長，誠不越乎此矣。夫帝王之道，豈不同條共貫哉？臣伏跡草野，
translation_en:
Your servant, Yin Tai.

Your servant replies: I have heard that emperors and kings follow no different Way in founding and preserving their rule over all under Heaven. It lies simply in the mind and in government. In governing the realm, founding and preserving belong to different times, and their principles may seem to lead in different directions. Yet to plan a great undertaking and retain possession of it, to bring those above and below into the clear light of the great Way, and to transmit the succession far into the future without decline—is founding alone difficult? Preserving is also exceedingly difficult. Once one understands this difficulty, everything one seeks within one’s own mind and extends to affairs of government must be directed toward avoiding any departure from principle; one can hardly treat the task lightly. Thus, the mutual assistance of mind and government in achieving good order is common to both founding and preserving imperial rule.

The mind is the unifying source of order, on which government depends for its emergence; government is the framework of order, through which the mind finds expression. The emperors and kings of antiquity constantly feared in their hearts that even a single person or thing might fail to receive proper care, or that they might leave behind the burden of a great and difficult undertaking. Their government, moreover, adequately supported and accorded with these concerns. Whatever they aspired to in their hearts, they spared no effort to realize in government. Thus their own times enjoyed excellent order, later generations celebrated their sagacity, and their achievements and virtue were recorded without end. This was the means by which they devised far-reaching plans for founding and preserving their rule and bequeathed them to the distant future.

Among later rulers, this Way was seldom complete. Their minds became habituated to partiality and selfishness; extended into government, these became obstructions that prevented their intentions from being realized. Their government exalted empty extravagance; examined against the mind, it proved erroneous and discordant. Under such conditions, to expect their broad approach to governing the state to leave later generations even a tenth of what the ancient emperors and kings had bequeathed, and thereby to make manifest a dynasty’s achievements in founding and preserving its rule—would this not be misguided? There were indeed reasons why later government failed to equal antiquity, why the realm seldom received its benefits, and why its allotted span of years was not fulfilled.

I have privately recited what is contained in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents, together with accounts recorded in the annals and biographies of earlier ages. I have often reflected with admiration that the methods by which the Three Dynasties founded and preserved their rule could not be surpassed. Their grounding in the mind and government, as the unifying source and framework of order, seems to me exceedingly clear. It was therefore fitting that the long duration of their dynastic fortunes should likewise have been beyond the reach of later ages.

When I consider how our imperial ancestors first founded the great edifice, and how the successive sage rulers thereafter inherited their glorious charge, I see that all the splendid models and grand designs they firmly established for countless ages proceeded from their single mind and found expression in the government of the realm. Only then do I understand that the Three Dynasties’ preeminence among those who possessed the Way truly went no further than this. Does not the Way of emperors and kings share the same guiding principles and common thread? Your servant has lived obscurely in the countryside…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
蓋嘗講圖末議志亦欲有所陳也今幸預有司推選獲進
詣
明廷備充數引對之列
陛下親賜綸制策詢之且勉令罄所知以告夫極帝王之規徵
往代之故明創守之說察理要之論皆非臣愚所能具也
然遇際
陛下明聖獨觀昭曠之道馳驅域外之議而臣得效淺淺之忠
無忌諱之患此自昔賢智士所希蒙之時也雖臣愚陋敢
不圖一言自獻乎臣聞古之人有言曰為君難夫創業之
難難矣守成之難難矣故天下莫難於為君蓋天生民物
不能自理於是焉託之大君曰大君統眾理物寔為天下
===
主是故或肇治于先則首制典度昭一代之典憲立經陳
紀遺萬世之法程是曰創業之難也或紹治于後則御土
宇之大思燕翼之惟艱撫神器之重念嗣服之匪輕是曰
守成之難也夫人君負大難於身苟其心之不敢自暇逸
則必思難以圖其易達之於政豈使有一不得其理者哉
聖制探求往世創守之迹則稽自三代以來迄于宋終蓋三代
之君所以創守天下者其具至明備矣是故其先必大聖
人開而造之暨其後嗣又克敬承無失是以能維持統紀
於數百餘年不墜然臣論之大要蓋不出乎心與政也是
故克艱祗承懋昭建極禹湯之心矻矻焉恒恐一失其理
將無以為天下屬也故其政之昭施至于平成天地允殖

不能自理於是焉託之大君曰大君統衆理物寔為天下
===

紀遺萬世之法程是曰創業之難也或紹治于後則御土
宇之大思燕翼之惟艱撫神器之重念嗣服之匪輕是曰
守成之難也夫人君負大難於身苟其心之不敢自暇逸
則必思難以圖其易違之於政豈使有一不得其理者哉
聖制採求往世創守之迹則稽自三代以來迄于宋終蓋三代
之君所以創守天下者其具至明備矣是故其先必大聖
人開而造之暨其後嗣又克敬承無失是以能維持統紀
於數百餘年不墜然臣論之大要蓋不出乎心與政也是
故克艱祗承懋昭建極禹湯之心矻矻焉恒恐一失其理
將無以為天下屬也故其敷之昭施至于平成天地允殖
punctuated:
蓋嘗講圖末議，志亦欲有所陳也。今幸預有司推選，獲進詣明廷，備充數引對之列。陛下親賜綸制，策詢之，且勉令罄所知以告。夫極帝王之規，徵往代之故，明創守之說，察理要之論，皆非臣愚所能具也。然遇際陛下明聖，獨觀昭曠之道，馳驅域外之議，而臣得效淺淺之忠，無忌諱之患，此自昔賢智士所希蒙之時也。雖臣愚陋，敢不圖一言自獻乎？

臣聞古之人有言曰：「為君難。」夫創業之難，難矣；守成之難，難矣。故天下莫難於為君。蓋天生民物，不能自理，於是焉託之大君，曰：「大君統眾理物，寔為天下主。」是故或肇治于先，則首制典度，昭一代之典憲；立經陳紀，遺萬世之法程，是曰創業之難也。或紹治于後，則御土宇之大，思燕翼之惟艱；撫神器之重，念嗣服之匪輕，是曰守成之難也。夫人君負大難於身，苟其心之不敢自暇逸，則必思難以圖其易。達之於政，豈使有一不得其理者哉？

聖制探求往世創守之迹，則稽自三代以來，迄于宋終，蓋三代之君所以創守天下者，其具至明備矣。是故其先必大聖人開而造之，暨其後嗣，又克敬承無失，是以能維持統紀於數百餘年不墜。然臣論之，大要蓋不出乎心與政也。是故克艱祗承，懋昭建極，禹湯之心矻矻焉，恒恐一失其理，將無以為天下屬也。故其政之昭施，至于平成天地，允殖
translation_en:
…I have at times considered humble proposals, wishing to have something to present. Now, fortunately, I have been selected by the responsible officials and permitted to advance into the illustrious court, merely making up the numbers among those summoned to answer. Your Majesty has personally bestowed an imperial decree, questioning us on policy and further urging us to report all that we know. To fathom the principles of emperors and kings, investigate the circumstances of former ages, clarify the teachings on founding and preserving a dynasty, and examine arguments concerning the essentials of governance—all these exceed what your foolish servant can fully expound. Yet I have encountered a time when Your Majesty, enlightened and sage, uniquely surveys the broad and luminous Way and ranges in thought beyond conventional bounds. Your servant can thus offer his modest loyalty without fear of transgressing a taboo. This is an opportunity that worthy and wise men since antiquity have hoped to receive. Foolish and uncultivated though I am, how could I fail to consider offering even a single word?

Your servant has heard that a man of antiquity said: “To be a ruler is difficult.” Founding a dynasty is indeed difficult; preserving what has been achieved is indeed difficult. Thus nothing under Heaven is harder than being a ruler. Heaven brought forth the people and all things, but they could not order themselves; it therefore entrusted them to a great ruler, saying: “The great ruler commands the multitude and orders all things; he is truly the lord of all under Heaven.” Thus, when a ruler first establishes government, he must institute codes and standards, making manifest the statutes of a dynasty; he must establish guiding principles and set forth regulations, bequeathing models for ten thousand generations. This is what is called the difficulty of founding a dynasty. When a ruler subsequently carries on that government, he must govern a vast territory, mindful of the difficulty of securing peace for his descendants; he must uphold the weighty sacred vessel of sovereignty, remembering that inheriting the royal charge is no light matter. This is what is called the difficulty of preserving an achievement. A ruler bears these great difficulties upon his own person. If in his heart he dares not indulge in leisure and ease, he will surely reflect upon the difficulties in order to find the means of resolving them. When he extends this disposition to government, how could he allow even one matter to fall short of its proper order?

Your Majesty’s sacred decree inquires into the precedents for founding and preserving dynasties in earlier ages. Examining the period from the Three Dynasties down to the end of the Song, we find that the means by which the rulers of the Three Dynasties founded and preserved their rule over all under Heaven were most clearly and fully provided. In each case, a great sage first opened the way and founded the dynasty; his successors then reverently carried on his work without fail. Thus they could sustain the governing order for several hundred years without its collapse. Yet, as your servant considers it, the essentials do not extend beyond the heart and government. Able to shoulder difficulties and reverently receive their charge, striving to make virtue manifest and establish the supreme standard, Yu and Tang labored unceasingly in their hearts. They constantly feared that, should they once depart from proper principle, they would no longer be able to serve as the focus of allegiance for all under Heaven. Thus the manifest effects of their government extended to bringing Heaven and Earth into harmonious order and truly nourishing…

title: 嘉靖十四年進士登科錄
text:
兆民四方無不祇服累子孫數十世尚不絕息凡以所積
而遺之者深矣況後王繼作又有若啟仲康者有若太甲
盤庚中宗高宗者咸有敬承繼戒之心克終永肩寅畏恭
默之心故能不隳其前王舊政率履不越以綿享國之祚
夫夏商創守之迹概可見矣使其後無甚不道之君或稍
扶持安全之則二代雖至今存可也若夫周之立國則自
后稷至公劉並以稼穡勤其民及太王遷岐文王邑豐盛
德蒸發益勃勃乎不可遏矣詩曰天作高山太王荒之彼
作矣文王康之此之謂也武王平暴亂拯民於水火周公
成文武之德興禮樂以相天下今讀周官六典之書想見
當時政治之迹蓋渢渢乎至仁流行哉所以然者其視民
===
如傷不泄邇忘遠之心與夫在宮在廟著於詩人所稱几
杖盤盂刀劍戶牖莫不設銘以立戒其中之所形見者已
若是至極也又篤棐俔勗迄終始相勉勸如君奭之誥所
陳則一時儆惕不懈之心君臣蓋亹亹焉夫其政澤漸被
至于今頌之不衰不有繇然乎迨其嗣王又得前人疾敬
德之訓所其無逸之訓毋冒貢于非幾之訓以早夜夾介
用持乃心于不怠故成康之際刑措囹空文武之澤益漬
濡于天下及乎中世業頗陵遲宣王中興飭治而作起之
觀雲漢諸詩見其畏天悲民之心惻然而不可巳宜不失
文武成康令緒以永厥聞于翼世矣夫周家所以創造天
下者累數王積數世其澤既深入而浹乎民後世又得不
